Three offices behind a Fayette County bill

Three offices share the work. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets each parcel's value. The Sheriff takes the current year's payment. Bills that run late go to the County Clerk. Lexington and Fayette County merged governments on January 1, 1974, so there is no separate city bill. One statement covers every taxing district.

The PVA works from 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, in Lexington (phone 859-246-2722, fax 859-246-2729). The PVA neither sets rates nor accepts payments. The sheriff's Property Tax Division is in Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse at 150 North Limestone, reachable at 859-252-1771. Counter hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday to Friday, with closing pushed to 6:00 p.m. during October. The office collects over 110,000 bills worth nearly $260 million a year.

The bill pays for the Commonwealth, Fayette County Public Schools, the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government, called LFUCG here, the county extension and soil conservation districts, the health department, Lextran and a park fund. Property in the Downtown Lexington Management District carries a further charge.

How the bill is calculated

Take the assessed value, subtract any exemption, and multiply by the rate for the property's tax district, per $100 of value. Values are fixed each January 1 at fair cash value, meaning what the parcel would most probably sell for on the open market.

Rates depend on which city services a parcel receives. The seven residential districts share the same state, school, general services, extension, conservation, health, Lextran and park fund lines. They differ only in refuse, street light, street cleaning or full-service charges.

Real property rates in Fayette County for 2026, in dollars per $100 of assessed value
Tax districtAdded city servicesTotal rate
1Full services1.2598
2General services only1.0868
3Refuse1.2238
4Street lights1.1138
5Refuse and street lights1.2508
6Street lights and street cleaning1.1228
7Refuse and street cleaning1.2328

Properties certified as abandoned and blighted by the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission pay an extra $1 per $100. Downtown Lexington Management District parcels pay an extra $0.10 per $100.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are payable through December, with a discount for paying early. Statements are mailed in the last week of September. If you have no bill by about October 10, call 859-252-1771 for a duplicate, since a missing bill is no excuse for nonpayment.

  • October 1 to November 1: pay the face amount less 2 percent.
  • November 2 to December 31: full face amount, no discount.
  • January 1 to January 31: 5 percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 10 percent penalty with a further 10 percent add-on.
  • After April 15: delinquent at 21 percent and handed to the County Clerk.

You can pay at the sheriff's counter (cash, check or money order), at any Lexington Republic Bank lobby through January 31 with the bill coupon, on the online portal (card or bank debit, with a convenience fee the sheriff does not receive) or by mail to PO Box 34148, Lexington, KY 40588-4148. A mailed payment counts at the amount due on its postmark date, and a postage meter stamp is not accepted as proof. The sheriff cannot take installments or grant extensions, and a returned check adds a $35 fee.

How to challenge your assessment

Speak with a PVA assessor first, and only afterward take an appeal to the County Clerk. The PVA reviews each of its roughly 300 assessment areas every three to four years under a state quadrennial plan, and neighborhood sales drive most reassessments. Many owners receive a notice in April that includes a map of recent sales close to the property.

The PVA conference and the clerk's appeal to the Local Board of Tax Appeals both fall in May. Kentucky's calendar places the tax roll inspection across the 13 days that start on the first Monday of May, so the window recurs yearly. Postmarks do not count for the appeal form, so deliver it to the clerk.

  • Bring comparable sales, a recent appraisal, photographs, insurance policies, construction costs, listings or sale contracts.
  • A paid representative must attach a letter of authorization from the owner.
  • Hearings take place at the LFUCG Phoenix Building, 101 East Vine Street, in a first-floor conference room, and the clerk mails each appellant a time.
  • After the roll is finalized, the PVA still accepts a request for review, though it cannot change the bill already issued for that year.

For the clerk's appeals desk, dial 859-253-3344.

Homestead exemption

A qualifying home loses $49,100 of assessed value under the exemption, a figure the state set for 2025 and 2026. An owner qualifies by turning 65 at any point in the calendar year or by being classed as totally disabled. It only applies to your primary residence.

The disability route needs total disability status under a public or private retirement system, payments across the calendar year, and a yearly confirmation to the PVA. A copy of the system's disability letter serves as proof. For age, a driver's license, birth certificate or registration, passport, school record or marriage record will do.

Each residence gets one exemption and each person gets one. Send applications by mail to the Fayette PVA at 101 East Vine Street, Suite 600, by fax to 859-246-2729 or by scan to the PVA's email.

Selling with taxes owed or due

Ownership on January 1 decides who is billed, so a seller may receive a statement for a year in which the buyer takes title. After a sale, the PVA tries to mail the bill in care of the new owner, though a closing near printing time can outrun the update. Take questions about the prorated share to the closing agent or attorney. The sheriff does not issue prorated bills or accept prorated payments.

Anything unpaid after April 15 lands at the County Clerk. Payment there must be cash, a money order, or a cashier's or certified check made out to the Fayette County Clerk. Partial payments are refused and interest accrues monthly. Owners who cannot pay in full can call the County Attorney's Office at 859-254-4941 about an arrangement.

Each summer the clerk offers eligible delinquent bills to third-party buyers, some time between day 90 and day 135 after the handover. Clerk and attorney charges pile on top of the penalties. A sale ordered by a court, including for delinquent taxes, goes through the Master Commissioner. The clerk also runs a free alert service that emails you when a filing is recorded under a name or address you register.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Fayette County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Housing and selling in Fayette County

Fayette County is a 286 square mile urban county in the central Bluegrass region, with Lexington as its seat and only city. Population is 329,751. There are 152,488 housing units, and 53.8 percent are owner-occupied. Median home value for owners is $293,500, and median gross rent is $1,164.

Nearly half of homes are rented, so a house needing work or carrying a tax balance can still find buyers. When a sale must close fast and without repairs, a buyer paying cash for the house as it stands can settle the tax out of the proceeds. Get a payoff figure from the sheriff first so the title company knows what to hold back.

Frequently asked questions

When is the 2% discount deadline in Fayette County?

The discount ends on November 1 of the assessment year. It runs from October 1 and cuts the bill by 2 percent. After that, the full amount is due through December 31.

Where do I pay Fayette County property tax in person?

Go to the Sheriff's Property Tax Division in Room 236 of the Fayette District Courthouse, 150 North Limestone, with cash, a check or a money order. Any Lexington Republic Bank lobby also takes payments through January 31 if you bring the bill coupon.

What is the Fayette County homestead exemption worth?

It removes $49,100 of value from a qualifying primary residence. The owner has to turn 65 during the calendar year or be totally disabled, and the PVA at 859-246-2722 processes applications.

Can I appeal my Fayette County assessment after the window closes?

Not for the current bill. The PVA conference and the clerk's appeal filing both fall inside the May inspection period. After that you can still request a review through the PVA, but a finalized assessment cannot change the bill for that year.

What if Fayette County taxes stay unpaid?

If still unpaid on April 15, the bill goes delinquent at 21 percent and transfers to the County Clerk, which adds monthly interest and fees. The clerk may then sell the bill to an outside buyer at the summer sale.

Which Louisville offices value and bill your house

The PVA values your house, and the Sheriff bills it. The Sheriff's office gathers about $1 billion a year from over 300,000 taxpayers for 13 taxing jurisdictions, among them the state, Louisville Metro, the school board and several fire districts.

The PVA is in the Glassworks Building, 815 W. Market St., Suite 400, Louisville, KY 40202, phone (502) 574-6380. The Sheriff's Property Tax Department is inside the Fiscal Court Building at 700 W. Liberty St., phone (502) 574-5479, and takes walk-in payers from 8 AM until 4 PM on business days.

The PVA measures fair cash value as of each January 1. Whoever the records name as owner on that date, or when the roll is printed, receives the bill.

Due dates and how to pay

Bills are due out by November 1. The 2 percent early-pay discount lasts until December 1, and then the stages step up on the Sheriff's calendar.

Payment stages for the current-year Jefferson County tax bill
DatesAmount owed
November 1 to December 1Bill less 2 percent
December 2 to January 4Bill at face value
January 5 to February 5Face value plus 5 percent
February 6 to April 15Face value plus a 10 percent penalty and a 10 percent Sheriff's add-on fee

When the last day of a stage lands on a Saturday, Sunday or office holiday, it rolls forward to the next open day. A missing bill still carries the late charges, so call the department if yours hasn't come.

  • In person: cash, check or money order, with the stub from your bill.
  • Mail: make the check out to Jefferson County Sheriff and send it to PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570.
  • Web portal: eChecks run $2, and cards run 2.25 percent, or a flat $1.95 when the payment is $86 or less.
  • Dropboxes sit at the downtown office and at County Clerk branches such as Dixie, Fairdale, Highview, East and Westport.

Installment-style payments toward a current bill are also taken between November 1 and April 15.

How to challenge a PVA valuation

The route starts with a PVA conference, not a board hearing. KRS 133.120 sets that order, the conference falls in the yearly open inspection period, and Jefferson County runs it through an online form.

  • File one conference per parcel ID.
  • Attach an appraisal, photographs, an insurance policy, repair quotes, construction costs or a listing agreement.
  • Pick comparable sales from about the last two years, matched on size and type. The PVA opens its sales search to the public free for the appeal window.
  • Results come back in writing within roughly one to two weeks.

If the conference result stands, complete the lower section of that form and deliver it to the Jefferson County Clerk. State law sets the filing deadline at one workday after the inspection period ends. The Local Board of Assessment Appeals hears the case, and skipping that board forecloses the Board of Tax Appeals. Paid representatives need written authorization and must fit a listed profession.

An appeal never pauses collection. Pay tax on your own claimed figure now. A higher number from the board brings a supplemental bill with interest.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jefferson County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption and West End help

The figure for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years is $49,100, subtracted from an eligible home's assessment. Eligible means 65 or older, or totally disabled, and living in the house.

The deduction shrinks a bill but never erases it unless the assessment is smaller than the deduction. Bring proof of age to the PVA, such as a passport, birth certificate or license. Disability claims need proof of benefits from a federal or retirement-system program.

West End homeowners may have another option. LHOME and the West End Opportunity Partnership offer a grant or 0 percent loan toward the residential bill in nine neighborhoods: Algonquin, California, Chickasaw, Park DuValle, Parkhill, Parkland, Portland, Russell and Shawnee. LHOME's number is (502) 882-8091.

City taxes on top of the Sheriff's bill

Often there are. The Sheriff's bill funds the state, Metro, schools and fire districts, while many smaller cities inside the county bill their own residents on top.

The PVA tallies 83 incorporated taxing jurisdictions among roughly 60,000 properties. Those cities offer services such as police, sanitation and parks, with rates posted by each city. State law has recognized just two city classes since 2015: first class, which is Louisville, and home rule cities, which are all the rest.

A seller in a place like St. Matthews or Jeffersontown should call city hall for a balance and a payoff letter. Looking only at the Sheriff's account can miss a separate city liability.

Selling with tax owed

The debt sticks to the owner and the land alike. KRS 134.015 calls it the taxpayer's personal obligation from the assessment date, and the KRS 134.420 lien can run 11 years no matter who holds title.

Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the Clerk, where monthly interest of 1 percent and extra fees start. An outside investor may buy the certificate at the summer sale, and the County Attorney's page estimates the added cost near 40 percent.

A County Attorney payment plan keeps a bill out of that sale, though plans for a given year open only after the Sheriff's collection period closes. Requests to waive certain penalties go in writing to the same office.

The usual closing split is that the seller pays a prorated share for the months owned, and the buyer settles the whole bill when it arrives. Read your settlement statement to see how the closing agent divided it. Closing doesn't wipe out a lien, so the title company will clear it from your proceeds. Get a current-year figure from the Sheriff and earlier-year figures from the Clerk.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jefferson County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Jefferson County housing in brief

Kentucky's most populous county counted 795,222 people in the 2025 estimate, inside borders it shares with Louisville Metro. Land area is 380.8 square miles.

  • Owned homes had a middle value of $248,400.
  • Owners live in 62.1 percent of homes.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,593 with a mortgage and $608 without.
  • Median household income: $69,866.
  • Housing units in 2025: 366,702.

Children attend Jefferson County Public Schools, or the Anchorage Independent district through eighth grade. Deed recording questions go to the County Clerk's Legal Records Division.

Before you list

Call the Sheriff for the current-year balance and the Clerk for anything older, and ask city hall about a separate city bill if your house is in one of the smaller cities. Put all the figures in writing so the title company can pay them from your proceeds.

If you think the PVA's number is too high, act during the inspection period, because a tax bill arrives too late to contest. Start with the online conference and use the Clerk petition only if the conference fails. A cash sale doesn't skip any of this, since liens and city balances still have to be cleared before the deed passes.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I hand in a Jefferson County tax payment?

Walk-in payments are taken downtown at 700 W. Liberty St. between 8 AM and 4 PM Monday to Friday, cash, checks and money orders only. You can also pay online, drop an envelope in a dropbox or mail PO Box 34570.

How long does the 2 percent early discount last?

The 2 percent discount covers payments received between November 1 and December 1 inclusive. Face value applies until January 4, and a 5 percent charge starts January 5.

Will the Sheriff take part of a bill now and the rest later?

Yes. Part payments on a current-year bill are accepted while collection runs, and once the bill moves to the Clerk the County Attorney decides who qualifies for a plan.

How early must I act to lower my assessment?

Act during the yearly inspection period, because a tax bill arrives too late to contest. File the PVA's online conference first. Only a failed conference opens the door to a petition at the Clerk.

Does closing on the sale wipe out a tax lien?

No. A lien outlives a sale, and the title company will insist on clearing it out of your proceeds. Obtain a current-year figure from the Sheriff and earlier-year figures from the Clerk.

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Campbell County?

Campbell County offices and who sets the rate

Three offices share a Campbell bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets the value, the Sheriff's Office mails and collects, and the County Clerk inherits what goes delinquent. Rates come from neither the PVA nor the sheriff: each taxing district's board figures its rate from the assessments inside that district.

The county runs along the Ohio and Licking Rivers and has two seats, Newport and Alexandria, with sheriff's windows in each. By law the PVA assesses at 100 percent of fair market value, meaning the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on. Field staff look at every parcel in person at least every four years, and new construction is reviewed when it appears. Which of the county's school districts serves a house changes the school line on the bill.

Rates move each year under House Bill 44. A district can take the compensating rate, which keeps revenue from existing property flat as values rise, or a rate that raises up to 4 percent more, which needs a public hearing. A rate above that can be put to a recall vote. A rise in your assessed value therefore does not automatically mean a bigger bill.

Payment calendar

Finished bills reach the sheriff by September 15, and mailing usually follows around November 1. The discount phase runs from November 1 through November 30, with payment before December 1 earning the discount.

Campbell County payment calendar
Payment periodAmount owed
NovemberFace amount less 2%
DecemberFace amount, no discount
JanuaryDelinquent, plus 5 percent
From February 1Plus 10 percent and a 10 percent sheriff's add-on fee
Older yearsSettled at the County Clerk, never the sheriff

One line item surprises owners: the 911 fee printed on the bill is exempt from the 2% discount and stays at full price. The sheriff mails only to the listed owner and cannot redirect a bill to a lender, so anyone with escrow should pass the bill along at once.

How to pay the Campbell sheriff

You can pay on the web, by mail, or in person at either sheriff's window. The Newport window is inside the County Administration Building, 1098 Monmouth Street. The Alexandria window is at 8330 West Main Street. Each is open weekdays, 8 in the morning to 4 in the afternoon.

An outside vendor runs the web payment page. Cards carry a 3 percent charge paid by the cardholder, e-checks cost $3, and e-checks over $30,000 are refused. None of that money goes to the sheriff. For a check by mail, make it out to the sheriff, write the bill number on it, and treat the canceled check as your receipt.

Should a check come back, the bill returns to unpaid status in both the sheriff's and PVA's records, and you must repay on the schedule printed on the bill. During a closing week, a bounced check can leave a lien open.

How a Campbell County appeal works

A PVA conference has to happen before the 13-day inspection period ends, and the appeal itself is filed with the county. Inspection starts the first Monday in May, and the Board of Assessment Appeals then meets for five days starting 25 to 35 days after it closes.

The filing deadline is the workday after inspection ends, but read the dates on your notice and get the exact last day from the PVA before filing. Anyone paid to represent you must be an attorney, appraiser, accountant, broker or similar professional under KRS 133.120.

Good evidence for a Newport or Alexandria house includes recent sales of similar homes, photos of damage and repair estimates. Ask the PVA for the list of sales used to value your home, and request it first.

Exemptions and corrections

Owners who reach 65, or who are totally disabled, can apply for a homestead or disability exemption through the PVA, which can state the filing cutoff for the year. Disability verification is due before December 31. If you are turning 65, contact the PVA before paying.

The PVA at 1098 Monmouth Street, (859) 292-3871, also fixes a wrong property address, mailing address or owner name. Corrections can be written on the return stub, which the sheriff forwards. An assessment or exemption can be changed only by the PVA.

  • PVA, 1098 Monmouth Street: value, address, name and exemption questions.
  • Sheriff, Newport or Alexandria: bill lookup and payment.
  • County Clerk, (859) 292-3845: any year that has gone delinquent.

Farm acreage is valued at its agricultural value, which can sit far below the market price per acre in urban areas. A seller with a few acres at the edge of Alexandria should ask the PVA how the parcel is classed.

Reading a Campbell County bill

Each line on the bill belongs to a different taxing district, and the district's own board set its rate. If a line looks wrong, ask who controls it. The PVA answers questions about the value the rates are applied to, as well as a wrong name or address. The sheriff can explain the amount due and the payment dates. Neither office can change a rate.

Keep an eye on the 911 line, which does not get the 2% discount. A buyer's agent comparing two houses should look at the total on the bill, not just the assessed value.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Campbell County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to the taxes when you sell

The debt follows the parcel. Before closing, the title company will ask for a payoff of the current bill and of any delinquent certificate. KRS 134.015 makes the tax a personal debt of the owner on the January 1 assessment date, and the delinquency lien continues under KRS 134.420 no matter who owns the house afterward.

A bill that outlasts the sheriff's season moves to the County Clerk carrying a 10 percent penalty, the sheriff's fee and 1 percent monthly interest. Clerk, county attorney and third-party purchaser fees pile on from there. The clerk at (859) 292-3845 gives the live figure.

Falling behind does not block a sale. You can still sell as-is and let the payoff come out of the proceeds, and early numbers from the clerk show what remains.

Campbell County housing market

Values are high in Campbell County. The 2020 to 2024 median for an owner-occupied home is $252,000, and 182 building permits were issued in 2025. The county is part of the Cincinnati metropolitan area, with 95,441 residents in 2025 and 43,090 homes counted in mid-2025. Owners live in 71.1 percent of homes. Typical rent is $1,145 a month, and typical owner cost with a mortgage is $1,627.

About 86.1 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, which points to more moves and more rentals. Owners of older Newport homes, duplexes or inherited houses can sell directly for cash when repairs or tenants slow a standard listing.

Before you list a Campbell County house

  1. Call the PVA at (859) 292-3871 to confirm the value, address, owner name and any exemption on the account.
  2. Ask the sheriff in Newport or Alexandria for the current bill and whether it has been paid.
  3. Call the County Clerk at (859) 292-3845 about any delinquent year.
  4. Hand the payoff amounts to the title company so the closing agent can settle them from your proceeds.

Doing these early means corrections can be made on the return stub or at the PVA before a contract is signed.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When do Campbell County tax bills go out?

Mailing typically happens around November 1. The 2% discount lasts through November 30, December is face value, January adds 5%, and after January 31 a 10% penalty and sheriff's fee apply.

Where do I take a Campbell County payment?

Visit the Sheriff's Office in Newport (1098 Monmouth Street) or Alexandria (8330 West Main Street), mail it, or use the vendor link on the sheriff's tax page.

Is the 911 fee discounted?

No. The 911 line on a bill is outside the 2% discount.

Who handles questions about my Campbell value?

The PVA, at (859) 292-3871. The sheriff only collects, and cannot alter an assessment, address or exemption.

Can a house with unpaid Campbell taxes still sell?

Yes. Delinquent bills sit with the County Clerk, and closing pays them from the proceeds. Ask the clerk, at (859) 292-3845, for the amount before fixing a date.

Offices and who does what

Property tax in Pulaski County runs through Somerset. The PVA (Property Valuation Administrator) puts a number on every parcel; call (606) 679-1812. The sheriff's tax office mails your bill and takes your money, weekdays 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM, with email at taxes@pulaskisheriff.com.

Rates are not set by either one. The fiscal court, the school board and other districts each choose a levy, and your bill adds them up. Pulaski County, Somerset Independent and Science Hill Independent are the three school systems here, so your address decides which school levy lands on you.

The sheriff also bills tangible property, franchise and gas taxes, undeveloped land, oil, and limestone, sand and gravel. Owning a mix of these? Ask whether every item arrives on a separate statement.

When you list a house, keep a folder with the current bill, last year's receipt and the PVA's phone number handy. Buyers and title agents ask for the same papers, and having them ready saves a few days.

Due dates and penalties

Mailing starts in early October. What you owe depends on the day you pay, and the 5 percent January charge matches KRS 134.015.

Pulaski County sheriff: amount owed by payment date
When paidAmount
October 1 to November 1Bill less a 2 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Base amount
January 1 to January 31Base amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Base amount plus 21 percent
April 16 onwardPay the County Clerk, (606) 679-2042

Walk-in payers can hand over cash, a check or a card (cards add a small fee). Installments are turned down, so show up with the entire balance. Mailing a check? Tuck in a stamped self-addressed envelope and a receipt comes back. Misplaced your bill? Replacements cost nothing.

Pulaski County at a glance

Somerset is the seat, and Burnside, Eubank, Ferguson and Science Hill round out the towns. Population was estimated at 67,384 in July 2025, a 3.6 percent climb since 2020. Owners occupy 72.5 percent of the 26,210 households. Typical home value is $166,900, and typical gross rent is $803. Only 129 building permits were issued in 2025, which leaves resale houses doing most of the work.

Lake Cumberland and its houseboat trade pull buyers to the south end. US 27 and Kentucky 80 cross the county, Interstate 75 sits about 28 miles east, and Lexington is 76 miles north. A house with roof, septic or shoreline trouble can go to a direct cash buyer, with any tax owed settled at closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Pulaski County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption and the state rate

Frankfort set the 2025 state rate at 10.6 cents per hundred dollars of assessed value. Your local districts pile their rates on top, and only your own bill shows the final sum.

Homeowners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, may deduct $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. File through the PVA at (606) 679-1812. Because the state adjusts the figure, check which amount applies this year.

The 2 percent early-payment discount covers the whole bill, not part of it. A seller still on title in October gets it by paying before November 2, and a buyer who closes later in the year inherits whatever is left on the bill.

How to appeal your assessment

Value looks too high to you? Begin at the PVA office, whether the parcel is a Lake Cumberland cottage or a farm near Eubank. The appeal cannot be filed before that sit-down. The assessment roll sits open for thirteen days from the first Monday in May. During the meeting the PVA walks you through the math, then writes down what you claim, what was agreed and how it ended.

  • File with the clerk on the workday right after the roll closes.
  • Neighbors who own property sit on the local board, which meets roughly thirty days afterward for as many as five days.
  • Bring paper proof: land and building descriptions, insurance policies, what construction cost, and sales listings. A file with none of these is thrown out.
  • If someone speaks for you, they must appear on the statutory list and hold your signed authorization.

Bills can print before the board decides. If the final value lands above your claim, a supplemental bill covers the gap.

Who owes the tax when a house sells mid year?

The fall bill belongs to whoever held the parcel on January 1, even if a closing prorates it between buyer and seller. Your closing attorney drafts the split in the contract, and a quick call to the tax office tells you if the parcel shows paid or open.

Under KRS 134.015 the tax is a personal debt of the January 1 owner. Under KRS 134.420 the lien sticks to the land for eleven years. Lenders with escrow accounts normally pay what they receive, yet the responsibility stays with you. Moved lately? Forward your bill to the lender.

Moving away? Tell the PVA right away. The older owner deduction follows the person, so the buyer must file a fresh application.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pulaski County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens after April 15?

On April 16 unpaid bills leave the sheriff's hands and land with the County Clerk as certificates of delinquency, each backed by a lien. An investor who buys one collects the tax, 12 percent a year, and costs like attorney and filing fees. Your house is not auctioned at this point.

The clerk charges 1 percent a month. Once notices go out, the county attorney's commission and postage join the total. The law puts the sale between 90 and 135 days after transfer. Pay the clerk before that day and no investor can take the bill.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax does not kill a sale. It just gets paid at the closing table. Here is how to line it up.

  • Get a written payoff for each open year. The sheriff has it until April 15, and the County Clerk has it after.
  • Give the number to your closing attorney so it can be subtracted from your proceeds.
  • If an investor already bought the bill, the payoff comes from that holder, with interest and costs included.
  • Scan the title for a lien ahead of signing, since liens travel with the land from one owner to the next.

A cash sale of a house in rough shape follows the same path, only faster. The buyer skips repairs and lender approval, and the tax debt is paid from your sale money when papers are signed. Bring your latest bill, your deed and a photo ID to the closing office. One week before closing, ring the tax office again so the payoff figure is current.

Frequently asked questions

Can I pay a Pulaski County tax bill by card?

Yes, at the sheriff's counter, with a small surcharge for cards. Cash and checks are fine too. Bring the full amount, since installments are refused.

What are the extra charges after January in Pulaski County?

January costs an extra 5 percent. From February 1 to April 15 the extra is 21 percent. Once April 16 arrives, you pay the County Clerk.

When does the Pulaski County early discount apply?

Pay between October 1 and November 1 and 2 percent comes off. From November 2 to December 31 the plain base amount applies.

Where do I claim the older owner deduction in Pulaski County?

Phone the PVA at (606) 679-1812 to file. It takes $49,100 off the assessment for owners 65 and up, or totally disabled, in 2025 and 2026.

Will the sheriff auction my house over unpaid Pulaski County tax?

Not at the sheriff stage. After April 15 the clerk can sell the bill to an investor, who then holds a lien earning 12 percent a year plus costs.

Who bills and who taxes in Boone County

The county Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values each parcel, the Boone County Sheriff bills and collects, and several overlapping districts levy the tax. The PVA sets the assessment as of January 1, and the sheriff mails the bill in the fall.

Your bill adds a state rate, a county rate, a city rate where one applies, and separate rates for the library, health department, extension office, fire district and school district. Neighbors can owe different totals if their parcels fall in different districts. Most of the county belongs to Boone County Schools, and a portion lies in the Walton-Verona Independent district, so the school share depends on the parcel.

Check which year's bill is in question. Kentucky taxes follow the January 1 owner, so a bill that shows up in September or October may carry the name of whoever held the house in January.

Due dates, discount and penalties

Boone's sheriff runs four payment stages, and they repeat annually because KRS 134.015 fixes the pattern, barring a delayed schedule approved by the state.

Boone County Sheriff collection stages
StageDatesWhat you pay
DiscountOctober 1 to November 1Bill minus 2 percent
Face amountNovember 2 to December 31The printed amount
First penaltyJanuary 1 to 31Printed amount plus 5 percent
Second penaltyFebruary 1 to April 15Penalty of 10 percent, plus the sheriff's 10 percent add-on

Because partial payments are refused, a bill is paid in one lump. Card payments online add a vendor charge, and e-checks add a smaller flat charge. The sheriff's office is on Conrad Lane in Burlington, with Saturday hours in October, and bills go in the mail before the end of September. The sheriff also listed Heritage Bank branches as places to pay.

A bill still open in April

If a bill remains unpaid at the close of business on April 15, the sheriff passes it to the County Clerk, and a lien is recorded. From there the account picks up a 20 percent attorney fee, a 10 percent clerk fee and interest at 1 percent monthly, and the debt may be sold to a private buyer the next summer.

  • The lien stays on the parcel for up to 11 years under KRS 134.015, no matter who buys the house.
  • Warning letters go to the owner of record, which means an outdated mailing address can keep them from reaching you.
  • Installment plans are available through the county attorney.

A parcel with an open certificate can still be sold. Payoff comes out of the seller's share, and it is the clerk who quotes the figure at that stage.

How to appeal your assessment

The PVA is step one, since no formal appeal is accepted before you have met with that office, and Boone's online request form is open from October 1 to May 1. You can also email appeals@boonecountyky.org to book the meeting.

The window is short. The tax roll sits open for inspection for two weeks beginning in the first week of May. If the meeting doesn't settle the value, you file with the County Clerk by the next business day after that window ends. A bill itself can't be appealed, because values must be final before rates are calculated.

  • Comparable sale prices from homes near yours are the strongest evidence, and the PVA's own model works from the same kind of data.
  • Show photos or repair bids if the house is rougher than the record assumes.
  • Ask for the sales list behind your value.

The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after inspection closes, under KRS 133.030. If you still disagree, its decision letter explains the next appeal step.

Why did my assessment go up?

Most increases trace back to sales. The PVA values homes from nearby arm's length transactions through a computer-assisted system, and every parcel gets a physical look within four years, so a jump often means several years of price growth arriving at once.

House Bill 44 caps growth in countywide tax revenue at 4 percent a year. That law acts on the tax rate, not the assessed value, so a rising valuation can come alongside a falling rate. Kentucky requires the PVA's values to land within 90 to 110 percent of sales prices, and a yearly ratio study tests it.

The 2020 population was 135,968, and the July 2025 estimate of 145,316 is 6.9 percent higher, spread across 56,021 housing units. The middle owned home is valued at $277,300, and the middle household income is $99,414.

Homestead and disability exemption

Homeowners turning 65 during the tax year, and those totally disabled, receive a flat deduction from assessed value. The PVA lists $49,100 for 2026, and the amount should print on the face of your bill once the PVA holds your form.

  • You must own the house and live there on January 1.
  • A household gets one deduction, even when both spouses meet the age test.
  • Disabled owners under 65 renew every year, unless the disability is a service-connected rating or a permanent finding by Social Security or a state retirement system.
  • The deduction is personal to the owner. Once the house sells, the PVA removes it from the old address and the buyer files a new request.

Don't pay a bill that lacks the exemption without phoning the PVA first. KRS 132.810 allows a refund for late approval, though fixing it first is simpler. The PVA accepts forms by mail, fax, email or its online form.

What to expect at closing

The usual practice is for the closing agent to pay the year's tax from the seller's funds and divide it by days of ownership. A bill for a house bought after January 1 may still arrive in the former owner's name, so the settlement statement is where the split gets recorded.

Three checks help. Find out whether this year's bill is paid, and ask the sheriff for a duplicate if yours never came, since that office can't see new deeds. Make sure a recorded deed or other document updates the owner name at the PVA, because name changes happen there. For an inherited house, the PVA accepts a death certificate to update the record.

Owners with a delinquent bill, a missing exemption or deferred repairs sometimes pick a direct sale to a cash buyer, who purchases the house in its present condition, with the tax payoff deducted at closing.

Getting your paperwork straight before listing

Burlington is where most of the pre-sale legwork happens. Request your parcel record from the PVA and read it the way a buyer's agent would: owner name, exemption, square footage, anything that seems off. Then ask the sheriff for the account history and confirm that nothing is carried over from an earlier year. If you moved out of the house and rent it, remember that notices go to the owner of record, so keep the mailing address current with the PVA.

When the numbers look right, give the closing agent the sheriff's figure in writing. A clean tax account is one less thing for a buyer's lender to question, and it makes the settlement statement quick to prepare.

Boone County offices

The cycle touches four offices. The PVA in Burlington values property and takes exemption forms and appeal requests at 859-334-2181. The sheriff collects bills at 859-334-2175, with an online portal at boonecountytax.com. The County Clerk files deeds, receives appeals and holds the bills that go delinquent in April.

Frequently asked questions

What dates matter for a Boone County bill?

Four stages apply each year. Paying by November 1 earns the 2 percent discount, the printed amount holds through December, and a bill still unpaid at the end of January moves to the larger penalty stage.

Can a Boone County assessment be appealed after the bill arrives?

No. Appeals belong to the May inspection period. Meet with the PVA first, then file with the county clerk by the next business day after the period closes.

How large is the Boone County homestead exemption?

The PVA lists $49,100 for 2026. It comes off the assessment, not the bill, and applies to owners turning 65 in the tax year or totally disabled.

Who receives the bill if I sold my Boone County house during the year?

The bill goes to whoever owned on January 1. The buyer should forward it or call the sheriff for a copy, and the settlement statement divides the cost.

Is a Boone County home with back taxes still sellable?

Yes. A lien attaches to the parcel, so the unpaid amount and any clerk and attorney fees come out of what the seller receives. Request an exact payoff from the sheriff or clerk before choosing an asking price.

Daviess County market snapshot

Daviess County is western Kentucky's river-city market, anchored by Owensboro on the Ohio River. It covers 477 square miles, 18 of them water. The north is mostly level river land, while the south rolls into hills and valleys. The county had 103,312 residents in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate of 104,898 is 1.5 percent higher.

There are 45,155 housing units across 41,639 households, and 68.1 percent of households own, so close to a third rent. A typical home is valued at $199,900 and typical rent is $918 a month. Typical monthly owner cost is $1,387 with a mortgage and $512 without. The county issued 253 building permits in 2025, which keeps some new inventory in the mix.

Who sends and collects the bill

Billing and collection both sit with the Sheriff's Office tax division, found at 212 St. Ann Street, Room 103, in Owensboro. The counter answers questions at 270-685-6133 on weekdays until 4:30 and closes on major holidays.

Bills are mailed during the first week of November. Even with a lender paying from escrow, you may get a bill, because servicers sometimes plan to pay without asking the sheriff to hold a copy. If you expect a bill and see none, allow a couple of days for postal delays, then look the parcel up on the sheriff's website, since the mailing address on file may be wrong. Call or email the tax counter with the parcel numbers to correct an address. Property inside Owensboro also owes city tax through the City of Owensboro Tax Office at 270-687-8537.

County tax rates for 2025

In August 2025 the Fiscal Court adopted the compensating rate for real property, which moved the county's figure from 12.9 cents to 12.2 cents per $100 of assessed value. Tangible personal property stayed at 13.8 cents, and motor vehicles and watercraft at 17 cents.

The county's share is only part of the picture. Schools and other taxing bodies add theirs, so the full rate on a parcel runs above 12.2 cents. Pull a parcel-level bill from the tax counter or the sheriff's website before quoting a buyer the carrying cost.

Payment windows and penalties

One state-approved calendar repeats yearly. Pay in the first window to save 2 percent, which is worth doing if you can. Every later window costs more.

Daviess County collection periods
Payment windowWhat you pay
November 10 to December 102 percent discount
December 11 to January 10Base amount
January 11 to February 105 percent penalty
February 11 to April 2521 percent penalty

Under KRS 134.119, a mailed payment with a U.S. Postal Service postmark inside the window is on time. A returned check costs $25, and the bill goes back to unpaid.

How to pay

Three channels work. Online, go to dcsoky.gov and use Pay Taxes Online. Several bills can share a cart, the options are card or electronic check, and the fee appears before you confirm. The office warns that payments sent through any other website will not be honored.

  • At the counter: cash, card, check, cashier's check or money order, with checks for the exact amount
  • By mail: checks payable to the Daviess County Sheriff's Office, drawn on U.S. banks only
  • Online: card or e-check on the sheriff's own site

Two bills for one parcel usually mean an exemption was added after the first printing. Read both and look up the balance online. If the amounts differ, ask the tax counter which one reflects the exemption before you pay, so you don't pay twice or miss a discount window.

How do I challenge an assessment?

Start by phoning the PVA at 270-685-8474. No appeal is allowed without a conference with the PVA or a deputy, and that has to occur during the thirteen-day May inspection window that begins the first Monday of May. What's being tested is fair cash value as of January 1.

When the conference settles nothing, file at the County Clerk's office, 270-685-8434, by the close of the following workday. The local board of assessment appeals sits 25 to 35 days after the window ends and rules on evidence, so bring comparable sales, an appraisal or repair quotes. A board ruling you dispute can go to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Daviess County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption

People at least 65, or classified as totally disabled, can claim it on the home they occupy. For 2025 and 2026 it is worth $49,100 off the assessed value.

The application goes to the Daviess County PVA. A driver's license, birth certificate or passport proves age. A disability claim needs proof that a federal agency or a retirement system classified you as totally disabled.

Selling after bills are printed

If you sold or bought after January 1 and think a bill came in error, the sheriff's office suggests asking the closing title company. Valuation fixes on January 1 under KRS 132.220, so paperwork can trail a sale. Your settlement statement should split the year's tax between seller and buyer.

A delinquent notice is sent on February 11. When business closes on April 25, unpaid bills pass to the County Clerk, carrying heavy fees and exposure to the tax sale. A delinquency can be paid off from the sale proceeds at closing.

Practical steps: ask the sheriff's counter for the balance on each parcel, ask whether an exemption was added or removed this year, and make sure the buyer's lender has a copy of the bill that was actually printed.

Some sellers short on time choose a straight as-is cash sale. The buyer takes the house without repairs, and the tax balance, whether current or delinquent, is paid from the proceeds at closing. That suits an inherited or vacant house. Even so, get every balance in writing first and check that it shows as its own line on the closing statement.

What a delinquent bill turns into

After April 25 the bill becomes a certificate of delinquency held by the County Clerk, with a lien on the parcel. The state process adds interest at 1 percent a month, a 10 percent clerk fee and a 20 percent county attorney fee. The county attorney mails notices by mid-May and mid-June, and installments may be possible.

From mid-July to late October the clerk may sell certificates to private buyers, after advertising the list in the local paper and on the clerk's website at least 30 days ahead. Once a buyer holds the certificate, the owner pays that buyer, who adds charges. Settle a delinquency before the summer sale dates if you plan to sell. The clerk's phone is 270-685-8434.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Daviess County 2 percent discount end?

December 10 every year. The window opens November 10, and bills are mailed in the first week of November.

What is the final day to pay a Daviess County bill before it goes to the clerk?

April 25, at close of business. After that the bill moves to the County Clerk with added fees and can be offered at the tax sale.

Can I pay Daviess County property tax online?

Yes, through the Pay Taxes Online link on the Daviess County Sheriff's Office site, dcsoky.gov. Card and e-check payments carry a fee that shows before you confirm.

Who do I phone when my Daviess County value looks too high?

The PVA at 270-685-8474, to book the conference that Kentucky requires before an appeal can be filed with the County Clerk.

Does Owensboro bill its own property tax?

Yes. The City of Owensboro Tax Office, 270-687-8537, bills city tax separately from the county bill the sheriff sends.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Jessamine County?

Which office does what

Jessamine County splits the work in two. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a value on each parcel, and the sheriff sends the bills and banks the payments.

The PVA doesn't set rates, mail bills or take payments. It values property at full fair cash value on January 1, logs deed transfers, updates parcel maps and handles exemptions. The sheriff's office at 201 North Main Street in Nicholasville, staffed weekdays from 8 to 4, collects the state, county, school and district levies on real and tangible property and passes each share to the right body.

The PVA also lists tangible personal property, with returns due May 15, and logs building permits that the city and county planning offices send in each month. Call the PVA when your value looks wrong. Call the sheriff at (859) 885-4139 when you need a payoff or a receipt.

How fast the tax roll has grown

The assessment roll has grown every year since 2013, and the 2026 total of about $6.71 billion is up 9.00 percent. Residential property is the biggest piece at roughly $5.22 billion, commercial adds about $1.04 billion and agricultural about $444 million.

Jessamine County assessment roll by year
YearResidentialTotalChange
2026$5,223,249,119$6,710,234,7399.00%
2025$4,786,456,183$6,157,159,0837.60%
2024$4,418,399,761$5,722,955,01010.80%
2023$4,065,270,187$5,308,263,3259.70%
2022$3,647,300,454$4,839,328,6956.88%

Residential value alone climbed from about $3.65 billion in 2022 to $5.22 billion in 2026. A house bought a few years back can carry a far larger assessment than at purchase, and each property class is reassessed on a four-year cycle, so a single bump may bundle several years of price movement.

The roll doesn't always rise. 2007 added 12.66 percent, 2011 and 2012 each slipped by about 1 percent, and 2024 added 10.80 percent, the biggest single-year gain since 2007. If you bought near a peak, don't assume next year's roll will match the last one.

How the PVA classifies property

Four classes cover everything taxable. Where a house falls depends on its location and its acreage.

  • Residential: homes inside Nicholasville or Wilmore, whether single-family, duplex, townhouse or an empty lot.
  • County Residential: homes or land outside those cities on under 10 acres, sometimes with trailers, barns or sheds.
  • Farms: tracts of 10 acres or more, where agricultural value is set.
  • Commercial and Industrial: businesses on commercial or industrial ground, plus golf courses, apartments and trailer park land.

A farm owner who wants use-value pricing files by March 1 of the year in question, and horticultural land qualifies from 5 acres. The program is meant to keep farms operating and preserve farmland through tax relief.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jessamine County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

Bills reach the sheriff by September 15. Pay by November 1 and the bill drops 2 percent under KRS 134.020, then it sits at face value through December. January adds 5 percent, and from February the add-ons are 10 percent plus a 10 percent sheriff's fee.

After the close of business on April 15, whatever is left moves to the county clerk as a certificate of delinquency, secured by a lien on the parcel. Monthly interest of 1 percent and attorney and clerk commissions start from there, with a summer sale where an outside investor can purchase the bill. The clerk's website carries a delinquent tax search.

Check dates with the sheriff each fall, since Kentucky permits a delayed schedule in some counties.

How to contest your value

First comes a talk with the PVA. Assessment notices usually go out in April, and the roll opens for inspection on the first Monday of May for 13 days, Saturdays included. The PVA office takes conferences by phone or in person at (859) 885-4931, and the notice and the Jessamine Journal carry the dates.

Bring something that backs a lower figure: an appraisal, photos, an insurance declaration, active listings or nearby sales.

  • Conference with the PVA during the open window.
  • If it fails, an appeal form goes to the County Clerk within one workday after the window closes, and a three-member Board of Assessment Appeals hears the case.
  • The last stop is the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals, whose members the Governor appoints.

The local board meets 25 to 35 days after inspection ends and turns away appeals that lack evidence. Every step falls in spring, so a fall bill can't be contested this way.

Homestead and other exemptions

Owners 65 and over, and owners ruled totally disabled, can deduct a fixed sum from assessed value. The amount for 2025 to 2026 is $49,100.

The cap is one exemption per household. The age exemption stays on the books while the first applicant owns and occupies the home, and it leaves with them at a sale. The disability version needs a fresh application every year. File at the PVA office or mail P.O. Box 530, Nicholasville, KY 40340, marked "Homestead Exemption" or "Disability Exemption", with a driver's license or birth certificate copy and, for disability, a Social Security award letter or similar proof.

Churches and charities use Revenue Form 62A023. Owners of business equipment file tangible personal property returns by May 15, and late returns draw 10 percent or 20 percent penalties.

Tax steps before you list

Start by asking the sheriff for a payoff on the current bill. The name on a September bill can still be the prior owner's, so agree on the split with the buyer in writing.

Then look the address up in the clerk's delinquent search for older years. If you hold the age exemption, tell the PVA about the sale so it can move to your next home.

Buyers keep arriving: the county had 57,147 people in the July 2025 estimate, up 7.8 percent from 2020, with 22,061 housing units, a $268,100 median home value and two thirds of homes owner-occupied.

What to expect at closing

The title company will want the sheriff's figure for the current year and the clerk's figure for anything delinquent. Any amount owed comes out of your proceeds, and the deed doesn't pass free of a lien until it is cleared. A cash sale goes faster only when these numbers are ready, so call both offices before you accept an offer.

Does the PVA mail the Jessamine County tax bill?

No. The PVA only sets assessed value. The sheriff mails and collects the bill, and the PVA sets no rates and collects nothing.

What is the discount deadline in Jessamine County?

November 1. KRS 134.020 gives 2 percent off for payment on or before that date, and the face amount is due through December 31.

Where does an unpaid Jessamine County bill end up?

With the county clerk after April 15, as a certificate of delinquency with a recorded lien and interest of 1 percent per month.

What does the Jessamine County age 65 exemption deduct?

$49,100 for 2025 to 2026. It applies to owners who live in the home, and the state adjusts the amount every two years.

Can I contest my Jessamine County value in the fall?

Not through the standard process. The PVA conference and the clerk filing both take place in May, before bills are delivered.

Where a Scott County bill comes from

Two offices split the work. The PVA fixes what a parcel is worth. The sheriff mails the bill and takes payment, and never sets a value. The sheriff collects for 28 districts, among them the state, the county, school systems, fire and library districts and, by contract, some cities. Mailing normally happens on November 1. Dispute a value? Call the PVA at (502) 863-7885. Have a payment question? Call the sheriff at (502) 863-7855.

Because the sheriff bills for so many districts at once, one statement can look larger than the county rate you expect. Ask the office for a line-by-line breakdown if you want to see how much goes to schools, fire protection and the library.

Georgetown adds its own levy. City hall's Clerk's Office takes payment over the counter, by post or by phone, and lookup and online payment run through the city's OpenGov portal. Bills from before 2025 are found through the city's Tax Master service. A house inside Georgetown carries a city bill in addition to the county one.

Scott County housing at a glance

Scott County lies north of Lexington and is counted in the Lexington-Fayette metro. Georgetown is the county seat and the largest city, with Sadieville and Stamping Ground as the smaller ones. The county grew from 47,173 residents in 2010 to 57,155 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 62,262, up 8.9 percent since 2020. Lexington is roughly 16 miles south by way of I-75, and Cincinnati about 69 miles north.

Prices sit well above the Kentucky norm. A typical owner-occupied home is $288,500 and typical household income is $85,158. The county has 22,642 households and an estimated 25,010 housing units. Owners hold 71.7 percent of occupied units, and middle rent is $1,247. Owner costs run $1,637 a month with a mortgage and $514 without one. Builders took out 393 permits in 2025, so a resale competes with new construction.

Toyota's Georgetown plant anchors the local job base. One district, Scott County Schools, serves the whole county, so families relocating here will ask which zone your address falls in. Look it up before you list.

Due dates and penalties

KRS 134.015 sets the calendar, and the sheriff follows it.

  • By November 1: a 2 percent discount for paying in full.
  • Through December 31: the face amount.
  • January: 5 percent added.
  • Later payment: 10 percent added.

Whoever held title on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a delinquent bill leaves a lien on the land itself. Spell out the split in your sales contract so the closing agent knows what to deduct from your proceeds. A spring closing usually means the buyer's side pays the bill that arrives the next November, and the seller credits their share of the months already passed.

What happens when a bill goes unpaid

Around April 15 the sheriff's unpaid bills move to the County Clerk. The county attorney writes in May, offering payment agreements to eligible owners, and again in June. Every year the sequence is the same, with only the dates shifting.

Scott County Clerk delinquent tax calendar
WhenStep
April 15Unpaid bills transfer to the clerk
May and JuneCounty Attorney mails notices and offers payment agreements
June 30Deadline to sign a payment agreement
July 1Advertising costs attach to remaining bills
Late AugustLast chance to pay, then the sale in the third-floor Fiscal Court Room

The clerk takes cash, cashier's checks, money orders and cards, and a 2.75 percent vendor fee applies to cards. For payoff figures call the clerk at (502) 863-7875, extension 2260, or the County Attorney at (502) 863-7870 about agreements.

Where to go in person

  • Sheriff (current-year bills): 240 Caleb Conley Way and 120 N Hamilton St, Georgetown, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm.
  • County Clerk (delinquent bills, deeds, motor vehicles): 101 E Main Street, Georgetown, weekdays 8:30 am to 4:30 pm.
  • County Attorney: 198 E Washington St, Georgetown.
  • Georgetown-Scott County Revenue Commission (occupational and business tax): (502) 603-5860.

Property and vehicle taxes are not collected at the county Treasurer's office.

How to contest a valuation or claim an exemption

A conference with the PVA comes first. Only after it can you petition the local appeals board, which wants comparable sales, repair bids or similar proof. An appeal does not suspend the bill, so pay on the value you claim while it runs. Gather your evidence before the meeting, and keep copies of everything you hand over.

Owners past 65 and those totally disabled can claim the homestead exemption through the PVA. The state's deduction is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, and the PVA can confirm the figure for the current year.

Georgetown city bills

If your house sits inside Georgetown, you have two bills to track. The county bill comes from the sheriff. The city bill comes from city hall, where the Clerk's Office takes payment over the counter, by post or by phone.

For a current-year city bill, use the OpenGov portal for lookup and online payment. For years before 2025, the city's Tax Master service is the place to search. Print both receipts before closing day, because a buyer's title agent will want proof that neither bill is open. A house outside the city limits has no city bill, which is worth telling buyers who are comparing addresses.

Selling with taxes owed

A delinquent bill will show up in the title search, so deal with it early.

  • Ask the County Clerk for a payoff, since it holds delinquent bills after April 15.
  • If the County Attorney offers a payment agreement, you must sign by June 30.
  • Give the closing agent the final figure so it comes out of your proceeds.
  • If you own a house inside Georgetown, check the city bill too, since it is paid separately.

Bring a few things when you visit an office: a photo ID, your deed or closing paperwork, and the bill itself or the parcel address. Staff can pull up the account faster with the address, and written payoff numbers are what the closing agent will ask for. If you share ownership with a spouse or heir, have the other owner's name ready too, since payment and records are tied to the owner of record.

A direct cash sale works well when back taxes and repairs are both stacked up, because the buyer does not wait on a lender and the tax is paid from the sale money.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes Scott County property tax payments?

For the current year, the Scott County Sheriff's Office at (502) 863-7855. Around April 15 unpaid bills go to the County Clerk, and Georgetown's own city bill is paid through the city.

When is the Scott County tax sale?

In late August each year, in the third-floor Fiscal Court Room. Pay before the day of the sale to keep a bill out of it, and ask the clerk at (502) 863-7875 for the current date.

Is there a payment plan for delinquent Scott County tax?

Possibly. The County Attorney mails a May notice describing agreements for eligible owners, and June 30 is the cutoff to sign one. The office answers at (502) 863-7870.

Does turning 65 give a Scott County owner the homestead exemption automatically?

No. File at the PVA, (502) 863-7885, with proof of age. The state deduction for 2025 and 2026 was $49,100.

Does Georgetown bill property tax separately from the county?

Yes, the city bills its own property tax. You can search and pay through the city's OpenGov portal or at the City Clerk's Office.

Who handles your Kenton County tax bill

Three offices split the work. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) assigns value. The Kenton County Sheriff mails and collects the bill. The Kenton County Clerk takes over any bill still open after April 15.

The PVA does not set rates, create taxing districts or take payments. Escrow questions and bill questions go to the sheriff. The summer sale and the delinquent lists belong to the clerk. The rate itself comes from the school district, city, county and fire district named on your bill.

The county has two seats, Covington and Independence, and the PVA keeps an office in each. In Covington the office sits at 1840 Simon Kenton Way, Suite 3300, open weekdays 8:15 to 4:15. The Independence one is at 5272 Madison Pike, open weekdays 8 to 4 and closed from 1 to 2. One number, 859-392-1750, reaches both.

Due dates and penalties

Collection runs from October 1 to April 15. The cheapest window is the first one, which ends November 1 and takes 2 percent off the face amount. Penalties begin in January.

What the sheriff charges, by date paid
Date paidYou owe
Oct. 1 through Nov. 1Bill minus 2 percent
Nov. 2 through Dec. 31Bill as printed
Jan. 1 through Jan. 31Bill plus 5 percent
Feb. 1 through Apr. 15Bill plus 10 percent, then another 10 percent

If April 15 lands on a weekend or holiday, the close moves to the next business day.

Where and how to pay

You can pay at the sheriff's Covington counter (1840 Simon Kenton Way, Suite 1200) or at the Independence courthouse. Heritage Bank branches accept cash or checks at the window. You can also mail a payment, pay by card or e-check online for a convenience fee, or let your mortgage escrow handle it. A bounced check costs $50.

No bill in hand by October 15? Phone 859-392-1800 and ask the sheriff's office to confirm the amount for your parcel.

The county rate and what else is on the bill

The county's slice is thin. In August 2025 the Fiscal Court voted to lower its real property rate from 12.5 to 11.5 cents per $100 of valuation. That was a fifth straight annual cut and the lowest since 1983. By the county's own example, a home valued at $275,000 pays $316.25 to the county.

The rest of the bill comes from bodies the Fiscal Court does not control: school districts, the health department, the library and fire protection districts. Cities add their own taxes, and Morning View has no city taxes. The sheriff's property tax page has a phone list for city tax collections. For a line-by-line breakdown on one address, call the sheriff.

How to appeal your assessment

Your first move is a review request sent to the PVA, which takes them from January 1 onward. It also counts as the mandatory conference that must happen before anything formal.

Conferences run by email or in person by appointment. You can file the Review Request Form online, in person or by phone. The burden of proof sits with you. Check the PVA's supporting documentation list before you gather evidence. Its site also posts sales dashboards and a comparable sales map for houses and condominiums. Nothing is accepted after the inspection period closes.

  • Formal inspection opens the first Monday in May and runs 13 days.
  • The conference period ends at the close of the PVA's business day on the last day of that window, and the filing with the clerk is due shortly after. Check the PVA's posted times each spring.
  • A conference record, Form 62A307, must accompany any filing with the clerk.

The Board of Assessment Appeals is separate from the PVA and runs through the County Clerk's office. A loss there can go to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals, which answers to neither the PVA nor any taxing authority.

Reassessment and the homestead exemption

The PVA follows a four-year review plan, so every parcel gets a physical look at least that often. Owners in Elsmere, Erlanger, Fort Mitchell, Lakeside Park and Park Hills may see inspectors working their areas, and the PVA lists the sales behind its re-evaluations for Bromley, Covington and Ludlow. The office also values about 5,000 commercial and industrial properties and prices motor vehicles at January 1 using NADA figures.

A homestead reduction is open to owners turning 65 within the year, filed through the PVA's online application. Owners who are totally disabled may also claim it. It follows the owner, not the property, which means a buyer must file a new application. Business personal property returns are due May 15, with no relief from a tax filing extension.

Selling with taxes owed

Once April 15 passes, the sheriff stops and the Kenton County Clerk picks up the file. Your unpaid bill is converted into a certificate of delinquency carrying a lien, and fees plus 1 percent interest each month keep adding up.

The clerk holds a yearly sale in July. A bill still open then can be sold to an outside buyer, and redeeming it costs substantially more. State revenue officials show the climb with a $1,000 example: $1,254 on transfer and roughly $1,388 if paid at the clerk's counter within five business days, before the county attorney's fee applies.

  • The county attorney's first notice goes out in the month after transfer.
  • A newspaper ad and a website list name the delinquent parcels ahead of the sale.
  • Expect the sale between 90 and 135 days after the clerk gets the file.

Before listing, pay off any old certificate so nothing jumps out at closing. Have the clerk put a payoff figure on paper, then pass it to your title company.

What happens to the tax bill at closing

After you sell, the next bill can still carry your name, or both names. The sheriff explains that the seller credits their share to the buyer or escrow agent at closing, and the owner of record then pays the whole bill. Before you close, confirm which year's bill is still unpaid and make sure the title company has the sheriff's current figure.

A cash sale skips the lender's escrow analysis and the usual wait on a buyer's loan, so the tax proration is a single line on the settlement statement. Bring the latest bill, any delinquent notice and your PVA exemption paperwork to the closing table.

Kenton County housing at a glance

Kenton is the third most populous county in Kentucky, with an estimated 175,779 residents in July 2025. It holds 74,593 housing units, and 70.7 percent of households own. The median home value is $244,400, and median gross rent is $1,069. Five school districts serve the county, from dense northern cities to rural southern areas, so tax bills on similar houses can differ by district.

When are Kenton County property tax bills due?

Pay by November 1 for the 2 percent discount. Face amount is due through December 31, penalties begin January 1 and the sheriff stops on April 15.

Where do I pay my Kenton County property tax?

At the sheriff's Covington or Independence counters, a Heritage Bank branch, by mail to P.O. Box 188070 in Erlanger, online, or through mortgage escrow.

Who do I call if my Kenton County tax bill is wrong?

The PVA at 859-392-1750 handles value and exemptions. The sheriff handles the bill itself, and the PVA neither collects nor sets rates.

How do I appeal my Kenton County assessment?

Request a PVA conference inside the 13-day May inspection window. The clerk filing is due one working day after the window closes.

What is the Kenton County property tax rate?

The Fiscal Court lowered its real property rate to 11.5 cents per $100 in August 2025. School, city, library, health and fire levies are billed on top.

Who sends and collects a Warren County tax bill

The job is split among three Bowling Green offices that take calls on weekdays. The PVA sets the value, the sheriff mails the bill and collects, and the clerk inherits whatever is still open after April 15.

  • PVA: 429 E. 10th Avenue, Bowling Green, KY 42101, phone (270) 843-3268, open 8:00 to 4:30.
  • Sheriff: (270) 842-1633, with a tax inquiry page for looking up and paying a bill. The business office keeps the same 8:00 to 4:30 hours.
  • County Clerk: P.O. Box 478, Bowling Green, KY 42102, phone (270) 842-9416. Property tax and valuation questions go to the PVA.

The sheriff collects under KRS 134.140 and 160.500, then passes the money on to each state, county, school and district authority.

Payment schedule and online fees

Expect your bill during the first week of October. Each stage below tracks the state calendar in KRS 134.015, and the 2026 discount window closed November 1, 2026.

  • October 1 to November 1: 2 percent off.
  • November 2 to December 31: the amount on the bill.
  • January: 5 percent more.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 21 percent charge that bundles the 10 percent penalty with the sheriff's fee.

Online payment carries a fee: $1.50 for a card payment of $60.00 or less, 2.49 percent above that, and $1.50 per ACH or e-check payment. American Express is refused. The site refreshes after 7:00 pm on business days, so a Friday payment may not show until Monday night. On a large bill, ACH avoids the percentage.

Why do two Warren County neighbors pay different rates?

Warren County has two public school districts. Warren County Public Schools serves the county and the outlying parts of Bowling Green, and Bowling Green Independent Schools serves most of the city proper. The city school levy is 84.80 cents against 52.20 cents for the county district, and that single choice moves the bill more than any other line.

Warren County 2025 real estate levies, cents per $100 of assessed value

The county levies add to 21.45 cents. Put together, the levies yield three totals: 84.25 for land outside any city, 104.55 for city land in the county school district, and 137.15 for city land in the city school district. Ask the sheriff which total applies to your address. Buyers comparing houses across the county will notice the gap.

Homestead exemption

Owners who are 65 and over, or totally disabled, claim the deduction at the PVA. It is $49,100 for each of 2025 and 2026. A birth certificate, license or passport backs up the age claim.

A disability claim is renewed yearly. Two groups never renew: owners with a service-connected disability, and owners rated permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems. If you sell, tell the PVA so the deduction comes off your old address.

When you visit the PVA, bring photo identification and the proof of age or disability described above. Ask the office to confirm the deduction is on your parcel for the current year before you list, because a buyer will not inherit it. The new owner has to apply for their own if they qualify.

How to contest a Warren County value

Your first stop is a conference with the PVA, (270) 843-3268, because state rules require it before anything else. The roll is open for viewing for thirteen days, beginning the first Monday in May. After meeting with the PVA, file at the County Clerk before the day after inspection ends.

  • Photos, insurance records, building costs and sales listings are the evidence the local board expects.
  • Anyone paid to speak for you must be a professional such as an attorney, accountant, appraiser or broker, and must carry written authority.
  • Hearings start 25 to 35 days after viewing ends and run no more than five days.

Any decision to raise or lower a value arrives with written reasons.

Unpaid bills after April 15

At the close of that day, the sheriff sends every open bill to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency carrying a lien. The clerk keeps accepting payment right up to the annual sale and publishes a PDF list of current delinquent parcels. The sale is held each August at the clerk's office, Suite 100 at 429 E 10th Ave, with buyer registration closing a few days earlier. Call the clerk for this year's date.

Once the bill moves to the clerk, charges stack up fast. Interest runs at 1 percent monthly. The clerk's commission is 10 percent of tax, penalty and interest, and the county attorney adds 20 percent unless the bill is paid within five business days. A $10 lien recording and release fee also applies.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Warren County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

The lien clings to the land for up to eleven years, so it does not disappear when the house sells. Pay it off at closing and get a release from the clerk. Ask the sheriff for a current payoff on this year's bill and the clerk for anything older, and bring both figures to the title company before you sign.

A cash sale can clear an old delinquency from the proceeds without you fronting the money first, which helps if penalties are already piling up. Expect the buyer's title search to turn up every open bill, so it is better to know the total before you list.

A simple order of work helps. First, look up the bill on the sheriff's inquiry page and confirm which school district your parcel sits in. Second, phone the clerk and ask whether any earlier year was sent over as a certificate of delinquency. Third, hand the payoff numbers to whoever handles your closing. Last, ask the clerk for the release once everything is paid, so the lien does not follow the title to the next owner.

Permits and local context

Warren County had 149,375 people in mid 2025, and 1,453 building permits were issued during the year. Median rent is $1,002 a month, and 55.6 percent of homes are owner occupied. The median home value is $258,000.

Permits matter at sale time. The county's Division for Building Services, at 1141 State Street, covers everywhere except Bowling Green and Oakland. It charges $0.15 per square foot with a $45 minimum, and sets a fine of at least $500 for work begun without a permit. Sheds from 120 square feet and all pools need one. Phone (270) 843-5360 to ask about a past project before you list.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes payment for Warren County property tax?

The Warren County Sheriff's Office takes it, at (270) 842-1633. Use the tax inquiry page on its website to look up and pay a bill.

Did the 2026 Warren County discount end?

Yes. The window was October 1 to November 1, 2026. After that the face amount stands until December 31, 2026, and January 2027 adds 5 percent.

Why is the Warren County school tax higher in some places?

The city school district levy is 84.80 cents per $100, against 52.20 cents for the county district. Parcels inside the city's own district pay the higher one.

Does Warren County charge extra to pay by card?

Yes. Card payments run $1.50 up to $60.00 and 2.49 percent over that. ACH and e-check payments cost $1.50, and American Express is not accepted.

What happens to Warren County taxes when I sell?

Any open bill carries a lien on the land for up to eleven years. Pay it at closing and get a release from the clerk.

Why a Frankfort house can have two tax bills

The City of Frankfort taxes inside its limits on top of the county. Everyone in Franklin County gets a county bill from the Franklin County Sheriff, and a house in Frankfort also gets a city bill from the Finance Office, which collects for Frankfort Independent Schools too.

The Franklin County PVA sets the values for both bills. It is at 313 West Main Street, 2nd Floor, Room 209, Frankfort, with a fax at (502) 226-5495 and a phone at (502) 875-8780, open weekdays from 8:00 until 4:30. The sheriff has moved to the Public Safety Complex at 974 River Bend Road and answers at (502) 875-8740. The sheriff's website offers a tax bill search with card payment, and the front door has a secure drop box under camera watch.

Frankfort uses the PVA's figure, which is 100 percent of fair market value as of each January 1. Questions about a value, an exemption or a mailing address belong with the PVA, not the city.

County and Frankfort payment calendars

The city does not copy the state schedule. County bills follow KRS 134.015, while Frankfort publishes its own dates, so a deadline that works for one bill can already be past for the other.

Sheriff bill and City of Frankfort bill side by side
