Selling a house in Meade County

Meade County was created in 1823 and covers 325 square miles. The Ohio River forms its 56-mile northern line, facing Indiana. Karst terrain with sinkholes covers much of the land, and the northwest sits on a plateau behind the Dripping Springs Escarpment. Brandenburg is the seat, Ekron and Muldraugh are the other cities, and Doe Valley and Fort Knox are census-designated places. Meade lies in the Louisville metro area, within reach of the job centers at Elizabethtown and Fort Knox, and workers travel a mean 33.0 minutes to their jobs.

Meade County Schools, with Meade County High School, teach most children, while families living on the Fort Knox base are zoned to the Defense Department's schools. The county keeps Eastern time.

Sinkholes are common in this terrain, and a house with one, or with deferred repairs, can stall a conventional sale. Ground conditions vary from one parcel to the next, so a buyer's inspection may ask about them. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can close without those fixes.

Location also shapes demand. Fort Knox and Elizabethtown employers are a short drive away, and the Ohio River frontage faces Indiana, so buyers from the Louisville side often compare Brandenburg listings with those in Hardin County. Priced against the $207,900 median, a well kept house with clear title and a current tax payoff tends to move faster than one with open questions.

Before you list

Start by phoning the PVA to confirm the parcel record and any homestead claim, then ask the Sheriff for the current bill. If the sale will close after April 15, plan to get the payoff from the County Clerk instead. Expect the title company to ask for both figures, along with a copy of the deed. When the owner has died, bring the papers showing who may sign the deed.

Showings go better when the house is ready for a walk-through, but you aren't required to fix anything for a cash sale. If the sinkhole question comes up, a buyer will want to know what you know about it, so be ready to answer plainly. Keep copies of your tax receipts for recent years. They show the title company the bills were paid and speed up the payoff check. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the buyer early and give the lease terms, since a lease may stay in force after the sale. Finally, ask the Sheriff about payment methods for your closing date, because the personal-check rule near the end of the season can matter if the closing falls close to April 15

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay the Meade County Sheriff?

Go to 516 Hillcrest Drive, Suite 14, in Brandenburg, or call (270) 422-4937. Suite 3, the PVA, can't accept payments.

When does the Meade County Sheriff stop taking personal checks?

From two weeks before April 15 onward. Cash, cards, money orders and cashier's checks are still accepted.

When is the homestead filing cutoff in Meade County?

The PVA sets a spring date each year for a place on the November bill. Call the office for the current cutoff.

What is the state rate in Meade County?

The state's 2025 rate is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value. County, school and district levies come on top.

What becomes of Meade County bills left open after April 15?

The Clerk receives them as certificates of delinquency and files a lien. Interest accrues at 1 percent monthly, and the Clerk may schedule a sale within 90 to 135 days.

Which office does what

Valuing a parcel and collecting its tax are handled by different offices in Montgomery County. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) answers value questions. The Sheriff's Office prints and collects the bills.

  • PVA, (859) 498-8710: value, the tax roll and exemption forms.
  • Sheriff, (859) 498-8704: amounts due. Checks go to 1 Court Street, Suite 4, Mt. Sterling, KY 40353, with the bill number written on them.
  • County Clerk, (859) 498-8700: recording a deed, and any bill that has gone delinquent.

The sheriff's website lets you view and print bills and receipts but offers no way to pay online. If you want a receipt mailed back, enclose a stamped, self-addressed envelope with the check.

Due dates and penalties

The sheriff mails bills in the last week of September, and they become payable October 1. Each year the collection calendar runs like this:

Sheriff's collection calendar
DatesWhat the bill becomes
October 1 through November 1Two percent comes off
November 2 through December 31Printed total, no adjustment
January 1 through January 31Five percent is added
February 1 through April 15Twenty-one percent is added

A payment made while the 10% penalty applies, before the bill is handed to the clerk, carries one more 10% sheriff's fee. At close of business on April 15, delinquent bills transfer to the County Clerk. From then on a 20% County Attorney fee, a 10% clerk fee and 1% interest each month apply, and the clerk may sell a bill still unpaid to a third party in the summer.

Once April 15 passes, the clerk owns the past-due bill and quotes the payoff. Owe an earlier year? Get that number before you choose a closing date. Where escrow or a former owner pays the tax, forward the bill to them so nothing is missed.

Montgomery County housing and the market

The county covers 197 square miles of the Outer Bluegrass, with Mount Sterling as the seat, 34 miles east of Lexington. Clark County gave up the territory in 1796. The 2025 population is estimated at 28,822, a gain of 2.5% since 2020. Interstate 64 clips the north edge of town, and U.S. 60 and U.S. 460 cross downtown. The average commute is 25.7 minutes, and the area belongs to the Lexington combined statistical area.

There are 12,422 housing units, and 53 building permits were issued in 2025. Homeowners live in 68.3% of occupied units, leaving close to a third to renters. The midpoint of an owned home is $172,200, and renters pay a midpoint of $830 in gross rent. Ownership costs are $1,242 a month for mortgage holders and $470 for owners with no loan. A seller with deferred repairs can expect a slower sale than one with a tidy house.

Zoning is uneven. There is no countywide planning and zoning, yet subdivisions within five miles of Mt. Sterling must meet the city's zoning and subdivision rules. Anyone planning to split a lot before a sale should call city hall first. Court Day each October brings roughly 130,000 visitors downtown over four days, which is worth remembering before scheduling showings that weekend.

How to dispute your valuation

Values are pinned to January 1. Under KRS 133.120 the first step is a sit-down with the PVA or a deputy, which may be held by phone. KRS 133.045 opens the tax roll for inspection for 13 days from the first Monday of May, unless the Department of Revenue picks other dates.

If that talk fails, put your complaint in writing and deliver it to the County Clerk. Identify the parcel, explain what is wrong and name the value you think is right. The hearing is before the county appeals board, and the burden is on you to bring evidence such as an appraisal, listings or a builder's estimate.

While the case is open, pay on the value you claimed. A higher final number means you owe the gap plus interest. Skipping the county hearing forfeits the later route to the state Board of Tax Appeals.

Homestead exemption

The state exemption is $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026, open to anyone 65 or over or classified as totally disabled. It lowers the value that rates are applied to.

The PVA takes the form at (859) 498-8710. Show your age with a birth certificate, driver's license or passport. Disability claimants must reapply each year, with carve-outs for owners with a service-connected disability and for people whom Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems has found permanently and totally disabled.

The tax bill at closing

The owner on January 1 is the taxpayer for the whole year, so a house bought later still has its bill under the seller's name. KRS 134.015 calls the tax a personal debt of that owner. A lien from unpaid tax can last 11 years under KRS 134.420 and passes to the next buyer along with the land.

  • Ask the sheriff whether this year's bill is settled, and what payoff applies on the day of closing.
  • Decide in the sales contract who bears which months of tax.
  • Enter the buyer's address for later tax mailings on the deed, since KRS 382.135 demands it.
  • Record the signed deed at the County Clerk's office.

Title searches turn up old bills, so clearing them early avoids a delay at the closing table.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Montgomery County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Back tax doesn't stop a sale. The closing agent pays it from your proceeds, so request the current figure from the sheriff, or the clerk once April 15 is past, and hand it over. If the bill has gone to the clerk, the attorney and clerk fees and monthly interest are part of that figure, and it rises each month, so ask for a figure dated near the closing day.

A cash sale as-is can suit an owner with deferred repairs, an inherited house or a bill already in collection, since it skips showings and lender repair demands. Bring the deed, your latest bill and, for an estate, the papers showing who may sign. After closing, the County Clerk records the deed, and the PVA should be told so the next bill reaches the new owner.

Getting a Montgomery County house ready to sell

Many buyers commute toward Lexington, so name the Interstate 64 exits, 110 and 113, and the drive time in your listing. The Montgomery County School District, which includes Montgomery County High School, serves the whole county. Midpoint values near $172,200 mean a clean, repaired house competes well, and one with open tax or lien questions tends to stall.

Before listing, pull your last bill and receipt from the sheriff's site, confirm the parcel on the PVA roll, and note any exemption on file. If you split a lot, check with city hall about subdivision rules first.

Mount Sterling has seen seven courthouses over its history, and the county records office downtown holds the deed trail for your parcel. Ask the clerk's staff how to look up a prior deed if the chain of title is unclear. Interstate 64, U.S. 60 and U.S. 460 make most addresses easy to reach, and showings work best away from the October Court Day crowds, when downtown parking and traffic are heavy.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the Montgomery County tax bill?

The Sheriff's Office, (859) 498-8704, mails it. The PVA, (859) 498-8710, is the number to use only if the value seems off.

Is online payment offered by the Montgomery County Sheriff?

No. You can look up and print bills and receipts on the sheriff's site, but money has to arrive by mail or in person at 1 Court Street, Suite 4, Mt. Sterling.

What are the penalty periods after December 31 in Montgomery County?

January adds five percent, and February 1 through April 15 adds twenty-one percent. After that the County Clerk takes the bill and tacks on attorney and clerk fees and monthly interest.

Is there zoning in Montgomery County outside Mt. Sterling?

There is none countywide. Subdivisions within five miles of Mt. Sterling follow the city's rules, so ask city hall before dividing land.

What does the state homestead exemption take off a Montgomery County home?

It removes $49,100 from assessed value for tax years 2025 and 2026. File at the PVA if you are 65 or older or totally disabled.

How does an owner contest a Wayne County value?

  • Proof of age can be a passport, license, or birth certificate.
  • Disability payments must have been received through the whole assessment period.
  • Owners with a service-connected disability, or a permanent total ruling from Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems, skip the yearly renewal.

The exemption goes with the person, not the parcel. After you sell, tell the PVA so it comes off, and the next owner can apply for theirs.

Do unpaid Wayne County taxes block a sale?

Not by themselves, but they come out of your proceeds. Under KRS 134.420 a delinquency lien can sit on the parcel for as long as eleven years, and any buyer's title company will insist that it be cleared.

Once at the Clerk the amount grows by a penalty, a Sheriff's add-on, and monthly interest. Clerk and county attorney commissions, mailing costs, and a lien recording fee follow, and a bill can climb well past its original size within weeks.

Beyond that, an investor can buy the certificate at a sale and add charges. Paying the Sheriff before April 15 sidesteps the path, and the sales contract should spell out who covers this year's bill.

Steps for selling with a tax balance

To get ready, call the Sheriff for this year's total and the Clerk for any earlier year that was turned over as a certificate of delinquency. Write down the amounts and the date you were quoted. Next, give those figures to your closing agent. The payoff goes on the settlement statement, comes out of what you receive at the table, and the lien is released so the buyer gets clear title.

An inherited cabin, a rental, or a house needing repairs can go to a cash buyer as-is, with the tax settled the same day. A cash sale skips the lender's inspection and repair list, so an old tax balance is one fewer thing that can stall the deal.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wayne County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

A tax year in Wayne County, start to finish

The calendar helps a seller plan. Assessment notices arrive in spring, and the roll is open to the public starting the first Monday in May. That stretch is your chance to question a value. Rates get voted afterward, and the bill comes in the fall.

Pay by November 1 if you can, since that is the only date that earns a discount. The printed amount holds through December. After that the cost rises: 5 percent in January, then 10 percent from February 1 until April 15. A bill still unpaid after that lands with the Clerk, and the added costs described above begin.

If you plan to list in the spring, check the November and December payment before anything else. A paid bill is clean on the title search, which leaves a buyer's agent with fewer questions.

Wayne County at a glance

Wayne County lies on the Tennessee border, with Monticello as its only city and the seat. Lake Cumberland and the Daniel Boone National Forest reach into the county. Wayne County keeps Eastern time, though its west and south edges trace the Central time line, so a lender or attorney across that line may be an hour apart.

Population was 19,597 in 2025, up 0.2 percent from 2020. There are 10,206 housing units against 8,074 households, and 69.1 percent of homes have owners living in them. Median home value is $135,700. Owners with a mortgage spend a median $1,100 a month and those without spend $342, which makes a paid-off house inexpensive to carry. Rents have a median of $727 a month. The county voted wet on November 3, 2020.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Wayne County PVA's hours?

At 55 N. Main Street, Suite 107 in Monticello, the PVA opens weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., plus the first and third Saturday of the month 8 a.m. to noon. The phone is 606-348-6621.

Is there a discount for paying Wayne County tax early?

Yes, 2 percent for paying the entire bill by November 1. The printed amount holds through December, then 5 percent and later 10 percent are added.

Must I talk to the Wayne County PVA before I can appeal?

Yes. You must confer with the PVA or a deputy first, and then file with the County Clerk by closing time on the day after inspection ends.

How big is the Wayne County homestead exemption?

It deducts $49,100 for 2025 and 2026 from the value of the home you live in. Owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, file at the PVA.

Who gets my Wayne County tax bill after April 15?

The County Clerk takes it as a certificate of delinquency backed by a lien. Interest and commissions accumulate, and an investor can purchase it at a sale.

Edmonson County tax offices

Three counters matter to a seller in Edmonson County, and all sit in Brownsville. Valuation belongs to the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), whose office is inside the courthouse on Main Cross Street at 270-597-2381. Payment belongs to the sheriff at 110 Jackson Street, 270-597-2157. Anything late, plus the land records, goes through the county clerk at 108 North Main Street, 270-597-2624.

County government keeps weekday hours starting at 7:30 and ending at 4:00. The PVA's website links a qPublic parcel search, which shows how a particular house is assessed before anyone picks up the phone.

No single office decides the total bill. The PVA supplies the value, while the levy comes from the taxing bodies, among them the fiscal court and the county school system. For the combined rate on one parcel, ask the sheriff.

The Edmonson County tax calendar

Bills leave the sheriff's office on October 30, later than the statewide default of September, so the whole calendar here runs a month behind the usual one. If you have no bill by November 15, ring the sheriff, who mails a duplicate right away. The slower start fits the alternative schedule in KRS 134.015, which gives each stage one month when bills are delayed.

What the Edmonson County Sheriff charges at each stage of the collection year
When you payWhat you owe
Paid by November 30Bill less 2%
All of DecemberBill as printed
All of JanuaryBill plus 5%
February 1 to April 15Bill plus 21%

That 21 percent is a 10 percent penalty with a 10 percent sheriff fee stacked on it. Whatever remains unpaid when April 15 ends goes to the clerk.

The sheriff takes cash at the counter, plus checks, money orders and cards (processing fees apply to cards, by phone or in the office). The office opens at 7:30 every day it is open, closes at 4:00 on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday, and closes at noon on Thursday and Saturday.

How an Edmonson County owner contests a valuation

Talk to the PVA first, and appeal second. Values are struck on January 1. Houses can be listed with the PVA through March 1, and business equipment through May 15.

  • The assessment roll lies open for thirteen days starting on the first May Monday, including Saturdays.
  • A conference with the PVA or a deputy unlocks the right to appeal. The appeal form then goes to the clerk's office, due the workday after the inspection window shuts.
  • The local board sits for no more than five days, opening between 25 and 35 days after inspection ends.
  • Evidence decides the outcome: insurance policies, building costs, listings and physical details of the land. An appeal with none is denied.
  • Skipping a scheduled hearing forfeits any further review.

If bills print while an appeal is pending, they use the owner's stated figure, and a supplemental bill covers any increase the board later sets.

Homestead exemption

The state deducts $49,100 from a qualifying home's value, and that figure applies to the 2025 and 2026 rolls. Owners qualify at 65 or when classified as totally disabled, and the PVA takes the application.

For proof of age, a birth certificate, license or passport will do. A disability claim rests on classification under a federal program or a retirement system, with payments received over the whole year. Disability claims are renewed every year, unless the owner has a service-connected disability or has been ruled permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

Selling an Edmonson County house while taxes are unpaid

The debt rides with the land. The lien outlives a change of owner: KRS 134.420 keeps it alive for up to 11 years on a parcel whose tax went unpaid, so a title search at closing will turn it up.

After April 15 the clerk holds the bill as a certificate of delinquency, interest builds by 1 percent each month, and the county attorney sends written notice well before a sale. Kentucky puts the sale 90 to 135 days after the handover. The clerk runs the list of unpaid bills in The Edmonson News in August and holds the sale in September at 11:00 a.m. Buyers register a few days ahead and post 25 percent of the face value of the certificates they hope to win.

Paying the clerk in full before the sale date ends the matter, and money that shows up later is sent back. Some bills are pulled from the list under KRS 134.504. Call 270-597-2624 for a payoff figure ahead of listing.

As grantor, the seller owes transfer tax of one dollar per $1,000 of price, which is how the $0.50 per $500 rate works out. The clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

Edmonson County housing in brief

Edmonson County has 12,749 residents in 2025, a gain of 5.1 percent on the 2020 count. It covers 303 square miles of land inside the Bowling Green metro area, and Brownsville is the seat and only town. About a quarter of the county falls inside Mammoth Cave National Park, and the Green and Nolin rivers shape the rest.

Owners occupy 80.1 percent of housing, across 5,099 households. A typical owned home is worth $160,300 and a typical monthly rent runs $778. Because most owners hold their houses long term, sales tend to be of older homes. A seller facing back taxes or repairs can compare a listing against a straight as-is sale for cash.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Edmonson County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What to do before you list

Start with the numbers. Call the sheriff at 270-597-2157 for this year's balance and the clerk at 270-597-2624 for any delinquent year. Look up the parcel on the PVA's qPublic search to see how the house is assessed, and phone 270-597-2381 if the acreage or building details look wrong. If you are 65 or disabled, check that the exemption is on the record, and keep copies of your payment receipts.

Then think about timing. A sale that closes in the middle of the collection year means the bill is split between you and the buyer, while a sale after February 1 means the 21 percent charge may already apply. An as-is cash sale can close quickly and pay the tax from your proceeds, which suits an inherited house or one that needs work.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Edmonson County tax discount end?

The 2 percent discount ends on November 30 under the sheriff's calendar, because bills are mailed October 30. December is face value, and January adds a 5 percent penalty.

Where does an Edmonson County owner send the payment?

Take it to the sheriff's office at 110 Jackson Street in Brownsville, or post a check or money order to that same address. The counter takes cash. Cards go through by phone or in the office and carry a fee.

Who sets my Edmonson County property value?

The PVA sets it, working from January 1 values. Its office is in the courthouse, phone 270-597-2381, and neither the sheriff nor the fiscal court has a say in the value.

Can I appeal my Edmonson County assessment later in the year?

No. Every appeal starts with a PVA conference while the May tax roll is open to inspection, and the clerk's filing window closes one workday after the roll does.

What does Edmonson County do with unpaid property taxes?

Bills left unpaid at the April 15 cutoff pass to the clerk, where 1 percent interest accrues monthly. The clerk advertises them in late summer and holds a tax sale, and payments must reach the clerk in full before the sale date.

Who values and who collects

Hopkins County splits the work between the PVA and the Sheriff. The PVA's staff lists every taxable parcel, measures and photographs buildings, values each one and builds the tax roll that the public may inspect. The office is in the Courthouse Annex, 25 East Center Street, Madisonville, KY 42431, telephone (270) 821-3092.

Billing and collection sit with the Sheriff's Office at 261 Responders Lane, phone 270-821-5661, open to taxpayers on weekdays from eight to four. Bills still open after April 15 belong to the Hopkins County Clerk, reachable at 270-326-2097.

Bills are written to the name on the parcel as of January 1. If you bought in spring, the old owner may still be receiving it and should forward it. The Sheriff can't see new deeds, so a buyer who hears nothing can ring the office or print a copy online.

Collection calendar and penalties

Bills normally go out about September 30, and the counter opens October 1. The Sheriff runs four stages through April 15.

Yearly tax collection stages at the Hopkins County Sheriff
Payment windowWhat changes
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 315 percent added
February 1 to April 1521 percent added

Call the Sheriff for an exact payoff before paying in February or March, since fees and commission can change the total.

Sheriff collection stops when business closes on April 15, and whatever is left moves to the Clerk.

Payment methods

The office takes online and counter payments, and it insists on the whole amount. A partial payment is turned down.

  • Accepted: cash, personal checks, money orders, cashier's checks and cards.
  • An outside processor runs cards and charges 2.5 percent plus 30 cents.
  • Online checks cost $1.50 to process.
  • Write checks to Hopkins County Sheriff.

Escrow doesn't lift the owner's duty. The taxpayer must get the bill to the mortgage lender, and a lender can't pay what it never receives.

Estimating and prorating a bill

The bill math is taxable assessment divided by 100, times the rate set for the year. Volunteer fire department fees or watershed taxes, where they apply, are added separately.

For a sale, the Sheriff suggests a simple split. Divide the last year's bill by 365 for a daily cost, then multiply by the number of days the seller lived in the house.

Some closing agents wait for the real bill. Compare their number with the Sheriff's method before you sign the settlement statement, and ask which year's bill each of you used. If the real bill is not out yet at closing, agree in writing on the estimate and who will settle any difference. A line in the contract is enough.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the PVA's office. Under KRS 133.120, a conference with the PVA or a deputy has to come first, before or during the inspection period, and you can ask to hold it by telephone.

  • The PVA walks through how the number was set and writes up the meeting.
  • If that fails, send the County Clerk a letter or petition no later than one workday after inspection closes.
  • Name the value you think is fair and back it up with land and building descriptions, insurance, cost records, listings, comparable sales or loan papers.
  • Show up for the hearing, personally or through an authorized representative.

The board may reject an appeal if you hold back information it reasonably asks for. Meanwhile, pay on the figure you claimed. Bring photos or an appraisal if you have one, and keep notes from the PVA conference, because the clerk and the board will want to know what was already discussed.

Homestead and farmland

A homeowner aged 65 or older, or totally disabled, who lives in the property can deduct $49,100 from the assessment for the 2025 and 2026 years. File the form at the PVA office with proof of age, most often a birth certificate or driver's license. Disability applicants must document benefits received from January through December.

Farmland is treated differently. KRS 132.010 values agricultural land by its production capability, and qualifying land means parcels of 10 acres or more used to raise livestock or grow crops, including timber. Nobody can claim more than one exemption on one property within one county and state.

When the Clerk takes over a tax debt

Once the Clerk holds the bill, it becomes a certificate of delinquency, and a lien is entered against the property. Selling the house doesn't remove it.

The Clerk holds the tax sale electronically each fall, and buyers register at the Clerk's office, 24 Union Street, Madisonville. Buyers pay $5 per priority bill or $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250 in combined fees, and the clerk sets the payment deadline at the sale.

A buyer of a certificate can load its own fees on the account, so clearing the bill with the Sheriff before the deadline, or with the Clerk afterward, costs less. Call the Clerk for current amounts.

Hopkins County housing in brief

Hopkins County is in western Kentucky, with Madisonville as county seat and largest city. Population was 45,127 in 2025, down 0.6 percent from 2020. Owners live in 70.7 percent of homes, and 18,397 households average 2.40 people each.

The middle owned-home value is $142,800 and median gross rent is $837. Median household income is $56,815. Persons 65 or older make up 21.0 percent of the population, so homestead claims are common. Builders took out 201 permits in 2025.

Monthly owner costs run $1,107 with a mortgage and $436 without, a useful figure when a buyer weighs your price against renting.

Selling with taxes owed

Before you list, find out which office holds your bill. In the fall and winter it sits with the Sheriff, and after April 15 it sits with the Clerk. Ask for a written payoff from whichever one has it, and give a copy to the title company.

At closing, the title agent pays the tax from your proceeds and the buyer's lender expects the lien to clear. If you are selling for cash and want to close quickly, the payoff is the one number you can't skip, so request it a week or two ahead and ask how long it stays good.

Keep your payment receipt and the Sheriff's or Clerk's confirmation with the sale file. Also check whether a homestead deduction is on the account. It ends with your ownership, and the buyer has to apply on their own if they qualify.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What day does the Hopkins County discount period begin?

Collection opens October 1, after bills go out around September 30. Paying through November 1 earns 2 percent off, and face value applies from November 2 to year end.

Will Hopkins County let me split a bill into pieces?

No. The Sheriff takes the whole amount only and refuses part payments. Cards, cash and checks all work, and cards carry a processor fee.

I closed last month and received no bill. Who do I call?

Call the Sheriff at 270-821-5661. Bills are issued to the January 1 owner and the office does not see new deeds, so a copy can be printed from the Sheriff's website.

Whom do I pay once April 15 has gone by?

Pay the Hopkins County Clerk at 270-326-2097, since open bills go there when April 15 ends.

Do older owners get any relief?

Yes: a $49,100 homestead exemption, filed at the PVA's office on East Center Street. Owners 65 and over who live in the house qualify, as do totally disabled owners.

Which Logan County office does what

Property tax in Logan County runs through three desks. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) appraises. The Sheriff takes payment on the current bill. The County Clerk picks up whatever is still open after April 15.

The Sheriff's Office is at 100 North Owen Street in Russellville and answers at 270-726-2244 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. A link on the county's Sheriff page leads to online payment. The PVA uses PO Box 307, Russellville, KY 42276, at 270-726-8334, and it neither sets rates nor collects tax. The Clerk's Office at 229 West 3rd Street keeps weekday hours until 4:30 and answers at 270-726-6061.

Rates come from the elected bodies that levy them: fiscal court, city councils, school boards, and districts like the extension office, library and health department. Once those rates are reported to the clerk, the bills go to print.

Selling a house in Logan County

Logan County is farm country with factories, lying against the Tennessee border. Its four cities are Russellville, Adairville, Auburn and Lewisburg. Russellville is the seat, with 7,164 people in 2020. Logan Aluminum is the largest employer, and dark fired tobacco built much of the county's early money.

The July 2025 population estimate is 28,669, up 4.5 percent since the 2020 census. Owners occupy 74.3 percent of homes, the middle home value is $164,900, and middle monthly rent is $751. The county held 12,461 housing units in 2020. Two school systems divide the county, Russellville Independent Schools and Logan County Schools, which matters to buyers choosing a side of the line.

How a Logan County tax bill is figured

Two inputs produce the bill: an assessed value from the PVA and a combined rate from each district that covers the parcel. Kentucky values real estate at what it would sell for in a voluntary sale on January 1, and farm ground can be valued by its agricultural use.

The PVA calls its online roll a working file, because appeals and assessments keep changing it. The value on that roll comes before exemptions, so subtract any exemption to find the taxable amount. Rates vary by city versus rural address, so ask the County Clerk for the exact set that applies to you.

One quirk helps buyers and sellers. If a property was bought last year, the price in the deed may stand as the listed value for the next assessment, unless the property changed. The number on a recorded deed can follow the house into future bills.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Logan County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and penalties

The Sheriff mails bills around the first of October. From there the state schedule moves through stages, and the amount owed rises as the calendar advances.

Logan County payment schedule
Payment windowAmount owedPaid to
Oct 1 through Nov 1Face amount minus 2 percentSheriff
Nov 2 through Dec 31Face amountSheriff
All of JanuaryFace plus 5 percentSheriff
Feb 1 through Apr 15Face plus 21 percentSheriff
After Apr 15Certificate of delinquencyCounty Clerk

A bill that has not turned up by mid-October is worth a call to 270-726-2244. Once the clerk holds it, the bill carries a recorded lien and grows by interest each month plus clerk and county attorney fees. The county attorney's first warning letter goes out by May 15, and an installment plan is still possible at that point.

How to appeal your assessment

Meet with the PVA first. Only owners who have held that conference may take a dispute to the clerk.

  • The roll is open to view for thirteen days beginning in early May, including Saturdays.
  • File the appeal at the clerk's office no later than the next workday after that window closes.
  • A panel of local board members hears the case between 25 and 35 days later, and the clerk sets the date.

Come with facts. Without them the panel must deny the appeal. Photos, a recent appraisal, insurance policies, construction costs, and listings or sale contracts all count as proof. Anyone paid to speak for you must be a recognized professional, such as an attorney, accountant, appraiser or broker, and must hold your written authorization. Written findings explain any change, and if you stay unhappy, the state tax appeals board is next. Skipping the local panel ends that route.

Homestead exemption and other relief

Seniors, and owners classed as totally disabled, take $49,100 off the home's assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Applications go to the Logan PVA at PO Box 307 in Russellville.

Disability filers generally reapply every year, with exceptions for service-connected veteran disability and for rulings of total, permanent disability by the federal or state retirement programs. The PVA also handles exemptions for certain religious, educational and government property.

Landowners with working acreage should raise agricultural valuation with the PVA, since the state allows farm ground to be valued by use.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Logan County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

The Logan County tax sale

Each year the clerk advertises the open bills and offers them to outside buyers. For the 2025 bills the sale was set for late July at 10:00 am in the old courthouse courtroom, after half-page notices in June and the full list later that month. Call the clerk for the date of the next one.

Buyers sign up ahead. The clerk charges $5 per prior-year bill and $10 per current-year bill, capped at $250, takes a 25 percent deposit on current-year bills, and wants full payment on prior-year ones. A winning bidder steps into the lien, and the owner pays that buyer, who may add heavy fees. State rules call for a 30-day notice from the county attorney, a second notice within 60 days if needed, and a sale date that lands three to four and a half months after the bills reach the clerk.

If your house appears on the list, call the clerk before the date. Paying first keeps the lien out of an investor's hands.

Clearing tax when you sell

Learn the balance before you sign anything, and let the closing agent show it on the settlement statement.

  • This year's balance comes from the Sheriff at 270-726-2244.
  • Older years sit with the County Clerk at 270-726-6061, with monthly interest and fees stacked on top.
  • For an inherited or vacant house, check whose name the tax roll shows before you list it.

Many local sellers are heirs, landlords or owners of older farmhouses. Ask each office for a written payoff and the date it is good through, then give both to the title agent. The faster you learn the exact payoff, the faster you can work out what you will net. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval, so the payoff and title check are the main things left to schedule before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where does a Logan County owner send the property tax payment?

Send it to the Sheriff at 100 North Owen Street, Russellville, or use the link on the county's Sheriff page. Once April 15 passes, the bill shifts to the County Clerk at 229 West 3rd Street.

How big is the early-pay discount on a Logan County bill?

It is 2 percent, for payments made from October 1 through November 1. Face amount applies November 2 through year end, a 5 percent penalty starts in January, and 21 percent starts February 1.

Can I still dispute a Logan County assessment after the roll closes?

No. The dispute needs a PVA conference and a clerk filing by the workday after the inspection window ends. The window opens again in early May the following year.

Does the Logan County PVA set my tax rate or take payment?

Neither. The PVA only assesses value and handles exemptions. Rates come from local taxing bodies, and the Sheriff takes payment.

What if a Logan County tax bill is already delinquent?

Call the County Clerk at 270-726-6061 for a payoff figure. The bill carries a lien, monthly interest and fees, and can be sold at the clerk's tax sale if it stays open.

PVA, clerk and sheriff in Marshall County

Valuation and recording share one address, 1101 Main Street in Benton, where the PVA and the County Clerk keep offices. Collection of the bill belongs to the sheriff.

  • PVA: appraises property and takes exemption filings. The county directory shows 270-527-4767 as an alternate phone, with the office open on weekdays until 4:30.
  • Clerk: holds every land record in the county and collects delinquent property taxes. Call 270-527-4740.
  • Sheriff: collects county tax. A bill lookup and payment link sits on the sheriff's page at marshallcountyky.gov.

Tax collection is one job among several for the sheriff, whose deputies patrol about 300 square miles and more than 900 miles of road, work the lake with marine patrols, and provide court security.

A house inside Benton brings a second bill. City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677), collects Benton's own property tax, and the city's website cautions residents against using its link for county taxes.

Kentucky Lake and Marshall County real estate

Water explains most of Marshall County's modern history. The Tennessee River and Kentucky Lake form its northeastern border, and 39 of its 340 square miles are water. In the 1940s the Tennessee Valley Authority impounded Kentucky Lake. Fishing resorts followed, and low-cost power from Kentucky Dam brought chemical and manufacturing plants to Calvert City. The impoundment flooded Birmingham and Gilbertsville, and Gilbertsville was rebuilt west of its first site.

Benton, the seat, is the biggest of the county's three cities, with Calvert City and Hardin the others. Gilbertsville is a census-designated place, and Aurora, Draffenville, Fairdealing and Briensburg are unincorporated. Owners of lakeside or second-home parcels should ask the PVA for the property's classification and last inspection date.

Housing and population

Marshall County leans older: one resident in four is 65 or over. Owners live in 81.6 percent of homes. The 2020 census counted 31,659 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is the same figure.

Marshall County housing and cost figures

2026 bill schedule

Rates had to be finalized before the bills could be printed, so the Sheriff's Office set a collection start of November 1. The schedule it published:

  • November 1 to 30, 2026: two percent discount.
  • December 1 to 31, 2026: face amount due.
  • January 1 to 31, 2027: five percent penalty.
  • February 1 to April 15, 2027: ten percent penalty.

Such a shifted calendar is permitted by KRS 134.015(3), under which the Department of Revenue can swap in new dates when billing falls behind. In a normal year the two percent discount ends November 1, and the face amount is good through December.

Whatever the year, trust the dates printed on your own bill. When the cycle ends, open bills pass to the County Clerk, and the Department of Revenue says they then accrue one percent interest monthly.

Disputing a value that looks too high

Walk into the PVA's office and ask for a conference, the opening move in KRS 133.120. Still unconvinced? Put your reasons and your own fair-cash-value figure in a petition to the County Clerk no later than one workday after inspection ends, then prepare for the board hearing described in KRS 133.030.

  1. Gather neighborhood sales, an appraisal or construction costs.
  2. Attend yourself, or send someone with written authority.
  3. Keep paying on your own figure until the board decides.

An owner who bypasses the county board loses the later state appeal, so the petition deadline carries weight. Working farmland may qualify for agricultural-use valuation under Section 172A of the state constitution; ask the PVA about it.

Homestead exemption

Many owners qualify. About one resident in four is 65 or older, so the exemption touches a large share of homes. The $49,100 deduction for 2025 and 2026 comes off the assessed value. File with the Marshall County PVA, attaching proof of age or a disability classification. The benefit follows the owner, so a qualifying buyer files again.

Prices and buyers around the lake

Marshall County sellers fall into two groups: families selling a primary home, and owners letting go of lake or second-home property. The first group sells to local buyers, often from Benton and Calvert City, where the plants bring steady work. The second group draws buyers who want water access, so condition and the shoreline setting count for as much as square footage.

Because the median home value is $173,800 and building permits were only 86 in 2025, there is not a flood of new houses to compete with. Still, a seasonal property may have a different classification at the PVA than a full-time residence, and a buyer's lender will ask about it. Ask the PVA for the classification and the date of the last inspection before you list, and fix any mismatch in the owner name or mailing address on the roll so the next bill reaches the right person.

Working farmland may sell on its own terms. Section 172A of the state constitution allows agricultural-use valuation, so the tax figure a buyer sees may be lower than the price per acre would suggest. Share the actual bill with serious buyers rather than guessing.

Liens, deeds and closing

A delinquency lien may remain for eleven years under KRS 134.015(5), so any unpaid year has to be cleared by closing. Because the Marshall County Clerk handles delinquent property tax, prior-year payoffs come from that office (270-527-4740) and the current bill from the sheriff.

Deeds are recorded with the same clerk, who first collects the grantor's transfer tax of fifty cents per $500 of value under KRS 142.050. The clerk lists open hours of 8 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays, with 270-527-4741 as a second line and 270-527-4746 for the vault. The homepage also promotes protection against deed theft, which any seller should ask about after closing.

Plan the order of your errands. Get the current payoff from the sheriff and any earlier-year payoff from the clerk, hand both letters to the closing agent, and bring the signed deed to the clerk with the transfer tax. If the city of Benton bills your house too, ask City Hall for that balance as well, because it is a separate account. A cash sale skips the lender's schedule, so these payoffs are usually the last items between you and the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I look up my Marshall County tax bill?

Use the bill lookup and payment link on the Sheriff's page of the county website. For value or exemption questions, ask the PVA at 1101 Main Street in Benton.

Do Benton residents pay a separate city property tax?

Yes. The City of Benton collects it separately, at City Hall, 1009 Main Street (270-527-8677). Do not use the city's link for Marshall County taxes.

What was the Marshall County discount for 2026 bills?

Two percent on payments from November 1 through November 30, 2026. Face amount applied through December 2026.

Which Marshall County office collects delinquent taxes?

The County Clerk, at 1101 Main Street in Benton. Interest of one percent a month starts once bills reach the clerk.

What is the Marshall County homestead exemption worth?

It takes $49,100 off assessed value for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years, for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who apply at the PVA.

Where and how to pay the Sheriff

Payment happens at the Sheriff's Office inside the courthouse at 100 South Main Street, Greenville, from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. The number is 270-338-3345, and the mailing address is PO Box 227, Greenville, KY 42345.

  • Bills normally go out October 30, and collection opens November 1.
  • Online payment is possible. Telephone payment is not.
  • A drop box behind the courthouse, near the elevator entrance, takes payments outside office hours.
  • Only full payment is accepted, so a part payment doesn't count.

What the property is worth is a separate question for the county Property Valuation Administrator (PVA). Assessed values can change before they become final.

Payment windows and penalties

KRS 134.015 sets the order the sheriff posts: a discount first, then the printed amount, then penalties.

Muhlenberg County bill totals by month paid
Month paidResult for the owner
Whole of NovemberSubtract 2 percent
Whole of DecemberPay the printed total
Whole of JanuaryAdd 5 percent
February 1 through April 15Add 21 percent

In any month the sheriff wants the whole bill paid at once. After April 15 the county clerk handles delinquent bills, so a seller with an old unpaid year should call the clerk for the payoff.

What shapes the Muhlenberg County market

The county covers 479 square miles of western Kentucky, 467 of them land. The Green River and Lake Malone are its two main waters. Greenville is the seat, and Central City is the largest community. Coal built the local economy: Kentucky's first commercial coal mine opened here in 1820 along the Green River at Paradise. Surface coal has been stripped out, and what remains lies deep. The north is gentle hill country with river flats, and the south has higher relief, gorges and sandstone outcrops. Lake Malone State Park sits near Dunmor.

Listings therefore range widely, from town lots in Greenville and Central City to ground near the lake and parcels in old mining country. Lake Malone gives some listings a recreation draw, and the river flats and swamp ground along Cypress Creek can mean flood and drainage questions from lenders and insurers. Greenville's courthouse square and Central City's downtown anchor the two town markets, and each has its own feel for buyers. One school system operates under the Muhlenberg County Board of Education, and a single Muhlenberg County High School has served the county since June 2009.

Housing numbers

The population estimate for July 2025 is 30,634, which is 1.0% below the 2020 base, and 21.3% of residents are past 65. Home prices are modest, and so are tax bills.

  • 13,640 housing units in 2025, with just 5 building permits that year.
  • Owners occupy 78.8% of homes.
  • The midpoint for an owned house is $127,400.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,167 with a mortgage and $396 without.
  • Gross rent has a midpoint of $718.
  • Household income has a midpoint of $51,927.

About 88.7% of residents did not move in the prior year. With so few new permits, a buyer here mostly picks among houses that already exist. A receipt showing the year's bill paid is the quickest answer to a buyer's first question about taxes.

Services and records for heirs

Many calls come from heirs. Central City has a convention center with an outdoor pool and spray park, and Muhlenberg County Public Libraries runs the Thistle Cottage Genealogy and History Annex in Greenville, a useful stop for anyone tracing an old deed chain. Workers spend a mean of 27.0 minutes getting to their jobs, and employment rose 6.7% between 2022 and 2023.

How to contest a valuation

The PVA sets value as of January 1. Under KRS 133.120, the owner first meets the PVA or a deputy during the tax roll's 13-day public inspection in May, which KRS 133.045 schedules. An owner who is still unhappy files a written petition at the County Clerk's office, listing the parcel, the reasons and the proposed value, by the workday after inspection ends.

The board can deny a case when the owner won't hand over the value information it requests, so collect sales comparisons, an appraisal or repair estimates early. A filed appeal doesn't postpone the due date, because the bill stays payable on the normal schedule while the case proceeds. A taxpayer who never appears before the county board cannot reach the state Board of Tax Appeals afterward. Tax is paid on the owner's claimed value, with any increase billed later plus interest.

Homestead exemption

A Greenville or Central City owner aged 65 or more, or totally disabled, may deduct $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026. The application goes to the Muhlenberg County PVA, and a birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability filers renew annually unless they hold a service-connected rating or have been ruled permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

Before the deed is signed

Whoever held title on January 1 owes that year's tax personally. A delinquent bill places a lien on the parcel for up to eleven years under KRS 134.420, regardless of owner.

  • Find out from the sheriff if the current bill is paid, and when.
  • Write the split of the year's tax into the sales contract.
  • Put the buyer's mailing address for future bills on the deed, which KRS 382.135 requires.
  • When a deceased owner's heirs sell, the executor first files an affidavit with the county clerk naming recipients and values.

If the bill is already at the clerk, ask for a payoff dated near closing, since interest and fees keep building. A cash sale as-is lets an heir skip repairs and showings, and the tax is settled from the proceeds at the table.

Coal country and what buyers ask

Buyers ask about jobs, schools and commuting. Coal made this county one of the biggest producers in the country during most of the 1970s, and mining in the county and its neighbors began to grow again as the 2000s opened. The Greater Muhlenberg Chamber of Commerce formed in January 2006 when the Central City and Greenville chambers merged. Schools consolidated in steps, from eight secondary schools to two high schools in 1990 and then to one.

Land near Cypress Creek has bald cypress swamps, and the southern gorges and sandstone outcrops can affect access and building sites. A buyer may ask what is underground on an old mining parcel, so tell them what you know and point them to the PVA and clerk records. The county lies at the southern edge of the Evansville, Indiana television market, which is where many listings get advertised.

Steps to close a sale

Begin at the sheriff's counter and confirm the current bill is paid. Hold on to the receipt. After April 15, call the clerk for the payoff on any delinquent year. Next, call the PVA to confirm the parcel details and any homestead claim on file. Put the tax split in the sales contract, hand the closing agent a written payoff, and record the deed with the buyer's mailing address for future bills.

Heirs should gather the documents that prove who may sign before listing, because the affidavit with the clerk comes first. When a house needs work, a cash buyer who takes it as-is can close on a schedule that fits the payoff, and the seller skips repair bills and open houses.

Frequently asked questions

Is telephone payment accepted by the Muhlenberg County Sheriff?

No. Payment can be made online, mailed to PO Box 227, carried to 100 South Main Street, or left in the courthouse drop box.

May an owner send part of a Muhlenberg County bill?

No. The sheriff requires payment in full.

How long is the Muhlenberg County discount window?

All of November. The printed amount is due in December, and the penalty starts January 1.

What hours does the Muhlenberg County Sheriff keep?

The courthouse counter in Greenville is open weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 270-338-3345.

What is the Muhlenberg County deduction for seniors?

Once a 65-year-old or totally disabled owner applies at the PVA, $49,100 is taken off assessed value for 2025 and 2026.

Who does what with a tax bill

Four county offices share the job. The PVA, at (270) 343-4395, assigns each parcel its worth. The sheriff, at (270) 343-2191, takes the money. The clerk, at (270) 343-2125, picks up bills nobody paid in time. The county attorney, at (270) 343-2121, mails the warning letters that come before the clerk's sale of delinquent bills.

A complaint about the number belongs with the PVA, while a question about where to send a check belongs with the sheriff.

Russell County for a home seller

Jamestown holds the courthouse, and Russell Springs is the larger town at 2,715 residents in 2020. The whole county counts as rural. Lake Cumberland and the Cumberland Parkway draw buyers, and the lake's drawdown years from 2007 to 2014 still prompt questions from lakefront buyers. Clocks here run on Central time while neighboring counties to the east run on Eastern, so confirm the hour when a distant buyer or title office schedules your closing.

Homes are modest in price and the stock is loose. The July 2025 estimate is 18,608 people, up from 17,991 in April 2020. There are 7,562 households, and owners live in 70.8 percent of homes. A typical owner-occupied value is $163,200, typical gross rent is $681, and owner costs with a mortgage run $1,219 a month. Median household income is $44,738. The 2020 count listed 10,088 housing units, with 26.0 percent vacant. Only 5 building permits were issued in 2025, so you are not competing with new builds.

Seasonal cabins, inherited houses and homes several years behind on tax deserve a written payoff from the clerk before you list. Lakefront sellers can also ask the county surveyor for help when a shoreline line is in doubt.

Due dates and penalties

Kentucky's statutory calendar, KRS 134.015, governs here. Mail arrives in October, and the sheriff stays open for payment right up to April 15 of the next year.

Russell County: charge by payment date
Payment dateWhat you owe
On or before November 1Printed bill minus 2 percent
November 2 through December 31Printed amount, no change
JanuaryPrinted amount plus 5 percent
February 1 onwardPrinted amount plus 10 percent
After April 15Clerk handles the unpaid bill

The law makes the January 1 owner personally liable, so spell out in your sales contract who repays whom.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Russell County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens if a bill is still open on April 15?

Your sheriff hands it off to the clerk, who turns it into a certificate of delinquency with a lien recorded on the parcel. New owners inherit that lien. The clerk commits to a sale before August ends, advertised in the paper and online. Private buyers who register with the state may buy the certificate and then chase the owner for payment.

  • Amounts on the clerk's delinquent list move monthly, so ask for a fresh payoff figure.
  • Interest of 1 percent per month runs on the certificate, with clerk and attorney commissions on top.
  • A title search will surface the lien, so settle it ahead of closing.

Challenging the PVA's value

Begin with an informal talk at the PVA; a phone call counts. When that goes nowhere, a written petition goes to the clerk no later than the workday following the end of roll inspection. Bring listings, building costs or loan papers. The appeal does not freeze collection, so pay on your own claimed figure while it runs.

Homestead exemption

Two groups qualify: owners 65 and over, and owners classified as totally disabled. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 the state's deduction is $49,100. About 22.6 percent of residents are past 65, so many local owners will want it.

Apply at the PVA. Anyone claiming disability needs a federal or retirement-system classification, and most renew each year. The state changes the dollar amount now and then, so confirm this year's figure.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Russell County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What changes at the closing table

Closing agents usually pull the current bill and any delinquent payoff, so ask for both early. A bill open before April 15 sits with the sheriff, and after that date it sits with the clerk, plus extra charges.

A buyer who spots a lien in the title search will demand its removal or leave. Pair your listing with a clean paper trail: a current bill, a payoff letter if needed, and a plain answer on any back years. Several unpaid years on an inherited house can eat most of the equity, which is the situation where a direct cash sale appeals to owners who want the debt paid at closing without making repairs first.

A year in the life of a bill

Knowing the sequence helps you decide when to list. October brings the mailbox surprise. If you pay everything by November 1, you keep 2 percent. December 31 is the plain deadline. Wait until January and 5 percent lands on top, and from February 1 it becomes 10 percent. April 15 ends the sheriff's turn.

After that the bill moves to the clerk, interest begins at 1 percent monthly, and the sale comes before August is out. A seller who closes in spring should assume the prior year's bill is still in their name, even if the contract says the buyer reimburses part of it.

Steps for selling with a tax bill

Whatever your situation, this order keeps things tidy.

  1. Phone the sheriff, (270) 343-2191, and find out if this year's bill shows paid.
  2. An older year still open? The clerk, (270) 343-2125, quotes a payoff with interest and fees folded in.
  3. While the house is still yours, ask the PVA, (270) 343-4395, if you qualify for the homestead deduction.
  4. Disclose each open amount to the closing agent before anyone signs.
  5. Reconfirm the payoff a few days ahead, because delinquent amounts move monthly, and bring a photo ID and your deed to the closing office.

Sellers with a lakefront cabin that sits empty much of the year often miss mail. Give the sheriff a current mailing address so bills and county attorney letters actually reach you.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling for cash when taxes are behind

A direct cash buyer does not need a bank to approve the house, so a lien or old tax debt does not stall the deal the way it can with a mortgage buyer. The title company still finds the lien. The payoff is simply taken from your sale money when papers are signed, and you leave with the rest. For an inherited house with several years unpaid, that route can end the problem in one meeting. Ask the title company to show the payoff line on your settlement statement so you can see exactly what was paid and to whom.

Frequently asked questions

Where does a Russell County tax payment go?

The sheriff's office takes it, (270) 343-2191, until April 15 of the following year. Past that date the county clerk, (270) 343-2125, holds unpaid bills.

What does a late Russell County payment cost?

January adds five percent, and ten percent applies from February 1. When the bill reaches the clerk, interest of 1 percent a month starts, plus clerk and county attorney fees.

Will a Russell County tax lien follow a house into a sale?

Yes. The lien stays on the parcel until the tax is paid or the 11-year limit in KRS 134.420 runs out, no matter who owns it. Your title search will show it.

What month does the Russell County clerk hold the tax sale?

It is held before August ends, with newspaper and website notices beforehand. Ring the clerk's office, (270) 343-2125, for the exact date.

Is the Russell County homestead exemption automatic once I turn 65?

No, you have to apply. Bring proof of age or disability to the PVA. The deduction was $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, and most disability claims renew yearly.

Which office does what

Three desks in Taylorsville share the work. The Property Valuation Administration (PVA) sets each parcel's value, the sheriff bills and takes payment, and the clerk's office picks up what is left after April 15. The sheriff never sets a value.

  • PVA, (502) 477-3207: assessments, exemption forms and questions about why a number changed.
  • Sheriff, (502) 477-3200: mails bills on October 1 and collects for the state, county and school districts, plus some cities and special districts such as fire protection and libraries when contracted to.
  • County attorney, (502) 477-3225: handles overdue bills from 7 West Main Street and sits with the PVA when an appeal reaches the local board.
  • County clerk, 2 West Main Street: keeps the certificates of delinquency and takes payment on any that remain unsold.

If the bill looks wrong, call the PVA first, and the sooner the better.

Bring your parcel number or the address when you call or visit, and write down who you spoke with. Each office holds a different piece of the file, so a seller usually needs a short conversation with the sheriff, the PVA and the clerk before listing.

Spencer County housing market

Spencer County sits in the Louisville metro area, borders Jefferson County to the northwest, and has Taylorsville as its seat. Taylorsville Lake, mostly inside the county line, is a leading local draw. The county has grown fast: 11,766 people in 2000, 17,061 in 2010, 19,490 in 2020 and 20,998 estimated for July 2025.

It is a commuter county. The average trip to work is 32.7 minutes, and most buyers earn their pay elsewhere in the metro area. Because nearly nine in ten homes are owner occupied, most sales here are one family selling to another.

Monthly cost of owning

Owning here costs more than in much of Kentucky. Typical monthly outlay is $1,795 for owners carrying a mortgage and $532 for those who own free and clear. Households average 2.75 people, and 91.6 percent stayed in the same home during the last year. Only 4.1 percent of the 7,430 housing units tallied in 2020 sat empty, so homes tend to sell to buyers who plan to stay.

Seniors make up 18.1 percent of residents, a group that can use the homestead break covered below. Ask the sheriff for the exact bill on your parcel instead of estimating from the county median.

Due dates and late charges

Bills carry a December 31 due date and go in the mail on October 1. The cost of timing is set by the collection statute:

  • Through November 1, pay 2 percent under the printed amount.
  • November 2 to December 31 is the printed amount, no more and no less.
  • January adds a 5 percent surcharge.
  • From February 1, the surcharge climbs to 10 percent and the sheriff's add-on fee joins it. The February to April 15 stretch carries a 21 percent penalty overall.

Escrow does not remove the need to look. The bill explains what to do when a mortgage company pays, and the sheriff's online lookup will show whether the lender actually sent the money before January begins.

When a bill goes delinquent

Anything unpaid at the April 15 cutoff goes to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency, and KRS 134.122 puts a lien on the real estate. The bill is also the personal obligation of the January 1 owner, with interest at 12 percent a year. Ninety days later, outside investors may buy it. The first offering is usually held in August or September.

Two things stop a sale: a payment agreement with the county attorney, or a foreclosure or bankruptcy case in which the county attorney is a party. The office also tries to reach the owner by regular mail ahead of any sale.

  • Still with the county: pay the full balance and accrued interest at the clerk's office, 2 West Main Street.
  • Already purchased: deal with the investor, who may tack on substantial administrative costs.
  • Payment plans: usually 4 to 8 months, and they must end before the next bill is due. Apply by the online form, by phone, or at 7 West Main Street, where an appointment shortens the wait. Sold certificates are not eligible.

How to contest your assessment

Book a conference with the PVA first, because the process cannot begin anywhere else. After that meeting, the written appeal is filed at the clerk's office during the May window for viewing the roll, with a one-workday grace period at the end. A board of local owners then hears it about a month later.

The board wants paper: closed sales near you, an appraisal, a contractor's repair quote, an insurance declaration. If you bring none, it denies the appeal. A bill printed early uses your claimed figure, and a supplemental bill follows if the board lands higher. Ask the PVA which home sales it used for yours. That list is the fastest way to test the comparison, and parcels are physically reviewed at least every fourth year.

Homestead exemption

Owners past their 65th birthday, along with owners on a total-disability classification, can knock a fixed amount off the assessed value of the house they live in. The Department of Revenue put that amount at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. File Form 62A350 with the Spencer County PVA by December 31. An approved application carries forward while the applicant stays in the home, and a buyer must file a fresh one.

Selling with taxes owed

Under KRS 134.015, a delinquent bill is the January 1 owner's own debt, and its lien can outlast a change of ownership for up to eleven years. Buyers and title companies look for zero balances. Ask the sheriff for this year's payoff, then ask the clerk if any certificate exists and whether an investor bought it.

When a payment agreement with the county attorney is active, say so up front so the closing agent can include the remaining balance.

A practical order of work helps. Get the sheriff's written payoff. Visit or call the clerk at 2 West Main Street about older years. Call the county attorney at (502) 477-3225 if a plan is in place. Then hand all three to whoever runs the closing. A cash buyer can take the house with the balance paid from proceeds, and you avoid the wait that comes with a buyer's lender.

Frequently asked questions

Who takes payment on a Spencer County bill?

The sheriff's office does, at (502) 477-3200. Look up the current bill on the sheriff's website, under the Property Taxes tab.

What changes once the April 15 cutoff passes in Spencer County?

The clerk takes over, a lien is recorded, and interest begins at 12 percent a year. After 90 more days an investor may buy the certificate, so call the county attorney before that point.

Does the Spencer County attorney offer payment plans?

Yes, for certificates that have not been sold. Plans generally last 4 to 8 months and must finish before the next bill is due. Call (502) 477-3225.

How big is the Spencer County homestead exemption?

The deduction is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period. Owners file with the PVA before the calendar year ends.

Can I list a Spencer County house that has past-due tax?

Yes. The balance is settled out of the sale, since the lien does not lift until it is paid. Line up written figures from the sheriff and clerk first.

Which offices deal with a Whitley County tax bill?

Whitley County splits the job three ways. The valuation administrator, called the PVA, sets each parcel's value, the sheriff mails and collects the bill, and the county clerk handles whatever is still open in spring. Call Property Valuation at (606) 549-6008 or 6009 and the sheriff at (606) 549-6006 or 6007. County offices share the courthouse at 200 Main Street, Williamsburg, and the sheriff's site has a bill lookup. The lookup opens your bill in a pop-up window, so switch off your browser's pop-up blocker before you search.

Housing market snapshot

Home prices run low here. The middle owned home is valued at $131,800, and the typical household brings in $44,615 a year. About two in three households own their homes, and the county's 2025 estimate of 37,297 residents is 1.6 percent above 2020. Williamsburg is the seat and Corbin is the biggest city, reaching into Knox and Laurel counties.

  • Housing units on the July 2025 count: 15,904.
  • Typical rent: $798 a month.
  • Monthly costs for owners: $1,156 with a mortgage, $346 without.
  • Permits for new homes in 2025: only 52.

With so few new homes going up, a seller mostly competes with other resales. Corbin and Williamsburg are the two places with retail alcohol sales, and the county is otherwise classed as moist. The University of the Cumberlands is in Williamsburg.

What happens when a Whitley County bill goes unpaid

The state schedule in KRS 134.015 runs from a 2 percent discount by November 1 to a 10 percent penalty after January. The person who held title on January 1 is personally liable for that year's bill, so closing in spring does not wipe it out.

When the sheriff is still unpaid on April 15, the clerk receives the bill, records a lien and files it as a delinquency certificate. Interest of 1 percent then builds every month, the clerk tacks on 10 percent, and the county attorney tacks on 20 percent. Any later owner inherits a lien that can last 11 years.

Whitley's clerk then sells the debt to private buyers in a September sale. Terms for the 2025 bills are in the table.

Whitley County Clerk terms for the 2025 tax bill sale
Sale termRule
Time and place9:00 a.m., courthouse Room 2
FormatLottery, up to three bills per buyer
Registration fee$10 per certificate, capped at $250 for 25 or more
Deposit25 percent of the certificates listed

The clerk takes no payments on the morning of the sale. Whoever buys your certificate collects from you and may add fees. Call the clerk for the date of the next sale.

Buyers with a stake in an earlier year can file a priority list, which needs a $5 fee per certificate and a deposit of the full price, and every certificate carries a $30 filing charge. Enrolling with the state revenue department is also required for a buyer seeking more than three certificates in the county, more than five statewide or more than $10,000 worth. A seller with a delinquent parcel should clear it with the clerk before the sale date, because paying off the lien is cheaper than paying a buyer who tacks on fees.

How to contest a Whitley County assessment

Kentucky bars an appeal unless you meet the PVA first. Values are set as of January 1, and the public viewing runs 13 days from the first May Monday, so schedule your meeting inside that stretch.

After that, file with the County Clerk by the next workday. A local board hears the case 25 to 35 days later and dismisses anything that comes without proof.

  • Recent sales of nearby houses like yours.
  • Photos and repair quotes where the house has defects the record misses.
  • Insurance or construction cost papers.

Before you file, ask which sales the PVA used on your parcel.

Homestead exemption

Homeowners at least 65 years old, and the totally disabled, take a set amount off the assessed value of their own residence. A couple gets one deduction. Turn in form 62A350 at the PVA office; an approved claim carries forward while the same owner stays. A buyer must apply again, and the PVA can quote the current deduction, which the state resets every two years.

If you are selling, mention it to your buyer early. Someone who qualifies will want to visit the PVA after closing, and the exemption is not something that transfers with the deed.

How the tax year runs for a Whitley County owner

Ownership on January 1 decides who is billed. The sheriff mails bills in the fall. Pay it all by November 1 for the 2 percent discount, expect the printed figure until year end, and plan on a 10 percent penalty once January is over. Each May the public viewing period gives you a window to question a value.

Listing in winter or spring? Check with the sheriff on whether this year's bill is settled and what any penalty has added. A balance that has reached the clerk carries a lien, interest each month, and the clerk's and county attorney's percentages. Paying it before the September sale keeps a private buyer out of the picture.

For the assessment, ring Property Valuation at (606) 549-6008 or 6009. For the amount owed, ring the sheriff at (606) 549-6006 or 6007. Having both numbers in hand before you list keeps the closing from stalling.

What a Whitley County seller should confirm before closing

Think of the tax as one more payoff, alongside any mortgage. It should be settled on paper before you hand over keys. Your title company requests balances from the sheriff and the clerk, and each is deducted from your proceeds.

  • Match the name on the bill to the deed.
  • Look for a bill on a garage, mobile home or other addition missing from earlier rolls.
  • On an inherited house, check whether the bill was mailed to someone who has died.
  • Ask the clerk if an earlier year was sold to a private buyer.

Get each balance in writing so the payoff matches the closing statement.

One more habit helps: keep copies of the paid bills for the years you owned the house, and bring them to the title company. If a record is missing from the sheriff's lookup or the clerk's list, the paper receipt settles it quickly.

A cash sale can handle a messy tax history without much delay. If a certificate has already gone to a private buyer, the payoff comes from that buyer instead of the clerk, and it includes the buyer's fees. Have the title company request that figure early, so nothing surprises you at the table.

Frequently asked questions

Where does a Whitley County owner send the tax payment?

To the sheriff, whose site offers an online lookup and whose office is at (606) 549-6006 or 6007. After April 15 the bill sits with the County Clerk.

Is it too late to pay a Whitley County bill after January?

No, but the cost rises. A 10 percent penalty applies after January, and after April 15 monthly interest and commissions come on top.

Can a Whitley County owner sell with a delinquent bill?

Yes. The title company gets the figures from the sheriff and clerk, and the balance is subtracted from what you receive. The lien stays until it is cleared.

When must a Whitley County assessment appeal be filed?

No later than the workday after the roll inspection ends. The roll opens for 13 days beginning the first May Monday, and you must meet the PVA before filing.

Which Whitley County office answers valuation questions?

Property Valuation, at (606) 549-6008 or 6009. The sheriff covers the amount due, and the clerk covers delinquent bills.
