Who values property and collects tax in Graves County

Two county offices share the work in Graves County, with a third stepping in later. The PVA appraises land and buildings. It does not set rates and does not take payments. Payments belong at the sheriff's counter, and a bill left unpaid past mid-April is turned over to the County Clerk.

Both the PVA and the Clerk operate from 1102 Paris Road in Mayfield, the PVA in Suite 2 at (270) 247-3301 and the Clerk in Suite 5, where the delinquent real estate tax line is (270) 247-1697. Each office keeps hours of eight to four-thirty. The sheriff keeps the same schedule on Central Time and accepts mailed checks, walk-in payments and online card payments. Cash, check and card are all taken at the counter. The sheriff cannot edit a bill's mailing address, because the PVA keeps that record.

Before you list, pull up your parcel there and read the owner name, acreage and any exemption flags. A mismatch with your deed is easier to fix before a buyer's title search finds it, and the PVA can correct the record.

Parcel data can be searched on the qPublic site that the sheriff's tax page recommends for Graves County records.

When bills go out and what if one never arrives

The sheriff starts taking payment on October 1 of the assessment year. If your bill has not turned up by October 10, request a duplicate, which you can collect at the sheriff's office or print from its website.

Bill addresses come from the PVA, not the sheriff. Anything changed after June misses the tax roll for that year, so a seller who moved over the summer may find the bill sitting at the old mailbox.

KRS 134.015 supplies the discount and penalty steps used everywhere in the state. Pay in full by November 1 and keep two percent. The bill sits at face value through the end of the year. January adds five percent, and later payments add ten. The January 1 owner is personally liable for that year's tax, so a buyer who closes in July or October should put the sharing arrangement on paper.

How to contest your assessment

Nothing can be filed until you have talked with the PVA's staff. The roll goes on public display for 13 days beginning in early May.

  • Ask for a PVA conference in or before that display window, and bring questions about how the number was built.
  • Get the appeal form to the Clerk's counter before it closes on the first workday after the display.
  • Assemble comparables, listings, photos of defects, insurance papers and building costs.
  • Make your case to the local appeals board, which sits about a month after the display and explains any change it makes.

Taxpayers may record the hearing on audio. A no-show after filing closes the door on the Kentucky Claims Commission.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Graves County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption

People who have turned 65, and people who are totally disabled, can knock $49,100 off the assessment for 2025-2026.

Exemptions are never granted on their own. Paperwork goes to the PVA first. Disabled applicants need to have been drawing disability benefits for the entire assessment period, and most must reapply every year.

The deduction follows the resident owner, so a buyer who qualifies files a fresh application.

What happens to a bill after April 15

At the close of April 15, the sheriff passes every unpaid bill to the County Clerk. The paper becomes a certificate of delinquency, and the Clerk records a lien on the parcel. Prior-year taxes cannot be collected at the sheriff's office after the transfer.

Notice and sale steps after transfer on a regular schedule
StepTiming
First attorney notice mailedWithin a month of transfer
Second notice naming the sale date20 or more days later, and inside 60 days
Published list of delinquent bills30 to 45 days ahead of the sale
Public saleBetween day 90 and day 135

From the day of transfer, one percent a month accrues, and the Clerk and the county attorney each take a commission. The amount owed climbs with each step, and it is lowest on the day of transfer. After the sale, a third-party certificate holder collects instead of the county.

Handling taxes at a Graves County closing

Say in the contract who pays the current year's bill. Dividing the year between seller and buyer is a private matter, since the sheriff bills only the January 1 owner. Ask the sheriff or Clerk for a payoff ahead of closing.

  • Ask the Clerk's delinquent line whether any earlier year is open, since that lien outlasts the sale.
  • Include the buyer's in-care-of address in the deed, which KRS 382.135 demands.
  • Confirm owner name and acreage on the qPublic record against the deed.

The deed also triggers a transfer tax payable by the seller, collected by the Clerk at filing.

On closing day, the title company usually carries the deed to the Clerk, pays the recording fee and tax, and sends the payoff for any open bill from your proceeds. Ask for a closing statement that lists each tax line separately, so you can see what went to the sheriff and what went to the Clerk.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Graves County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling after the 2021 tornado

On December 10, 2021, a long-track tornado went through the county and caused widespread damage in Mayfield. The Graves County Courthouse was among the buildings hit hard. Owners rebuilding or clearing a lot should ask the PVA how destroyed or rebuilt structures are valued as of each January 1.

Rebuilt property gets a new value, so a seller of a rebuilt house should expect the assessment to change and should bring building costs and photos if a conference is needed. Cash purchasers do buy storm-damaged or half-finished houses as they stand, and the new deed is still filed at the Clerk's office on Paris Road.

Graves County housing market

Mayfield is the county seat, with Wingo the only other city, and the county sits at the state's southwestern edge in the Jackson Purchase. Population is 37,050, up 1.1 percent from 2020, across 14,139 households. Owners occupy 76.1 percent of homes. Median home value is $147,800 against median gross rent of $775, and 83 new-home permits were issued for 2025.

With so few permits against more than 14,000 households, most sales here are resales, and clear title and condition matter to buyers. A seller with a back tax balance, an open mortgage release or a damaged house can price in the extra time a conventional sale needs, or consider a cash buyer who closes as-is and pays the lien from the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Where do Graves County property taxes get paid?

The Graves County Sheriff's Office handles current-year bills by mail, at the counter and online. After April 15, the County Clerk handles whatever is open.

What if my Graves County tax bill did not come in the mail?

Request a duplicate from the sheriff if nothing has arrived by October 10. Addresses come from the PVA, and changes made after June are left out of that year's bills.

Does the Graves County homestead exemption apply on its own?

No. A written application to the PVA comes first, at (270) 247-3301, and the $49,100 deduction follows only for owners who have turned 65 or are totally disabled.

When does a Graves County bill move to the County Clerk?

On April 15, at closing time. The Clerk records a lien, the bill is relabeled a certificate of delinquency, and interest starts at one percent monthly.

Can I sell a Graves County house that has unpaid taxes?

Yes. The buyer's title company pays the lien out of the proceeds, so call the Clerk's delinquent line at (270) 247-1697 for the figure.

Who sends the bill and who answers questions

Almost every LaRue County tax office sits inside the courthouse complex on West High Street in Hodgenville, and Hodgenville homeowners get a second bill from City Hall. The sheriff sends and collects the county bill, the PVA sets the value, the clerk takes in bills left unpaid, and the county attorney works on delinquent ones.

  • Sheriff's Office. 209 West High Street, Suite 6; open weekdays from morning until four; (270) 358-3120.
  • Property valuation administrator. Value, exemptions and appeal conferences; (270) 358-4202.
  • County clerk. Suite 3 at the same address; open until 4:30 on weekdays; (270) 358-3544.
  • County attorney. Suite 8; (270) 358-9223.
  • Hodgenville City Hall. 200 S. Lincoln Blvd.; (270) 358-3832 for the city bill.

Call the PVA before paying when a figure looks off. The sheriff collects whatever amount the bill shows and has no say over value.

LaRue County housing at a glance

LaRue is a rural county of gentle hills just outside the Bluegrass, with Hodgenville as the seat. It grew from 14,867 residents in 2020 to an estimated 15,184 in July 2025 and holds 6,763 housing units. The median home value among owner-occupants is $183,500, and 79.4 percent of the 5,996 households own. Median rent is $860. Higher values mean larger tax bills at the same rate, which makes a clean payoff worth the effort before listing. LaRue is also a dry county, which matters to anyone selling a building for restaurant use.

Due dates and discounts

The county attorney's office says bills typically mail in October, carry a December 31 due date, and can be paid at the sheriff's desk from November 1 through April 15. The 2026 bills went out on October 30, 2026, and the city bills were mailed around the same time.

Payment steps for 2026 LaRue County bills
Paid betweenAmount owed
Nov. 1 to Nov. 30, 20262% discount off the bill
Dec. 1 to Dec. 31, 2026Exactly the bill amount
Jan. 1 to Jan. 31, 2027Bill amount with 5% added
Feb. 1, 2027 onwardBill amount with 10% added, plus a possible 11% sheriff's fee on county bills

A card payment online adds a 2.5 percent fee. Inside the courthouse foyer, a drop box takes payments at any hour. By mail, enclose the bill or its number, plus a stamped return envelope if you want a receipt. These steps are reset each year, so check the bill itself.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Larue County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Is there a separate Hodgenville city tax bill?

Yes. A parcel inside the city gets a county bill from the sheriff and a city bill from City Hall, and the two are paid in different places. City payments go to City Hall, the city website or the city drop box, and the same November 30 cutoff earns the 2 percent discount. A parcel outside the city limits gets only the county bill.

When you buy or sell in Hodgenville, ask the closing agent to confirm that both bills are paid or prorated. The sheriff's office also has a fire dues waiver form. The online portal cannot remove fire dues, so an owner seeking a waiver files it at the sheriff's office.

How to appeal your assessment

Ask the PVA, at (270) 358-4202, for a conference. Kentucky requires one before any appeal. The valuation date is January 1, and the tax roll opens for inspection in early May. After that conference the appeal goes to the county clerk right after the inspection period ends, and a board of local property owners hears it within weeks.

The board denies a case that arrives without evidence, so assemble recent sales of similar homes, an appraisal, repair bids or insurance values. The county attorney's office helps the PVA with assessment appeals.

What happens to an unpaid bill

A bill still open on April 15 passes to the clerk as a certificate of delinquency, which is a lien on the real estate under KRS 134.122. Whoever owned the property on January 1 of that tax year also owes the bill personally. Penalties and fees are added, and interest at 12 percent a year under KRS 134.125 makes the total rise every month.

  • The county attorney mails two notices before any certificate is sold.
  • After 90 days, KRS 134.452 lets outside buyers purchase it by paying the amount due.
  • The first batch of certificates is usually offered at a tax bill sale in August.
  • An unsold certificate is paid at the clerk's office, Suite 3, 209 W. High Street.
  • A certificate that has been sold must be paid to the buyer.

A certificate cannot be sold while a payment agreement with the county attorney is in place or while the parcel is tied up in foreclosure or bankruptcy litigation that includes that office. The county attorney arranges payment plans on unsold certificates at (270) 358-9223.

Homestead exemption

The state set the deduction at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. It is available to owners who have reached 65 or who are totally disabled under a retirement system, for a home they own and occupy on January 1. Apply to the PVA, (270) 358-4202, by the end of December.

The deduction lowers assessed value, so the savings depend on the combined county, school, city and district rates on your parcel. Heirs who take over a house should ask the PVA what changes once the title moves.

Who pays what when a house changes hands

The January 1 owner is the person on that year's bill, so a spring closing still leaves the seller named. The settlement statement usually divides the year, and the closing agent pays the sheriff. The deed must carry an in-care-of address for the transfer-year bill under KRS 382.135(1)(d), which means giving the buyer's mailing address.

Before listing a LaRue County house with back taxes, collect two numbers: the current-year amount from the sheriff and any delinquent certificate balance from the clerk. Houses that were inherited, behind on payments or too worn for a standard listing can often close faster in a direct cash sale, and the payoffs come out of that one closing as long as they were requested ahead of time.

Paying at the courthouse: a short checklist

Walk-in payments go to Suite 6 at 209 West High Street. Bring the bill, or at least the bill number, so the clerk behind the desk can pull the right parcel. If you live in Hodgenville, plan on two stops or two payments, since City Hall takes the city bill at 200 S. Lincoln Blvd. Keep both receipts with your closing file.

If you are selling, call the sheriff and the clerk before you set a closing date. Ask for the current-year amount, ask whether any certificate is open, and ask how long each figure stays good. A written payoff from each office lets the title company work from real numbers instead of estimates, and it keeps a late discovery from pushing your sale back.

Frequently asked questions

Who takes LaRue County property tax payments?

The sheriff's office at 209 West High Street, Suite 6, by mail, online or in the courthouse drop box. Hodgenville city bills go to City Hall at 200 S. Lincoln Blvd.

When does the 2026 LaRue County discount end?

Payments made through November 30, 2026 earn a 2% discount. December 1 through 31 requires the face amount, January 2027 adds 5%, and after that the penalty is 10%.

How fast does a late LaRue County bill grow?

After April 15 it becomes a certificate of delinquency that earns 12 percent interest a year, plus penalties and fees. The county attorney can discuss a plan if the certificate is unsold.

Where do I sign up for the LaRue County homestead exemption?

At the PVA, (270) 358-4202, before December 31. Qualifying owners are 65 or older, or totally disabled under a retirement system, and must own and occupy the home on January 1.

May I sell a LaRue County house while taxes are overdue?

Yes. The lien stays on the parcel, so the payoff is deducted at closing. Get written amounts from the sheriff and the clerk before picking a date.

Selling in Marion County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Marion County?
We buy Marion County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Tax offices at 223 North Spalding Avenue

Lebanon's county government offices for taxes sit under one address, 223 North Spalding Avenue, so a Marion County owner can finish most paperwork in a single trip. Suite numbers tell you where to go.

  • Sheriff's Office, Suite 101 (270-692-3051): bills and payments, weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30.
  • Property Valuation Administrator, Suite 202 (270-692-3401): value, name and address changes, and exemption filings, on those same weekday hours.
  • County Clerk, Suite 102 (270-692-2651): deed recording and delinquent bills. The clerk's own site lists 8:20 to 4:20 on weekdays and a Saturday morning session.

Questions about value or how a bill was figured get routed to the PVA. Anyone asking about delinquent bills, or about buying a lien, is sent to the clerk.

The Marion County housing picture

Marion County is thinly settled, with roughly 57 people per square mile on 343 square miles of land. Lebanon, the seat, is the largest of three cities, followed by Loretto and Bradfordsville. One school district, Marion County Schools, serves every address.

A century of slow growth left the population at 19,820 in 2010 and 19,581 in 2020. The July 2025 estimate of 20,115 is 2.8 percent above the 2020 base. The county has 8,652 housing units and 7,724 households. Owners occupy 77.7 percent of homes, and over nine in ten people lived at the same address a year earlier. The median home value is $168,100, median gross rent is $726, and owners with a mortgage pay a median of $1,243 a month. Only 56 building permits were issued in 2025, which leaves resale listings with little new competition.

Selling a farm adds a twist. Section 172A of the state constitution values crop and pasture land by its yield. Outbuildings and fencing are priced at replacement cost less wear. Before you set an asking price on a farm, have the PVA tell you how each acre is classed.

Due dates and penalties

The sheriff mails statements ahead of October 1. If nothing has arrived by October 10, call the office and ask for a duplicate.

Marion County sheriff collection calendar
Payment windowWhat you pay
Oct. 1 through Nov. 1Face amount minus two percent
Nov. 2 through Dec. 31Face amount
All of JanuaryFive percent added
Feb. 1 through Apr. 15Twenty-one percent added
After Apr. 15Balance goes to the clerk

Anything unpaid on April 16 moves to the County Clerk. The twenty-one percent combines the ten percent penalty of KRS 134.015 to the sheriff's collection add-on.

Write the bill number on a mailed check, and enclose a stamped return envelope if you want a receipt. Card payments are taken only at the counter, with the card company's fee charged to you. Partial payments are not tracked by the sheriff's system, so pay the full amount in one go.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Marion County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who pays when the house sells

That year's bill carries the name of the January 1 owner. Once the house sells, the sheriff expects the seller to forward the bill to the buyer, and a buyer who never got one can request a copy from the office. The office carries no responsibility when a bill is missed during a closing.

No copy goes to the mortgage servicer. The homeowner gets each bill and has to pass it to the lender in time.

For earlier years, call the clerk at 270-692-2651. Overdue bills are transferred there, and the clerk's site advertises a free Online Deed Room. KRS 134.420 lets a tax lien stay on the land for eleven years, so a title company will insist that it be paid from the seller's proceeds.

Disputing the PVA's value

Call 270-692-3401 and ask for a conference. The meeting is the required first step of any appeal under state law, and KRS 133.120 then sends an unresolved case to the clerk as a written petition and on to a hearing. KRS 133.030 opens that hearing between 25 and 35 days after inspection wraps up.

PVA staff are expected to inspect every Marion County parcel in person within four years, so ask when yours was last visited. Appraisals and nearby sales carry weight. Payment stays due on the amount you claim.

Before the meeting, gather what a stranger would need to agree with you: photos of the house, an appraisal if you have one, repair estimates, and the prices of nearby homes that sold. Write down the value you think is fair and be ready to explain how you reached it. If the sit-down does not change the number, the petition to the clerk is your next step, and the clerk will tell you when the hearing is set.

Homestead exemption

For 2025 and 2026 the exemption takes $49,100 off assessed value. The PVA takes applications from owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who live in the house. About 19.5 percent of Marion County residents are 65 or older, so the exemption reaches a sizable share of owners. It stays with the owner, so a buyer applies separately. Take proof of age or a disability classification with you, and ask what else the office needs so one visit is enough. After a mid-year sale, let the PVA know so the exemption comes off the house you no longer own.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Marion County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording a deed at the clerk's counter

The clerk first collects the grantor's transfer tax, which KRS 142.050 sets at fifty cents for every $500 of value or part of $500. Taxes paid at the clerk's counter can use cash, check, debit or credit card, and the clerk's site warns that cards carry extra fees. No tax is due on foreclosure sales, on transfers between spouses in a divorce, or on a parent's deed to a child for token payment.

Steps for a seller with a tax question

Begin at the sheriff's counter in Suite 101 and ask if this year's bill is paid. Then walk down the hall to the clerk in Suite 102 and ask whether any earlier year was transferred there. Finish at the PVA in Suite 202, where you can check the owner name, mailing address and any exemption on the roll.

Request each balance in writing along with the date it is good through, because interest and penalties shift the figure as weeks pass. The title agent takes those letters and pays every amount from your proceeds at closing. Cash deals can move fast, so get the payoff papers ready before you accept an offer.

If you inherited the property, check whose name the roll shows, and bring proof of your authority to act for the estate. The office will not guess who should receive a bill, so a name change on the roll keeps statements from going astray before the sale.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Marion County Sheriff's tax office?

Go to 223 North Spalding Avenue, Suite 101, in Lebanon, or phone 270-692-3051. Put the bill number on any payment you mail.

How much extra does a Marion County bill cost in February?

Twenty-one percent is added between February 1 and April 15, following 5 percent in January. A bill still open on April 16 moves to the clerk.

Does the Marion County sheriff accept partial tax payments?

No. The sheriff's system does not track partial payments, so send the full bill in one payment.

Which office handles Marion County exemptions?

The PVA, reachable at 270-692-3401. Homestead and disability questions get sent there by the sheriff.

Where do I look up a Marion County delinquent bill?

Phone the County Clerk, 270-692-2651, since overdue bills are transferred to that office. Its website also offers a free Online Deed Room.

Pendleton County, KY Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Pendleton County, KY Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Pendleton County, KY Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Pendleton County, KY Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Pendleton County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Pendleton County?

Three Falmouth offices that touch a sale

A sale involves three offices in Falmouth. Bills come from the sheriff, values come from the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA), and the deed goes to the county clerk, who also takes over any bill that turns delinquent. The county's website links to the PVA's own page for parcel lookups and exemption forms.

  • Sheriff: 202 Chapel Street, with tax calls taken at 859-654-4511.
  • County Clerk: Room 1 at 233 Main Street, box 112, Falmouth 41040, telephone 859-654-3380. Weekday service runs 8:30 to 4:00. Saturday service falls on the second and last Saturday of a month, 8:30 until noon, except around holidays.
  • Planning and Zoning: answers for Falmouth and the unincorporated county on floodplains, addresses, code enforcement and plan review.

Only the owner is mailed a statement. Lenders are not on the list, so if your taxes are escrowed, check with the servicer about its copy.

Pendleton County housing in brief

Rural and small, Pendleton County counted 14,800 residents in mid-2025, a gain of about 1.1 percent over April 2020. Falmouth is the seat, with Butler about ten miles north on the Licking River.

  • Housing stock totals 6,341 units, and 74.7 percent of homes are owner-occupied.
  • An owner-occupied house has a midpoint value of $159,800, against $793 for gross rent.
  • Owners pay $1,172 a month with a mortgage and $475 without one.
  • Typical household income is $64,669, and the typical trip to work takes 36.4 minutes.

Zero building permits were logged for 2025, so a buyer here is almost always buying an older house. Because the planning office handles floodplain rules, a house near the Licking should have its flood zone confirmed before listing.

Due dates, discounts and penalties

Statements go out around the end of September, in plain envelopes with blue lettering reading "Pendleton County Tax Statement." The sheriff asks owners still waiting around October 12 to call. Payment is taken in cash, by check, or on a debit or credit card, though cards add a convenience fee and American Express is refused.

Pendleton County Sheriff payment schedule
Payment madeSheriff's posted rule
During October, through November 12% discount
November 2 until the year endsFace amount
All of January5% penalty
February 1 to April 1521% added

Counter service stops on county and state holidays and the weekends beside them, such as Thanksgiving week, Christmas week, New Year's, Martin Luther King Day and the afternoon of Good Friday. A drop box at the front door is watched on video. If you leave a check, tuck in the stub torn from the top of your bill plus a phone number, and add a stamped return envelope if you want a receipt. Leave cash out of it.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Pendleton County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Appeals and the homestead exemption

Any dispute begins with a sit-down at the PVA, either with the office or a deputy. If that fails, file at the clerk's office no later than the workday after public inspection of the roll wraps up. Inspection opens the first Monday of May and runs thirteen days. The board decides on documents, so bring insurance policies, what the house cost to build and comparable listings.

Owners aged 65 and up, plus anyone classified as totally disabled, qualify for the homestead exemption, worth $49,100 off assessed value in the 2025 and 2026 years. The PVA hands out the application.

Selling with unpaid tax

A delinquent bill becomes a lien that survives a sale, and KRS 134.015(5) lets it last up to eleven years. The closing title search turns it up, and the payoff comes out of the seller's proceeds.

Once April 15 is behind you, the clerk takes over the bill. Interest builds at one percent every month, and Revenue tacks on a clerk charge of 10 percent and an attorney charge of 20 percent. Advertised delinquent bills are posted through a link on the clerk's site. If you are behind, get a written payoff from the clerk before you sign a sales contract. Should an outside investor buy the certificate first, you owe that investor, with more fees added.

What the seller pays the County Clerk at closing

The grantor owes the state fifty cents on each $500 of declared value (KRS 142.050), paid to the clerk ahead of recording.

  • A deed is $50.00 to record, with $3.00 more per page beyond five.
  • A mortgage is $80.00, and releasing one is $46.00.
  • A deed needs a sworn consideration statement from both parties, plus an address where the next tax bill can be sent (KRS 382.135).
  • Transfers between spouses and foreclosure deeds are among the exempt ones.

Fees can shift a little, so ring 859-654-3380 for an exact figure ahead of closing. Then check two things: with the sheriff, whether this year's bill is settled, and with the clerk, whether a delinquent certificate is attached to the parcel. The title company needs the actual tax statement to work out the proration.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pendleton County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who gets the bill if the house sells midyear?

Each year's value and owner are locked in on January 1. The statement therefore goes to whoever held the house that day, so someone who closes in spring or summer still gets that year's bill. The common fix is a proration at closing, where the buyer repays the seller for the months after the sale and the title company uses the real bill. Hand the statement over early, and give the closing agent the sheriff's number in case a payment has not posted yet.

With escrow, the lender is not on the mailing list. Ask the servicer for its copy of the statement and a record of payments, so the proration rests on real figures.

A short seller timeline

  1. Phone the sheriff, 859-654-4511, to confirm this year is paid and nothing older remains.
  2. Ask the clerk, 859-654-3380, if any certificate or lien is on record.
  3. If the house is near the Licking, have Planning and Zoning confirm its flood zone.
  4. Gather the tax statement and deed details for the title company.
  5. Request one written total for clerk fees and transfer tax.

Selling for cash can skip a lender's inspection and appraisal. It does not skip the tax, lien and recording steps, which all have to finish before the deed is filed.

What to have in hand when you list

A sale goes quicker when your papers are in order. Put together the latest tax statement, proof of payment, your deed and any exemption approval.

Make a note of anything that could change the assessed value and keep photos and receipts. If you disagree with the value, the window to act is the spring inspection, so a sale in the fall means paying the bill as it stands and sorting out the difference with the buyer.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When do Pendleton County tax statements go out?

Near the end of September. Anyone without one by about October 12 should call the sheriff at 859-654-4511.

How large is the late charge after January in Pendleton County?

The sheriff posts 21% for February 1 through April 15, while a bill paid in January carries 5%.

Where is a deed recorded in Pendleton County?

In Falmouth, at the County Clerk's office, 233 Main Street, Room 1. It is open weekdays 8:30 to 4:00 and, on the second and last Saturday, 8:30 to noon.

Who bears the Kentucky transfer tax on a Pendleton County sale?

Kentucky puts it on the seller (the grantor): fifty cents per $500 of declared value, collected by the clerk first.

Is a PVA conference required before a Pendleton County appeal?

Yes. You meet with the PVA or a deputy first, and only then file with the clerk, no later than the workday after inspection ends.

How to pay the Pike County Sheriff

The sheriff's Tax Division, at 146 Main Street, Suite 204 in Pikeville, takes payment of Pike County taxes. The main number is 606-432-6260 and the tax line is 606-432-6212. Mail goes to the Pike County Sheriff's Office, Tax Division, P.O. Box 839, Pikeville, KY 41502, with checks made out to "Pike County Sheriff."

Ways to pay the Pike County Sheriff
Payment typeWhere it is accepted
CashIn person
Check or money orderAt the counter or through the post
Visa or MastercardIn person, by phone or online
Cash AppIn person, by phone or online

Online payment adds a 3% convenience fee on credit and debit cards, and the card statement shows the charge as "Kentucky Land Records." Search for the bill by number or by name, tick the box beside it, and press pay. The sheriff only collects, so questions about values and exemptions go to the Pike County Property Valuation Administrator (PVA).

Pike County at a glance

Pike is Kentucky's easternmost county and its largest by land area, at 786.73 square miles. Pikeville is the seat, and Elkhorn City and Coal Run Village are the other cities. Population has been falling, and housing is inexpensive.

  • Population fell from 58,669 in 2020 to an estimated 54,721 in 2025, a 6.7% drop.
  • The 2020 census listed 28,693 housing units, 14.5% of them vacant, and 28.0% of occupied homes were rentals. The 2025 estimate is 29,481 units.
  • The median value of an owned home is $112,000, median gross rent is $858, and owner costs are $1,278 with a mortgage.
  • Household income is $44,312 at the midpoint.

With so many empty units, sellers who can show a well-kept house and a clean tax record stand out.

Pike County property tax schedule

Pike County follows Kentucky's statewide timetable. Paying everything by November 1 earns a 2% discount, the face amount holds until year end, and a 5% penalty arrives in January. Payment after January 31 carries a 10% penalty under KRS 134.015. Taxes count as a personal debt of the owner from the day they come due.

For a mid-year sale, remember that the bill follows the deed's mailing address in the year of transfer. Call the Tax Division for the exact mailing date, because it shifts from year to year and a delayed year uses a month-by-month schedule. The sheriff's books close at the end of business on April 15, which is the cut-off for what the clerk inherits. Because the deed carries an in-care-of address for the bill in the year of transfer, give the closing agent a mailing address that will still work after the sale.

How to appeal a valuation

The path begins at the PVA's counter, since Kentucky bars an appeal until the owner has conferred with the PVA or a deputy. After that conference, the owner files with the county clerk no later than closing time on the workday after roll inspection ends. The roll is on view for thirteen days beginning with the first May Monday, and the local board sits between 25 and 35 days afterward.

  • Bring evidence: sales of similar homes, insurance policies, a contractor's repair estimate, photographs.
  • A paid representative must hold a qualifying professional credential, such as attorney, CPA or certified appraiser, and carry the owner's written authorization.
  • An owner may record the board hearing on audio.

The board must explain in writing any value it raises or lowers. A supplemental bill follows if the final number exceeds what the owner claimed.

Homestead exemption

Eligible owners are people 65 and up, along with anyone classed as totally disabled. For 2025 and 2026 they subtract $49,100 from the assessed value. The PVA takes the application, and a birth certificate, license or passport proves age.

If you are the seller and already hold this exemption, tell your closing agent so the proration reflects the lower bill. If you are the buyer, ask the PVA what you need to bring to apply for yourself.

When a Pike County tax bill goes unpaid

Once April 15 closes, unpaid bills pass from the sheriff to the Pike County Clerk, who records a lien and calls each bill a certificate of delinquency. Interest begins at one percent a month, and a clerk fee and county attorney fee are added. The county attorney's first notice goes out within 30 days and a second within 60, and the clerk must advertise the list in the newspaper beforehand.

For a county on the normal schedule, the sale can be set on any business day from July 14 through August 28. Clerks who also sell delinquent oil, gas or unmined mineral bills get 60 more days, with a deadline of October 27. Pike County has large coal and natural gas reserves, so a seller with mineral interests should ask the clerk whether any such bill is attached. A seller who still owes a bill should get a payoff from the clerk before listing, since a certificate bought by an investor adds substantial fees.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Pike County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What a seller pays at closing

The grantor owes the transfer tax, which works out to a half dollar for every $500 block of the deed's price (KRS 142.050). The Pike County Clerk lists a deed at $50 and a mortgage at $80, with $3 added per page past the fifth for a deed.

The clerk can be reached at 606-432-6211. The Pikeville office opens Monday to Thursday from half past eight until half past four and stays open until 5:30 on Fridays. Three branch offices keep shorter schedules:

  • Belfry: Tuesday 9:00 to 4:00 and Friday 9:00 to 6:00.
  • Phelps: Monday 9:00 to 4:00 and Wednesday 9:00 to 5:30.
  • Elkhorn City: Tuesday 9:00 to 4:00 and Thursday 9:00 to 5:30.

The clerk's deed page lists what a deed must carry, including a notarized consideration statement and an address for the next tax bill, so ask the closing agent to check the form first.

A seller's checklist for Pike County

  1. Call the Tax Division at 606-432-6212 and confirm this year's bill is paid and nothing older is open.
  2. Ask the clerk, 606-432-6211, whether a certificate of delinquency is recorded against the parcel, and whether any oil, gas or mineral bill is attached.
  3. Choose the branch office or the Pikeville office that fits your schedule.
  4. Give the closing agent a mailing address that will still work after the sale.
  5. Ask for one total covering the deed fee, extra pages and transfer tax.

Selling for cash avoids the wait for a buyer's financing, but the lien, the recording and the tax still have to be handled at closing, so these calls apply either way.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Pike County property tax?

At the Pike County Sheriff's Tax Division, 146 Main Street, Suite 204, Pikeville. Payments sent by post use box 839, and the tax line is 606-432-6212.

Is there a fee for paying Pike County taxes by card?

Yes, a 3% convenience fee applies to credit and debit cards, and the charge appears as Kentucky Land Records.

Who pays transfer tax on a Pike County sale?

The seller, as grantor, at a half dollar per $500 block of the deed's price. The clerk takes it before recording.

When do unpaid Pike County bills reach the clerk?

After the close of business on April 15, when the sheriff transfers them to the county clerk as certificates of delinquency.

Where is the Pike County Clerk's office?

The clerk's number is 606-432-6211, with offices in Pikeville, Belfry, Phelps and Elkhorn City, each on its own weekly schedule.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Washington County?
We buy Washington County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which Springfield offices touch a Washington County tax bill?

Three desks in Springfield split the work. The Property Valuation Administrator, or PVA, decides what each parcel is worth. The Sheriff takes money from October until April 15. After that date the County Clerk holds whatever is still open. Nobody at the PVA's counter can accept a payment or change a rate.

Phone numbers to keep handy: 859-336-5420 for the PVA (acreage, assessment, wrong name or address on a bill), 859-336-5400 for the Sheriff (payments, missing bills), and 859-336-5425 for the Clerk (payoff on a prior-year delinquency). Mail and drop-box payments go to 124 East Main Street, Springfield, KY 40069. The Sheriff's tax page has the details.

The bill follows the person listed in PVA records, normally the owner on January 1. If you bought or sold during the year and a bill lands with the wrong household, call the PVA or Sheriff quickly so it gets rerouted.

If you never receive a bill, that does not excuse the tax. Call the Sheriff after the middle of October and ask for a duplicate, then pay before November 1 to keep the 2 percent discount. Owners who mail a check should write the parcel on it and keep the receipt envelope for their records.

Due dates and discounts

The Sheriff cannot take a payment until the bills come over from the Clerk, which happens somewhere between October 1 and mid-October. Plan on a bill in hand around the 15th. Each bill prints four due dates, each with its own dollar amount, under KRS 134.015.

What a Washington County owner pays, by when the Sheriff receives the money
Payment receivedAmount owed
Through November 1Bill minus 2 percent
November 2 through year endPrinted amount
All of JanuaryPrinted amount plus 5 percent
February 1 through April 15Printed amount plus 10 percent

If the state's mailing slips, Revenue can substitute a schedule counted from the mailing date.

Can I use a card or pay online?

No to both. The office explains that card fees would be handed down to taxpayers, so it declines cards, and it runs no web payment system. What it does take is simple.

  • Checks and money orders payable to the Sheriff's Office there; cash only at the window.
  • The yellow postcard stub from your bill, included with any mailed payment, even when one envelope covers several parcels.
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope inside the mailing, if you want a receipt back. Walk-ins are handed one.
  • The outdoor drop box, available after hours.

Postmarks count: an envelope stamped by the due date is honored. Partial payments get mailed back, so a seller cannot park half a bill with the Sheriff and expect the account to clear.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Washington County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to question an assessment

Start with a sit-down at the PVA, then use the clerk's counter for the formal appeal. Public viewing of the roll runs 13 days from the first Monday in May. The clerk wants the written appeal by closing time the next workday. The board of assessment appeals hears cases about a month after that.

  • Bring paper: building and land descriptions, insurance policies, what construction cost, recent listings.
  • Attend the hearing. A no-show gives up any later review by the Kentucky Claims Commission.
  • Hire help only if the person qualifies under Kentucky's representative list, which includes attorneys, CPAs, and appraisers.

Should the board set a figure above yours after bills print, a supplemental bill covers the difference.

Who qualifies for homestead relief?

The test is age 65 or a total disability, plus living in the house you own. Frankfort fixed the deduction at $49,100 through the 2026 assessment year. The disability route asks for the Social Security notice of award, shown at the PVA office.

The state's rate was 10.6 cents per $100 for 2025, down from 10.9 cents in 2024. Local rates for the county, schools, and districts come on top, so ask the PVA for the full sum on your parcel.

Bring a birth certificate, license, or passport to the PVA. After a sale, tell the office so the credit leaves your old address.

What if taxes are still open when the house sells?

They travel with the land. The state calls the bill the owner's personal debt from the assessment date, and a delinquency lien clings to the parcel for eleven years (KRS 134.420). The title search will show it. Phone the Sheriff about this year and the Clerk about older ones before signing a contract.

At the April 15 handoff the Clerk records a lien, adds 10 percent plus the Sheriff's fee, and starts 1 percent monthly interest. County attorney notices go out. A sale of the certificate can come 90 to 135 days after the handoff, and the purchaser may tack on charges.

For the year of sale, a closing here usually has the seller pay a pro-rated slice for months owned, with the buyer picking up the full bill later. Check the closing statement for how it was split.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Washington County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a Washington County house with a delinquent bill

An older farmhouse, a house needing repairs, or a parcel with a bill sitting at the Clerk can sell as-is for cash, with the tax cleared at closing. Before you accept an offer, gather the payoff figures: the Sheriff's number for the current year and the Clerk's number for any prior year. Ask for each in writing or note the date and amount you were quoted.

On closing day the title company pays the taxes out of your proceeds and records the release. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, so an open tax bill rarely holds up the closing the way it can with a financed buyer. Confirm with the PVA afterward that the new owner's name is on the roll and that your homestead credit has come off.

Local context

Washington County, carved from Nelson County in 1792, has Springfield as its seat, joined by Mackville and Willisburg. The county voted wet in November 2024, ending its status as a dry county with one wet city.

It had 12,368 residents in 2025, up 2.8 percent over 2020. There are 5,325 housing units, and owners occupy 77.6 percent of homes at a median value of $179,200. Median monthly cost with a mortgage is $1,122, and median gross rent is $744, a useful benchmark if you rent out a house. The county issued 26 building permits in 2025, so a seller competes mostly with other resales.

Frequently asked questions

When will my Washington County tax bill arrive?

Expect it around October 15. The Sheriff gets the bills from the Clerk in early to mid October and cannot accept payment before that. If nothing shows up within 10 days of mailing, call the Sheriff for a duplicate.

Does the Washington County Sheriff take credit cards?

No. Payment is by check, money order, or cash in person, and there is no online option, because card fees would be passed to taxpayers.

Whom do I call for prior-year Washington County taxes?

The County Clerk at 859-336-5425 gives payoff amounts for earlier years. Unpaid bills reach the Clerk after April 15 with added penalties and interest.

Do buyer or seller owe the year's tax after a mid-year sale in Washington County?

The contract decides. Many sellers pay a pro-rated share at closing for months owned while the buyer pays the full bill when it comes. Read the settlement statement.

Is there a senior tax break in Washington County?

Yes. Owner-occupants 65 or older, or totally disabled, can deduct $49,100 from assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Apply at the PVA, 859-336-5420.

Bath County offices and what each one does

A few courthouse offices in Owingsville run property tax for Bath County. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values land and houses, the sheriff collects the bill, and the county clerk records deeds and receives bills that go delinquent. Every office uses a separate post office box, so a payment or an appeal needs to go to the right desk.

Who to call about a property tax bill

County AttorneyLetters and payment plans on delinquent bills(606) 674-2454

The clerk's website also carries a page of delinquent taxes, handy for checking whether a parcel is listed.

Tax calendar

Value is set as of January 1. In May the roll opens to the public, and that is when conferences and appeals take place. Bills go out in the fall. Under KRS 134.015, paying by November 1 earns a 2 percent discount, the printed amount stands until December 31, and after that come penalties of 5 percent for January and 10 percent once January is over. The sheriff stops collecting on April 15.

In a year when bills are late, the state may approve a different calendar with one month per stage. Bills for omitted property, or for a value raised on appeal, come due on the day they are prepared.

How to appeal your assessment

Book a conference with the Bath County PVA during the May inspection period. If you both agree on a figure, you're done. If not, file at the clerk's office and state the value you believe is right.

Under KRS 133.030 a three-member local board convenes at the county seat. Its first day goes to training and a review of recent comparable sales, and members may visit disputed properties. Five days is the ceiling unless the Department of Revenue permits more, and the decision arrives by certified mail.

  • Bring last year's sales of comparable homes, pictures of defects and an appraisal if you have one.
  • Ask how the PVA turned recorded sales into your number.
  • If the record misses a roof, well or septic problem, add a repair estimate.

The bill itself can't be contested, since the filing window closed months before it arrived.

Homestead exemption

Turning 65, or being totally disabled, lets a Bath County owner claim it on the home they live in. Apply to the PVA in the year you want it, with proof of age or disability attached.

KRS 132.810 gives one exemption per residential unit and counts a mobile home or manufactured house as a unit, a good fit where so many owners live in one. The figure tracks the cost of living and is revisited every two years, so ask the PVA what applies. An owner approved after paying gets a refund for the exempt portion. Report a sale or a death to the PVA, then the buyer or heir files a separate application.

Before you list a Bath County house

  1. Ask the PVA for your parcel record and compare it with what you know about the house. Fix wrong details while you can.
  2. Call the sheriff for the current balance and any earlier years still open.
  3. Check the clerk's delinquent page to see whether the parcel appears.
  4. If you hold a homestead exemption, plan to tell the PVA when the sale closes.
  5. Agree with the buyer on who covers which part of the year's bill, and get the closing agent to record the split.

All four offices are in Owingsville, so one afternoon of calls usually settles where you stand. Send paperwork to the correct box, because a letter to one office does not reach the others.

What happens to unpaid taxes

Come April 15, the sheriff turns every unpaid bill over to the clerk, and it is recorded as a delinquency certificate and lien. From then on interest accrues at 1 percent per month, and the state's worked examples stack commissions of 10 percent for the clerk and 20 percent for the county attorney on top.

Letters go out, parcels are advertised, and in summer a private buyer can purchase the certificate and add charges of its own. KRS 134.015 also makes the tax a personal debt of the January 1 owner and lets the lien trail the property for 11 years. Ask the clerk for a payoff and the county attorney about a payment plan.

Bath County homes and buyers

Bath County had 12,750 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 13,176 adds another 3.4 percent. The 2020 count found 5,445 housing units, with 10.4 percent of them vacant. Half of owner-occupied homes are worth more than $129,800, owners occupy 74.7 percent of homes, and renters pay a median $659. Median household income is $56,541. No building permits were logged for 2025.

With almost no new construction, the houses that change hands are mostly old ones. Age brings deferred repairs, and a PVA record that was never updated can misstate a house in either direction.

Cave Run Lake and the Daniel Boone National Forest take up a large share of the land, and rural lots, small farms and homes near the lake and forest make up much of the market. Interstate 64 crosses the county, and Owingsville is the seat and largest city.

Selling rural land, farms and forest-edge parcels

Many parcels here include acreage. Working farmland is taxed at agricultural value instead of market value, a rule drawn from Section 172A of the state constitution, and buyers will want to know whether your acreage keeps the classification. Ask the PVA before you list.

Look at the roof, the well and the septic system the way a buyer's inspector will. Where something needs work, a written estimate in your file helps in two places: it supports a lower assessment if the PVA's record assumes better condition than the house has, and it gives you a number to use when a buyer asks for a price cut.

Federal land owes no property tax, and much of the county lies within the Daniel Boone National Forest. On a rural tract, confirm that the boundary agrees with both the recorded deed and the PVA map. Sellers of rural land can also ask the county clerk what is recorded against a tract before they list it.

An older house with repairs pending and a bill sitting at the clerk's office can still sell. The payoff comes from the proceeds at closing, and the clerk quotes it for the month. A cash offer and a listing can be compared on what you net after repairs, back taxes and carrying costs.

Frequently asked questions

Where do Bath County tax payments go?

To the Bath County Sheriff in Owingsville, at (606) 674-2931. Bills are mailed in the fall.

How long is the Bath County appeal window?

Only while the tax roll is open for inspection in May. Meet the PVA first, then file with the clerk on the next business day after the period closes.

How pricey is a Bath County home?

Half of owner-occupied homes are worth more than $129,800, and owners live in 74.7 percent of homes.

Does Bath County give a break to seniors?

Yes. An owner who is 65 or totally disabled can apply to the PVA under KRS 132.810 for the home they live in.

What follows once the clerk takes a Bath County bill?

Interest and fees are added, and the bill can be sold to a private buyer at a summer sale. Ask the clerk for a payoff and the county attorney about a payment plan.

Carter County housing in brief

Carter County covers about 412 square miles of northeastern Kentucky. Grayson is the seat, Olive Hill is the only other city, and Interstate 64 and US 60 carry traffic through. The 2020 census counted 26,627 people, and the 2025 estimate is 26,149.

Most homes sit outside town limits and many are decades old. Of the 10,664 households, 75.7 percent owned their home, and 12.6 percent of the 12,206 housing units were empty. Only about one resident in five lived in an area the census treats as urban. For a seller, that means a lot of rural parcels, farm tracts and older frame houses, where acreage, wells, septic and road access can matter as much as the building.

Who bills and collects the tax

Three courthouse offices split the job. The Property Valuation Administrator values each parcel, the county clerk prints bills and inherits the unpaid ones, and the sheriff takes payment through autumn and winter. All three are at 300 West Main Street in Grayson, so a single trip can settle most questions.

Calling the wrong desk wastes a morning. Questions about worth belong with the PVA, questions about this year's bill with the sheriff, and anything already late with the clerk.

Carter County offices that handle property tax
OfficeAddressPhoneHours
Property Valuation Administration300 West Main Street, Suite 214, Grayson(606) 474-5663Mon to Fri 8:30 am to 4:00 pm; last Saturday of the month 8:30 am to noon

The clerk also runs an Olive Hill location with its own Saturday hours.

What you owe, and when

Under KRS 134.015 the calendar is the same every year. A bill appears around the first of October, and what you owe shifts with the date of payment.

  • Up to November 1, full payment earns a 2 percent reduction.
  • From November 2 through year end, you pay the amount on the bill.
  • Any day in January adds 5 percent.
  • Once February starts, the penalty is 10 percent and the sheriff's add-on fee kicks in.

Tax is your personal debt from the assessment date, and a lien on the land lasts eleven years regardless of who buys the house. If a bill never turns up, call the sheriff at (606) 474-5616 and ask how mailed and in-person payments are handled.

How to contest a valuation

Your first call is to the PVA, since a conference there opens the door to every later step. The roll is open for public viewing for thirteen days starting the first Monday of May, and your conference must take place inside that period.

When the PVA won't budge, hand the clerk a written petition no later than the workday after viewing ends. Identify the parcel and give your opinion of its open-market price. A local board hears the case about a month later and wants proof: sale listings, construction costs, insurance policies. Petitions with no evidence get denied. Owners who skip the board lose the right to go on to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Filing doesn't pause the bill. You keep paying on the figure you claimed until the case ends, and a higher final value triggers a supplemental bill.

What happens to unpaid bills after April 15

Every bill still open on April 15 moves from the sheriff to the county clerk and becomes a certificate of delinquency. The clerk reports that totals jump by about 40 percent once the added charges are counted. Personal checks are refused on these bills. Cash, money orders, company checks and cards (with a user fee) are accepted.

The clerk will sometimes set up a payment plan: a third of the balance up front and the rest within 90 days. Miss that deadline and the bill goes back on the delinquent list, with the money already paid kept and credited, not refunded.

  • The clerk advertises about 30 days before the sale and posts the list online.
  • The sale is held in late summer, in the fiscal courtroom at 10 am.
  • Bidders register at least ten days ahead, and the lien assignment fee is $46.

Whoever wins a certificate gains the right to collect from you. Paying before April 15 is far cheaper.

Homestead exemption

The break goes to owners who live in the house and are at retirement age or totally disabled. A fixed sum comes off the assessed value before the rate is applied. That sum stands at $49,100 for assessment years 2025 and 2026, with a new figure every second year.

Apply at the Carter County PVA, which also knows the current figure. A birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability applicants renew every year, with exceptions for owners with a service-connected rating and owners found permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

Selling a Carter County house that still owes tax

Yes. The balance is paid out of the sale price by the title company. First get this year's payoff from the sheriff. Then check with the clerk for any earlier year filed as delinquent, because a recorded certificate appears in a title search and must be paid or released to give the buyer a clean title.

Timing changes the cost. A bill still with the sheriff carries only the 5 or 10 percent penalty, while one at the clerk adds fees and interest. When the house is inherited, vacant or needs work, a cash purchaser who takes it as it stands can settle the tax from your proceeds, so you needn't bring money to closing.

Written balances from both offices should go to the closing agent before you sign a contract. Ask that the payoff and any release be shown as separate lines.

What to have ready

A little preparation shortens the process. Gather your parcel number or street address, your most recent bill and your deed. If you plan to claim the homestead exemption, bring a photo ID, and for a disability claim bring the paperwork from the agency or retirement system that classified you.

Visit before the last Saturday of the month if you need a weekend slot: the PVA, sheriff and clerk open that morning until noon, and the Olive Hill clerk office keeps its own Saturday hours. Weekday hours at the courthouse end at 4:00 pm, so don't leave a payoff request to the last hour of the day when a closing is close.

If a cash sale is on your list, a buyer who purchases as-is skips repairs and showings. You still need the payoff letters, so request them early.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes Carter County property tax payments?

The sheriff, at 300 West Main Street in Grayson, phone (606) 474-5616. Bills unpaid past April 15 are handled by the county clerk.

What if my Carter County tax bill never arrives?

Call the sheriff's office with your name or parcel number. Ask how it takes payments by mail, and confirm the address before you send a check.

How late can I file a Carter County assessment appeal?

The petition goes to the clerk by the next workday after the May inspection window closes. A conference with the PVA must come first.

Will the Carter County clerk accept my personal check on a delinquent bill?

No. Personal checks are refused on delinquent bills. Cash, money orders, company checks and cards are accepted, and cards carry a user fee.

Can I list my Carter County house while back taxes are open?

Yes. The payoff is taken from your proceeds at closing, so get written balances from the sheriff and the clerk before you sign a contract.

Who to call about a Floyd County tax bill

Two offices handle it. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) decides what a parcel is worth. The sheriff's tax division handles the bill itself. Neither one chooses the rate applied to that value.

The PVA appraises real and personal property at fair market value and stays out of rate setting, tax calculation and collection. Its counter is at 149 S. Central Ave., Room 5, in Prestonsburg, and the phone is (606) 886-9622. The sheriff keeps the tax division in the same building, takes mail at P.O. Value is a PVA question. Money owed is a sheriff question. Sending a value complaint to the sheriff only wastes a trip.

If you are getting ready to sell, plan two stops. The sheriff's tax division gives you the payoff or paid receipt, and the PVA has your parcel record and any exemption on file. Bring the deed or your last tax bill so the staff can pull the right parcel quickly, and use the McDowell office if that is closer to the property.

Floyd County housing market

Eastern Kentucky coal shaped the Floyd County housing map. The county topped 53,000 people in 1950 and has lost residents in almost every census since. The estimated 2025 population is 34,401, down 4.3 percent since 2020. Prestonsburg is the seat, and just 21.8 percent of the 2020 population counted as urban, so many sellers own hillside or hollow land instead of a town lot.

Prices are low, most owners live in their homes, and almost nothing new is being built. The typical value of a house its owner lives in is $98,700. Owners occupy 72.2 percent of housing, and there are 17,753 housing units, with 13.8 percent sitting empty when the 2020 count was taken. Median gross rent is $672, and only 2 building permits were issued in 2025.

On a house worth about $98,700, a few thousand dollars of back tax eats a visible slice of the price. Clearing it early protects what you walk away with.

Due dates and penalties

KRS 134.015 sets the calendar, and it favors early payers. A full payment made by November 1 earns a 2 percent discount. After that the printed amount applies until December 31. January costs an extra 5 percent, and anything later costs 10 percent.

Payment opens October 1, and you can pay through a link on the sheriff's website. If a lender escrows your taxes, check that the servicer actually received the bill. Owners who pay on their own should mark November 1 on the calendar, since the early credit is the only discount offered and it disappears the next day.

Every bill still open on April 15 moves from the sheriff to the county clerk. The clerk records a lien, and interest builds at 1 percent a month. The clerk adds a 10 percent commission, and once the county attorney has sent a notice, a 20 percent attorney commission follows. Expect a tax sale by the clerk about three to four and a half months after that.

Contesting your assessed value

See the PVA first. State rules demand a conference there before any appeal is filed, and the PVA has to explain how it valued the parcel.

  • The written appeal goes to the county clerk, and the cutoff is the end of the first business day after viewing closes.
  • A local review board takes cases roughly four to five weeks after viewing ends. Use that gap to gather photos, repair quotes and nearby sale prices.
  • If you miss the hearing, you lose the later step to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

Treat the PVA conference as the real chance to settle things. Many disagreements end there once the owner shows the condition of the house, repair estimates or what comparable homes nearby sold for. If you still disagree afterward, the written appeal to the clerk keeps your case alive, and the deadline is short, so file as soon as the conference is done.

KRS 133.120 limits paid representatives to a short list of professions, and they must hold your written permission.

Homestead exemption

Seniors 65 and over, and owners who are totally disabled, get $49,100 taken off assessed value for 2025 and 2026. A formal application is required, and the disability route is for people who are 100 percent disabled.

As proof of age, bring a birth certificate, license or passport. Someone applying on disability grounds needs proof of a total-disability classification and has to reapply annually. Owners with a service-connected military disability and people whose disability is permanent under Social Security rules are spared the yearly paperwork. Applications go to the Floyd County PVA, which keeps the exemption on file for later years. If you sell, the new owner has to apply in their own name, so tell the PVA about the sale.

Selling a Floyd County house with unpaid taxes

Clear the balance yourself, or let the closing agent do it from your proceeds. Under KRS 134.015 a delinquency lien stays on the parcel no matter who holds title, and the buyer's title company will turn it up.

  • Call the sheriff's tax division at (606) 886-8965 for the exact payoff.
  • Pay before April 15 if you can. Clerk and attorney commissions start only after the transfer.
  • Put the current year's bill in the sale contract. The state treats the tax as owed by the person who held the property on January 1.
  • If repairs and arrears are both piling up, a direct buyer that purchases as-is can fold both into one closing.

The county clerk explains how to record the deed. Afterward, send the PVA the new owner's name and mailing address. The next bill then reaches the buyer instead of coming back to you.

A cash sale does not hinge on a lender's appraisal or an inspection list, which helps when the house needs work. The title company still pulls the tax record, so ask the sheriff for the payoff letter before anything else. With that letter in hand, the closing agent pays the balance out of your proceeds and the lien comes off.

Where do Floyd County residents pay their property tax?

At the Floyd County Sheriff's tax division, 149 S Central Ave. in Prestonsburg, by mail to P.O. Box 152, or online from the sheriff's home page. The tax division's number is (606) 886-8965.

Does the Floyd County PVA set my tax rate?

No. The PVA does not determine rates, calculate taxes or collect them. It values property and processes exemption applications at (606) 886-9622.

When does Floyd County's 2 percent discount end?

On November 1. From November 2 through December 31 the bill is due without a discount, and penalties start in January.

How large is the homestead exemption for a Floyd County home?

The reduction is $49,100 for both 2025 and 2026. Eligible owners are seniors and the totally disabled, and the paperwork goes to the Floyd County PVA.

Can a Floyd County house sell while tax is still owed?

Yes, as long as the balance is settled at closing. Ask the sheriff for a payoff first, because an open bill keeps the lien on the parcel.

Who handles a Gallatin County tax bill

Gallatin County housing and the local market

At about 105 square miles, Gallatin ranks near the bottom of the state by size, on the Ohio River across from Indiana and part of the Cincinnati metropolitan area. Warsaw is the seat, with Sparta and Glencoe the other communities. Interstate 71 runs through with three exits around Sparta and Glencoe, joined by US 42 and US 127, and the commute averages 29.5 minutes. A good share of residents work elsewhere in the region.

Payment goes to the sheriff, and KRS 134.015 sets one schedule for every owner. A bill paid whole by November 1 drops 2 percent. Between then and December 31 you owe the printed figure. Each late month costs more: 5 percent in January, 10 percent past that.

If bill mailing slips, the Department of Revenue can replace the usual dates with a compressed schedule of one month at a discount, one month at face and one month at 5 percent, so go by the dates printed on your own bill. After a sale, give the sheriff the buyer's name so future bills land with the right person.

You can pay at the sheriff's office on North Main, mail a payment to PO Box 1025, or look up the bill on the sheriff page first to confirm the amount. How to dispute your value

Begin at the PVA office, 200 Washington Street. A PVA conference must come before an appeal, and it is easiest to go right after assessment notices arrive. The tax roll then opens to public view for 13 days in early May.

Once you have talked with the PVA or a deputy, put the appeal in writing and give it to the County Clerk's office by the end of the first business day after public viewing closes. A local review board then convenes roughly four to five weeks on and can sit up to five days.

If you sell, tell the PVA so the exemption is removed from your name. The buyer can apply for their own if they qualify, and the form has to be filed with the Gallatin County PVA office in Warsaw rather than with the sheriff or the clerk.

Selling with unpaid taxes

Unpaid tax does not disappear at closing. The owner personally owes the tax from the assessment date under KRS 134.015, and a lien for delinquency under KRS 134.420 rides along with the parcel whoever takes title.

Every open bill is handed from the sheriff to the County Clerk on April 15 as a certificate of delinquency. The county attorney then sends a first notice inside 30 days and a second inside 60. A clerk's sale can follow 90 to 135 days after the handover. A third-party buyer at that sale can pile on substantial fees.

  1. Phone the sheriff, (859) 567-5751, for a payoff before listing.
  2. If the house is in Warsaw, ask the city whether a water, sewer or city tax bill is open too.
  3. Give the title company that number and it will pay the balance from your proceeds.
  4. Keep the paid receipts. The title search lists any unpaid balance as an exception to clean title.

Cash buyers who take a house as-is do not wait on a lender, and the tax is settled at the table. That suits an owner facing repairs and back taxes together. With no appraisal step, timing rests on the title work and the payoff letter.

Where do I send a Gallatin County property tax payment?

Mail or bring it to the Gallatin County Sheriff, 106 North Main in Warsaw, or PO Box 1025, Warsaw, KY 41095. The county's sheriff page links a tax bill lookup.

How do I reach the Gallatin County PVA?

Call (859) 567-5621 or visit 200 Washington Street in Warsaw. The PVA handles value questions, exemption forms and owner records.

When is the early-payment date in Gallatin County?

The date is the same statewide: November 1. A full payment by then saves 2 percent, and the printed amount is owed until December 31.

Does the City of Warsaw send its own tax bill?

Warsaw offers an online page for water, sewer and property tax bills. If the house is inside the city, check with both the city and the sheriff about which bills apply.

Does a tax lien survive a sale in Gallatin County?

Yes. The lien stays with the property after a sale until the tax is paid or the KRS 134.420 period runs out, so clear the balance at closing.

Green County tax offices

Green County splits the work between two offices near the courthouse. The Green County Sheriff collects the bill at 203 W Court Street, Greensburg, KY 42743, phone (270) 932-5641. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values every parcel from 103 South 1st Street in Greensburg, phone (270) 932-7518.

The PVA keeps the records and sets the assessment. The sheriff only takes payment. Go to the PVA for address changes, exemption forms and any question about how a value was reached. Call either office ahead to confirm hours, and ask for a payoff or a parcel record before you list the house.

The Green County tax calendar

The tax year starts with the January 1 assessment date and ends with the sheriff's settlement the following September. For a homeowner the dates that count are mid-September, when the sheriff receives the bills, November 1, when the discount ends, and January 1, when penalties begin. Delinquent certificates are normally offered for sale between July 14 and August 28.

Green County real estate tax calendar
StepDate or window
Public inspection of the roll, with PVA conferences13 days from the first Monday in May, Saturdays included
Assessment appeals board sits5 days, starting 25 to 35 days after inspection
Bills handed to the sheriffBy September 15

If bills are mailed late, the state may move to a slower schedule that gives each step a 30-day stage.

Appealing a Green County value

The first stop is the Green County PVA and the second is the county clerk. Kentucky closes the local board to anyone who skipped the conference, and conferences take place during the May inspection window.

  • Let the PVA explain how the figure was reached, then state the value you think is right. The conference record shows the starting value, your claim and any changes you both accept.
  • File with the clerk before the workday ends on the day after the inspection period closes.
  • Come to the hearing with proof: lot and building details, insurance papers, build costs and listings of comparable houses.
  • When the board raises or lowers the value, it must give you a written reason.

Anyone you hire to speak for you must be on the state's list of qualified representatives and hold your written authorization. Skipping the filing or the hearing ends the path to the Kentucky Claims Commission. If the case finishes late and the board lands above your claim, expect a supplemental bill.

Exemptions and the homestead break

Section 170 of the Kentucky constitution exempts public property in public use, burial grounds, church property, charities, schools not run for gain, public libraries, household goods and crops in the producer's hands. A separate break serves owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who keep the house as a permanent residence.

That break is worth $49,100 off assessed value in assessment years 2025 and 2026. Apply at the PVA with a birth certificate, license or passport. Disability claims need payments received through the whole assessment period and a yearly renewal, except for service-connected disabilities and owners with a permanent total disability finding.

If you move out, give the PVA your new mailing address so assessment notices and tax bills reach you.

Selling with taxes owed

A tax debt travels with the land and lands on the buyer unless it is cleared first. The owner on January 1 is personally liable, and the lien on a delinquent bill can survive 11 years under KRS 134.015 and 134.420, whoever holds title.

Timing drives the cost. If you pay the sheriff before April 15, you owe only the penalties already earned. After the transfer, the clerk adds 1 percent monthly interest, a 10 percent commission, a county attorney commission and a lien fee. The state's own worked example shows a bill growing quickly once the attorney's first notice goes out.

The county attorney writes at the 30-day and 60-day marks, and a sale follows 90 to 135 days after the transfer. Before listing, get both payoffs in writing, one from the sheriff for the current year and one from the clerk for anything transferred. The closing agent can then pay them from the sale proceeds. A cash sale that closes in a couple of weeks can head off the clerk's added charges if your bill is still with the sheriff.

Reading the penalty schedule as a seller

The calendar tells you what a delay costs. Closing before November 1 means the bill can still be paid with the discount, so a seller who has the bill in hand can pay early and hand the buyer a clean record. From November 2 through December 31 the face amount is due and nothing extra is added. January adds 5 percent. After January 31 the penalty rises to 10 percent, and the sheriff's own 10 percent add-on comes with it.

After April 15 the sheriff no longer collects. The bill moves to the clerk, and from then on interest, commissions and fees pile up month by month. If your closing date falls near one of these steps, ask the sheriff or clerk which figure applies on that exact day.

Green County at a glance

Green County is in south central Kentucky. Its only incorporated city is the seat, Greensburg, and Summersville is a census-designated place. The land covers about 286 square miles, and the Green River crosses it from east to west. Population was 11,644 in July 2025, up 4.8 percent from 2020, with 4,421 households. About 77.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Median home value is $125,000, and median owner costs run $955 a month with a mortgage and $361 without. Median gross rent is $610.

The county sits on the Central and Eastern time zone line, with LaRue and Taylor counties to the north on Eastern time, so check which clock an appointment uses.

What to have ready before you list

Gather your last tax bill, the parcel number if you know it, and any exemption paperwork. Ask the sheriff whether the current year is paid, and ask the clerk whether older years were transferred after April 15. Have the PVA confirm your mailing address so notices follow you after the sale.

Buyers and title companies look at the same records, so surprises are rare when you check first. A house with a recorded lien can still sell, but the payoff comes out of your proceeds at closing, and a written figure from the clerk prevents a last-minute scramble.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Green County discount end?

On November 1. The calendar lets owners pay 2 percent less through that date, face amount from the next day to December 31, and adds 5 percent in January.

Who takes tax payments in Green County?

The Green County Sheriff, at 203 W Court Street in Greensburg, phone (270) 932-5641. The PVA at (270) 932-7518 values property and handles exemptions but takes no payments.

What happens to a Green County bill after January 31?

A 10 percent penalty and a 10 percent sheriff fee apply. The clerk takes over on April 15 and charges monthly interest.

How large is the Green County homestead exemption?

Owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, get $49,100 off assessed value for 2025 and 2026. Apply at the PVA with proof of age or disability.

When does Green County sell delinquent tax bills?

The standard calendar lists July 14 through August 28, which falls 90 to 135 days after the April 15 handoff to the clerk.
