Mail to the sheriff goes to PO Box 318, Greenup, KY 41144. The sheriff's tax page takes online payments with your bill number and mailing address. The processor, not the sheriff, keeps the convenience fee added to an online payment. Refunds and account problems are handled in person at the sheriff's office, and staff do not process them by phone.

What a bill costs after April 15

Any bill left unpaid when April 15 arrives leaves the sheriff for the County Clerk, and the amount owed begins to rise. That date is the final one for paying at the Sheriff's Office. Bills turned over to the Clerk pick up fees that the original bill never showed, and the sheriff's page cites House Bill 262 as the reason for the April 15 date.

The state's worked example follows a bill through the stages, and each one costs more than the last: payment within five business days of transfer, payment after the county attorney's first notice, a second month of interest in May, newspaper advertising in June, and finally purchase by a third-party buyer at the sale. The example assumes a 4 percent sheriff commission, so your actual figures depend on the local rate.

Once a certificate exists, 1 percent interest is added each month. The sheriff's site keeps links to earlier bills for tax years 2015 through 2019, which helps when you trace an old balance. The Clerk's sale of delinquent bills must fall 90 to 135 days after the transfer, which in a normal year means July 14 to August 28. If you hold a bill that reaches the sale, ask the Clerk's office for the third-party purchaser rules.

Challenging a Greenup County value

Begin at the PVA, because Kentucky lets only owners who held a conference take a case to the board. Every property is revalued each year and physically examined at least once every four years, so a value can move even when your house has not changed.

  • Conferences happen while the roll is open in May, a 13-day window starting the first Monday. Staff can meet earlier once notices are mailed.
  • Then file with the County Clerk before the office closes on the next business day.
  • The board convenes four to five weeks after inspection ends and sits at most five days unless the state agrees to more.
  • Bring documents the board can weigh: building costs, insurance policies, listings and photos. No documents, no reduction.

Taxes equal assessment times rate, so if the rate holds, a higher value means a higher bill and a lower value a lower one. Rates come from the county, city and school boards, not the PVA. Keep your mailing address current with the PVA, and never treat a missing bill or notice as a reason to skip payment.

Homestead exemption

A resident owner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled, has $49,100 taken off the assessed value for 2025 and 2026.

What to settle before closing

Ask each office for a payoff, because which office holds the bill depends on the date. Before April 15 it sits with the sheriff. Afterward the Clerk has it, and the Clerk's delinquent tax page links purchaser information and the application.

The January 1 owner owes the year's tax. Under KRS 134.420, a delinquent lien can trail the house for as long as 11 years after it sells. A buyer's title search will find a lien that has not been released, and a recording and release fee comes with clearing it.

Your closing agent will work out how the current bill is divided between you and the buyer. Any bill still open at the Clerk should be paid from your proceeds. A written payoff from the Clerk shows the full price of clearing title on a house with several years behind. If back taxes are piling up and repairs are not affordable, a cash buyer who takes the house as is can close on a short timeline and settle the liens at the table.

Paying the bill step by step

Start by finding the bill. If it has not come, the sheriff's office is the place to ask, and you will want your bill number and mailing address ready. Pay at the counter, by mail to the PO Box, or online. Online payment is quick but adds a processing fee, and the sheriff cannot waive it.

Keep the receipt or confirmation. A title company asking for proof that the year is paid is the most common reason to need it. If you overpay or a mistake shows up on your account, go to the sheriff's office in person, since that is the only way refunds and account fixes are handled.

Greenup County at a glance

Greenup County lies along the Ohio River in the northeast corner of Kentucky, in the Huntington-Ashland metropolitan area. Greenup is the county seat and Flatwoods is the largest city. Median owner costs are $1,186 a month with a mortgage and $483 without, and median gross rent is $860.

Most sellers here own a modest, long-held house, and the figures above suggest that taxes are a manageable cost. Still, a bill that slips past April 15 can complicate a listing, because the buyer's lender and title company will want the lien cleared before funds change hands. Checking the account early gives you time to fix a problem.

US 23 follows the river through Russell, Flatwoods, Raceland, Wurtland, Greenup and South Shore, which makes those river towns the busiest part of the market.

Where is Greenup County property tax paid?

At the Greenup County Sheriff's Office through April 15, in person, by mail to PO Box 318, Greenup, KY 41144, or online. Call (606) 473-9833. Processors charge convenience fees on online payments.

The PVA at (606) 473-9984, in Room 209 of the courthouse, 301 Main Street, with weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

What changes on April 15 in Greenup County?

The sheriff hands every unpaid bill to the County Clerk, which adds fees the original bill never showed. Call (606) 473-7394 for the total.

What is the Greenup County homestead amount?

The 2025 and 2026 figure is $49,100 off assessed value, open to owners 65 or older or totally disabled.

Will the Greenup County sheriff refund money by phone?

Mason County tax offices in Maysville

All three offices are in Maysville. One sets the value, one collects this year's bill, and the third records deeds and inherits any bill that stays unpaid.

  • PVA: 220 1/2 Sutton Street, (606) 564-3700, staffed through the workweek. It handles value, mailing and property addresses, and exemptions.
  • Sheriff: 120 West Third Street, in the old Health Department building, 606-564-3309, doors open at nine on weekdays, and a drop box takes checks only.
  • Clerk: 27 West 3rd Street, PO Box 234, (606) 564-3341, opening at eight on weekdays and closing for lunch between 11:30 and 12:30.

Before disputing a bill, know what the PVA controls. The office writes no laws and sets no rates, and it does not take payments either, so keep your checkbook for the sheriff. Fiscal court members, city officials and school boards vote the rates, so a rate complaint goes to them.

The Ohio River and the Mason County market

Mason County is a river county in northeastern Kentucky, with the Ohio River along its northern edge, facing Brown and Adams counties in Ohio. Maysville is both seat and largest city. Dover, Germantown and Sardis are the other incorporated places, and Mays Lick is a census-designated place.

Population has eased: 17,490 in 2010, 17,120 in 2020, and an estimate of 16,936, which is 1.1 percent under the 2020 base. The county has 8,276 housing units and 7,131 households, and owners live in 66.1 percent of homes. The median home value is $161,500. Median gross rent is $727, and owners with a mortgage pay a median of $1,245 a month, compared with $405 for owners without one. Only 26 building permits were issued in 2025, so resale homes make up most of what a buyer sees. Expect buyers to compare your house with older river-town homes in Maysville and with houses in the smaller towns, and expect their lenders to ask for the tax bill. Mason County Schools is the single public district.

Due dates and penalties

The sheriff's Taxpayer's Notice sets out four periods, and the bill itself arrives on a yellow postcard.

Mason County payment periods
PeriodAmount owed
October 1 to November 1Face amount minus a two percent discount
Next two monthsFace amount
January onlyFace plus a five percent penalty
February to April 15Face plus a twenty-one percent penalty

The usual timetable is set out in KRS 134.015. After April 15, real estate bills pass to the County Clerk, where a County Attorney fee of 20 percent, a clerk fee of 10 percent and interest of 1 percent monthly are charged, and an investor may buy the delinquency. A prior-year bill is paid at the clerk's counter, and the payoff number is 606-564-3341.

Past-due reminders are never mailed. A bounced check costs $50 and returns the bill to unpaid. Cards work through the online link with a surcharge. If escrow or a new owner is responsible, pass the notice along at once.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mason County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Appealing your value

Appeals begin at the PVA: talk the value over, review how it was figured, and take it to the Board of Appeals if nothing is resolved. The city of Maysville seats an appointee on that board and lists the PVA, (606) 564-3700, as the contact.

Appraisers see each property at least every four years and may measure a building's outside when nobody is home. In the statute, KRS 133.120 sets the order of steps, and KRS 133.030 puts the board's first meeting 25 to 35 days after inspection closes. Carry evidence of value and keep paying on your claimed figure until the board rules. A paid representative has to come from the professions the statute lists.

Good evidence is concrete. Bring photos of any damage or deferred repairs, recent sale prices of comparable houses nearby, an appraisal if you paid for one, and the property record card the PVA can show you. Compare the square footage, bedroom count and condition on that card with the house you actually own, since a wrong detail is the easiest error to correct. Ask the PVA to note your concerns in writing at the conference so the board sees them.

Homestead exemption

For 2025 and 2026 the exemption is $49,100 off assessed value. Qualifying owners live in the house and are 65 or older, or totally disabled. Applicants go to the PVA page on the county website, which also hosts a property search and a vehicle-tax exoneration affidavit. An approved age claim normally carries on while the same owner stays in the house; a buyer files afresh.

Liens, deeds and closing

The sheriff quotes this year's balance and the clerk quotes earlier years, and both come out of the sale proceeds. Under KRS 134.015(5) a delinquency lien can survive eleven years whoever holds title, so title agents insist on payoff.

Deeds are filed with the clerk at 27 West 3rd Street. The seller's transfer tax is fifty cents on each $500 of value under KRS 142.050. For electronic filing the clerk lists Hopdox, CSC, Simplifile and ePN. Confirm what each deed needs before sending it.

Before you sign, use the property search on the county's PVA page to check that the owner name and mailing address on file match what the deed will say, and ask the PVA to correct any mismatch so the next tax bill reaches the right person.

Preparing to sell

Start with three calls. The sheriff gives you the current balance, the clerk tells you whether any earlier year is open, and the PVA confirms the name, address and exemption on the roll. Ask each for a written figure and the date it stays good, because the sheriff's notice and the clerk's fees move the number as the calendar advances.

Bring the deed, a photo ID and your latest bill, and if the house came to you by inheritance, bring whatever shows your authority to sell. Give the payoff letters to the title agent so each amount is paid from the proceeds at the table. With a cash sale there is no lender waiting on an appraisal, so a clean tax record is the main thing that keeps the closing on its date.

If a bill is missing, call the sheriff for a copy, since reminders are never mailed and a lost postcard does not stop penalties from running. If an escrow account pays your tax, ask the lender to confirm the payment went out before you list, and ask the closing agent to refund any unused escrow balance to you after the sale. Keep your receipts in one folder for the title agent.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Mason County Sheriff's office hours?

The office opens at nine on weekdays, at 120 West Third Street in Maysville. Call 606-564-3309. A drop box takes checks only.

What does a bounced check cost on a Mason County tax bill?

It costs $50. The bill returns to unpaid status, and your repayment should follow the payment period printed on it.

Does the Mason County Sheriff mail past-due notices?

No. None is mailed, so watch the dates. Real estate bills still open after April 15 pass to the County Clerk with added fees.

Who sets tax rates in Mason County?

Elected bodies do: the fiscal court, city officials and school boards, among other taxing authorities. The PVA neither sets rates nor decides the total to be raised.

Can a Mason County bill be paid by card?

Yes, through the online link on the sheriff's site, where the card company adds a charge. Counter payments, mail and the check-only drop box also work.

Who buys homes in Metcalfe County

Metcalfe covers about 290 square miles of south central Kentucky. It was organized in May 1860 as the 106th Kentucky county. It sits in the Glasgow micropolitan area, so a seller may meet buyers who work toward Glasgow or Bowling Green. Edmonton lies on the Louis B. Nunn Cumberland Parkway, about 29 miles from Interstate 65, with Glasgow 16 miles west and Louisville 113 miles away.

The county had 10,286 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 10,583 for mid-2025. Edmonton had about 1,586 residents in 2010 against 10,099 for the whole county, so most owners live outside the city. The 2020 count showed 4,691 housing units, 11.6 percent of them empty. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $110,200 and typical rent is $582. Homeowners live in 77.7 percent of homes, and owner costs run $1,066 a month with a mortgage and $368 with none. About 19.0 percent of residents are 65 or older, which is the group that can claim the homestead exemption.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the PVA while the roll is on public view, which runs 13 days from the first Monday of May and includes Saturdays. If the conference fails, go to the county clerk, and do it by the next workday after the viewing period closes.

The appeals board has three local members, named by the mayor of the county's largest city, the fiscal court and the judge executive. Since Edmonton is the only city, its mayor makes one of those picks. A change by the board must come with a written explanation, and you may record the hearing. Bring:

  • Sale prices and dates of similar homes near yours.
  • A contractor quote for repairs that the PVA record omits.
  • The dollar value you claim, written on the form.

If you file and then skip the hearing, you can't take the appeal further.

Rural land and acreage

State rules send PVAs to every parcel at least every four years and put new buildings on the roll each year. Farm land can be assessed at what it is worth as agriculture instead of its fair cash value.

On nearly 290 square miles with about 10,500 residents, many Metcalfe County sales include acreage. If any part of a parcel is farmed, ask the PVA about its classification before you list.

Homestead exemption

An owner who turns 65 during the year, or is classified as totally disabled on January 1, applies at the PVA for the home they own and live in. KRS 132.810 allows a single exemption for each residential unit and includes mobile homes and manufactured houses.

A disabled owner under 65 reapplies yearly, except someone with a service-connected total disability or a permanent disability finding. Applying before payment reduces the bill, and applying afterward earns a refund.

After a missed payment

Unpaid bills reach the clerk's office at the end of April 15 as certificates of delinquency, each with a lien on record. Interest of 1 percent a month builds up, and clerk and county attorney fees of 10 and 20 percent follow. A public listing is required at least 30 days before the sale.

The January 1 owner is personally liable, and the lien can trail the property for 11 years. A private buyer who gets the certificate collects from the owner and may add fees.

Selling with back tax owed

It doesn't have to stop a sale. The sheriff quotes the payoff before April 15 and the clerk afterward, and the amount grows monthly once the clerk has it. Request a written figure dated close to closing.

January 1 settles tax ownership, so a late-year sale leaves the bill with the previous owner until next year. Many Metcalfe County sellers hold older houses with repairs put off. To weigh a cash offer against a listing, work out each net after repairs, tax and months of carrying cost.

Before you list, gather your deed, latest bill and any exemption approval. Call the PVA to check the acreage and building description, and ask the sheriff for the current balance. If the house is inherited, bring the papers showing who may sign. After closing, tell the PVA the new owner's name so the bill is mailed to the right place.

Steps from listing to closing

A typical Metcalfe County sale runs in a clear order. First, confirm with the PVA what is on record for the parcel, including any homestead claim and the farm classification if there is acreage. Second, ask the sheriff for the bill and the balance. After April 15, ask the clerk instead, because the bill has moved there. Third, decide in the contract who pays the year's tax, since the January 1 owner is the one on the bill. Fourth, give the closing agent a written payoff dated close to the closing day so the tax is settled out of the sale money.

Roads matter in this county. Edmonton is on the parkway and U.S. 68, with Kentucky routes 80 and 163 also serving the town, so buyers commuting to Glasgow or Bowling Green often judge a house by drive time. Mention the route and distance in your listing. A cash buyer can skip the repair list that a lender might require, which helps with older houses where work was put off, but expect a lower price in exchange for that speed.

Frequently asked questions

Who takes payment of Metcalfe County property tax?

The county sheriff, whose mailing box is P.O. Box 371 in Edmonton. The phone is (270) 432-3041.

Is there a city property tax in Edmonton?

Edmonton is the county's only incorporated city. Call the Fiscal Court at (270) 432-3181 to ask whether a city bill applies to your parcel.

How do I reach the Metcalfe County PVA?

Call (270) 432-3162 or write to P.O. Box 939, Edmonton, KY 42129. The office site is www.qpublic.net/ky/metcalfe.

When can a Metcalfe County owner contest a value?

During the 13 days that begin on the first Monday of May. A PVA conference has to come before any filing.

How long does a delinquent tax lien last?

Up to 11 years under KRS 134.015, through any change of owner.

This is the Monroe County in Kentucky, on the Eastern Pennyroyal Plateau.

Offices to call or visit

All of these are in Tompkinsville, KY 42167.

  • Sheriff: tax collection. 200 North Main Street, Suite E, phone (270) 487-6622.

Regular due dates

The delinquent tax sale

Right after April 15 the clerk issues a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record against the property. That happens on or about April 16. Interest climbs monthly, so an early payment costs less.

The clerk holds a sale of unpaid certificates each fall in the clerk's office, and the clerk can tell you the date. A certificate unpaid at the sale may go to a private party who adds heavy administrative costs. The county attorney or a buyer may pursue foreclosure.

  • By mail: money orders only.
  • In person at the clerk's desk: check, cash or credit card, and card fees may apply.

The clerk can also tell you by phone whether a certificate was bought and by whom.

The Monroe County market

Monroe covers about 329 square miles along the Tennessee border, formed in 1820. Fountain Run and Gamaliel are the other cities, and the county sits in the Upper Cumberland hills along the Cumberland River. The Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site draws visitors.

The 2020 count of 11,338 was above the 10,963 recorded in 2010, but the mid-2025 estimate of 11,191 is 1.3 percent lower. There are 5,300 housing units. Owners live in 70.9 percent of homes, which leaves more room for rentals. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $115,900 and typical rent is $657. Owner costs run $1,056 a month with a mortgage and $397 without one. Jobs counted in 2023 came to 2,649, which is 1.9 percent below 2022.

How to challenge your value

A PVA conference comes first, and the state requires it before anyone can file. The roll opens to the public on the first Monday of May for about two weeks, and the clerk's office accepts filings through the next workday after it closes.

The filing states your own opinion of value. Should bills go out before the appeal ends and the final figure beat your claim, a supplemental bill covers the gap. Across 329 square miles and 34.4 people per square mile, many Monroe County sales come with land. The PVA must visit every parcel at least every four years and add new construction yearly. Parcels near the Tennessee line, along the river or up in the hills can differ widely. If the roll shows a building that was torn down, or misses a barn you added, raise it at a PVA conference.

Homestead exemption

Anyone who owns and lives in a house and has turned 65, or carries a total disability classification, may claim it. Apply at the Monroe County PVA with proof, on the state's form.

KRS 132.810 sets one exemption per unit, even if the owner is both elderly and disabled, or several older residents share the unit. The amount follows a federal price index and is rechecked every two years. Report a sale or the owner's death to the PVA.

Selling a house that owes tax

It can be done, and the usual route starts with a written payoff. The sheriff supplies it before April 15, and the clerk does afterward, when the figure rises monthly and carries the clerk and attorney fees.

Under KRS 134.015 the person who owned on January 1 owes that year's tax personally, and a lien can follow the property for 11 years. Houses in Monroe County that need work, or came to heirs, can change hands with a bill still open, so build the payoff into your numbers when you compare a listing with a cash sale.

Gather your deed, your last bill and any exemption approval before you start. Ask the PVA to confirm the parcel details, since acreage and outbuildings are common sources of mismatch. If the owner has died, bring the papers that show who may sign. After closing, tell the PVA the new owner's name so the next bill is mailed correctly and the old exemption ends. A cash buyer can often close without repairs, which helps when a roof or other work would stall a lender.

Steps from listing to closing

Start by calling the sheriff for the current balance and, if April 15 has gone by, the clerk, since the bill will have moved there. Ask whether a certificate exists on the parcel and whether any buyer holds it. If one does, the payoff includes that buyer's costs, so get the figure in writing and dated close to closing.

Next, decide in the sales contract who pays the year's tax, because the January 1 owner is the one billed. The closing agent then pays the tax out of the sale money and the clerk records the new deed. A buyer who plans a conventional loan will usually want the tax cleared first, while a cash buyer can close around it.

Monroe County has a mix of town lots in Tompkinsville, small-town homes in Fountain Run and Gamaliel, and rural tracts. A town lot rarely needs more than a payoff and a clear deed. A tract with acreage may also need the PVA to confirm its classification and boundaries before a buyer will commit.

Frequently asked questions

Who accepts Monroe County property tax payments?

The county sheriff, in Suite E at 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. Call (270) 487-6622.

When is the Monroe County tax sale?

The clerk holds a sale of unpaid certificates each fall. Phone (270) 487-5471 to learn the date and whether a certificate was sold.

Is an installment plan available on a late Monroe County bill?

Yes, through the County Attorney's office, provided the certificate was not sold at the tax sale.

Can a delinquent bill be paid to the clerk by check in the mail?

No, mailed payments must be money orders. Checks, cash and credit cards work only at the clerk's office.

Where is the Monroe County PVA?

Suite A, 200 North Main Street, Tompkinsville. The office phone is (270) 487-6401.

Offices near the courthouse

Three counters in Mount Vernon handle a tax account. The Property Valuation Administration (PVA) sets parcel values; reach it at (606) 256-4194 or write to P.O. Box 977, Mt. Vernon, KY 40456. The sheriff, at 205 E. Main St., Box 2, (606) 256-2032, sends and collects the bills. The County Clerk, (606) 256-2831, Box 6 in the same building, takes over any bill that goes delinquent.

None of the three picks a rate. School and special districts choose their own levies, and the sheriff bills the total. The Fiscal Court meets monthly on the second Tuesday at 1:00 p.m. in the courthouse. Anyone who wants to speak asks for a place on the agenda a day ahead.

Deed and lien searches start at the County Clerk, who holds the county's official records. Trash service and animal control sometimes come up when a house changes hands, and the health department, dog warden and solid waste office each keep a separate number. The Fiscal Court's occupational tax office, (606) 256-8374, deals with employers.

Due dates and penalties

December 31 is the due date under KRS 134.015, and the sheriff collects. A delayed mailing can shift the calendar, but normally the stages go like this.

Your bill shows which stage applies. Values are fixed as of January 1, so a late winter closing normally leaves the prior year's bill in the seller's name. Before closing day, get an exact payoff from the sheriff.

Rockcastle County housing

Mount Vernon is the seat and the largest city, with Brodhead and Livingston as the other towns. The county covers about 317 square miles, partly in the Daniel Boone National Forest, and counts as rural throughout. July 2025 population was estimated at 16,148, up 0.7 percent from 2020. What a median home might cost to carry

Kentucky lowered the 2025 real estate rate to 10.6 cents for every hundred dollars of assessment. School, county and district rates sit on top of that, and only the sheriff's bill for a given address shows the sum.

Older and disabled owners can subtract $49,100 from the assessment. On a house valued near $123,600 that removes a large share of the base, so a qualifying owner gains by filing at the PVA early.

A sale changes who pays. The bill follows whoever held the parcel when the year began, so the contract should assign that year in writing, and any open balance belongs at the closing table.

How to appeal your assessment

You cannot file an appeal until you have met with PVA staff, so start there. They must explain the law, the procedure and how your number was derived, and a written record captures your claim and the outcome.

  • Watch for the published inspection notice. The roll opens on May's first Monday and can be viewed for thirteen days.
  • Meet staff in that window, or sooner if an assessment notice has already arrived.
  • File the appeal with the clerk the next workday after viewing ends.
  • Attend the local board hearing, about a month after viewing.

The board considers only evidence presented with both sides there. Insurance papers, construction costs, listings and property descriptions count as proof, and a case with none fails. If the board sets a number above yours after bills are out, a supplemental bill arrives.

Homestead exemption and other breaks

Owners 65 and older, plus owners whose total disability is recognized by a federal or retirement program, can take the homestead deduction on their residence. It is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. File with the PVA and bring a license, passport or similar proof of age.

An age claim stays in force while the first applicant keeps living there. Most disability claims must be refiled yearly, but people with a service-connected disability and people permanently disabled under Social Security or the state retirement system are excused. A couple counts as one claimant, and a buyer files separately because the break travels with the person.

Churches, schools, charities and governments may be fully exempt under sections 170 and 171 of the Kentucky Constitution, after an application to the PVA.

What unpaid taxes turn into

Delinquency starts when April 15 ends. The sheriff sends the list to the County Clerk, each bill becomes a certificate of delinquency, and the lien in KRS 134.420 lasts eleven years, through any resale of the house.

Interest runs 1 percent a month, and commissions for the clerk and the county attorney follow. The statute puts the sale between three and four and a half months after transfer. A 30-day letter goes out before it, then a second letter if needed, then newspaper advertising of at least 30 days.

A buyer of the certificate may add costs, so paying the sheriff before the April deadline keeps the total small.

Selling with taxes owed

A sale does not erase back taxes, but it is a good moment to clear them. Ask the sheriff for a payoff while the bill is still with that office. After April 15 ask the clerk instead, since interest and fees have usually been added by then.

  • Give the payoff figure to the closing agent so it is paid from your proceeds.
  • Search the clerk's records for any lien on the parcel before you sign a contract.
  • Put the year's tax split in writing, because the bill follows the January 1 owner.

A buyer paying cash can skip bank appraisals and repair demands, and the balance owed still comes out of the sale money at the table. Bring your deed, your latest bill and a photo ID to closing. If the house was inherited, have the paperwork showing who now holds title, since the clerk's records must match before anything can be paid off or recorded.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I send a Rockcastle County tax payment?

To the sheriff's office at 205 E. Main St., Box 2, Mount Vernon, (606) 256-2032. The PVA at (606) 256-4194 only sets values and does not collect.

How much does early payment save in Rockcastle County?

Two percent of the bill, when all of it arrives by November 1 on the regular schedule. After that only the printed amount is owed until year end, and penalties begin in January.

What is the older owner deduction in Rockcastle County?

It is $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, subtracted from assessed value. Owners 65 or older, or with a total disability, apply through the PVA.

When can I speak to the Rockcastle County Fiscal Court?

At its monthly meeting on the second Tuesday, 1:00 p.m., in the courthouse. Ask for a place on the agenda 24 hours ahead.

What if my Rockcastle County bill remains unpaid after April 15?

The County Clerk receives it as a certificate of delinquency with a lien. Interest starts at 1 percent a month, and clerk and attorney commissions are added.

Courthouse offices and payment methods

The PVA and the sheriff both work out of the Rowan County Courthouse at 600 West Main Street in Morehead, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. The PVA, (606) 784-5512, assesses all taxable real and personal property, tracks ownership changes, keeps parcel maps and handles exemptions. The sheriff, (606) 784-5446, mails and collects the bills.

At the sheriff's window you can pay with cash, a check or a money order. Cards go through an outside vendor that charges 2.49 percent on amounts above $60 and a flat $1.50 on anything smaller. Anyone with a bill number handy can also pay online through the county's property tax page.

Once a bill turns delinquent, the County Clerk and the County Attorney take over from the sheriff. The county's delinquent taxes page describes how the three offices fit together.

Due dates and penalties

Rowan County's discount window runs later than the usual November 1 cutoff and closes on November 30. Bills go out at the start of November.

StageWhat applies

When a mailing runs late, the Department of Revenue can shift the calendar under KRS 134.015, so dates may move from year to year. The debt attaches to whoever held title on January 1, so a spring seller should plan to settle that year's bill.

Rowan County housing at a glance

Morehead is the seat and Lakeview Heights is the other city. Morehead State University and Cave Run Lake bring steady activity, and part of the Daniel Boone National Forest lies inside the county line. July 2025 population was estimated at 24,476, which is 0.7 percent under 2020. Owners live in 61.5 percent of homes across 9,592 households. A typical home is valued at $161,800 and typical gross rent is $825.

New construction is thin, with eight building permits in 2025, so most listings are existing houses. Because under two thirds of homes are owner-occupied, many parcels are rentals, and a landlord who sells will be asked who covers the year's bill.

Homestead exemption and the state rate

The state set its 2025 real estate rate at 10.6 cents per hundred dollars of assessment. Other taxing bodies stack their rates on it, and the sheriff can quote a combined figure for any address.

The deduction matters most for older owners on fixed incomes, and it does not carry over to a buyer. If you sell, the new owner has to file a claim of their own, so mention it during the closing conversation.

Owners from age 65, and owners who are totally disabled, can subtract $49,100 across 2025 and 2026. Apply with the PVA at the courthouse and bring a license or passport.

How Rowan County pursues delinquent taxes

After April 15 the bill rests with the County Clerk, and the county attorney follows a published timetable. Two letters go out on set dates, and the sale usually lands in mid August.

  • May 15: the County Attorney mails a 30-day notice.
  • June 15: a 60-day notice follows for bills still open.
  • Second week of August: the customary sale, where outside investors may buy a bill and add fees.
  • Each month: the delinquent amount climbs by 1 percent until it is paid.

The owner of record can sign a delinquent tax contract with the County Attorney's office up to three days before the sale. The county requires 10 percent of the bill that day and spreads the rest over monthly payments. A contract signed ahead of the clerk's sale keeps investors from buying the bill.

The County Attorney also presses the county's tax claim in foreclosure cases, where it holds priority.

How to contest a valuation

The first step is a required sit-down with the PVA or a deputy. The roll is open for inspection for thirteen days beginning May's first Monday, with the dates and appeal instructions advertised in the county's largest newspaper. At the sit-down the PVA explains how your figure was built and writes it up.

  • File the appeal with the clerk on the workday after viewing ends.
  • Prepare evidence: land and building descriptions, policies, construction costs, listings or sales. A case without any is rejected.
  • The hearing comes roughly a month after viewing, before a panel of local owners.
  • A hired agent must come from a statutory group, among them attorneys, CPAs and appraisers.

Bills printed before a ruling use your claimed value, and a supplemental bill follows if the board lands higher.

Does selling a Rowan County house clear back taxes?

It does not. KRS 134.420 puts a lien on the parcel once taxes turn delinquent, and the lien lasts eleven years under any owner. A title search at the County Clerk reveals it, and it is normally paid off at closing.

Debt grows fast after April 15, because interest, the clerk's commission and the county attorney's fees all join the bill. Paying the sheriff on time avoids that.

An owner who is behind has three routes before the August sale: pay the sheriff, pay the clerk, or sign a contract with the County Attorney. A direct cash sale is a fourth when repairs or inherited debts stand in the way, with the balance taken out of the proceeds.

Preparing to sell

Gather the paperwork before you list. A current bill, proof that prior years are paid and a copy of your deed answer most buyer questions. Here is a simple order to follow.

  1. Call the sheriff at (606) 784-5446 and confirm the current year shows paid or open.
  2. If any year is behind, ask for a payoff before April 15, or from the County Clerk after that date.
  3. Check with the clerk for any lien recorded against the parcel.
  4. Hand the payoff figure to the closing agent so the debt is paid from your proceeds.
  5. Decide in the contract who pays the current year's bill, since it follows the January 1 owner.

If the house is a rental, tell the buyer's side early which tenant, if any, stays after closing. The year's bill and any lien get sorted out in the same meeting, so it helps to have the lease and the tax paperwork on one desk.

Owners who inherited a house should also bring whatever shows who holds title now. The sheriff and the clerk will only deal with the owner of record, and a payoff quote cannot be finalized until the records match the person signing.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Rowan County discount end?

The county lists a 2 percent discount for bills paid before November 30. The printed amount is then due through December 31, and 5 percent is added in January.

Can I pay the Rowan County sheriff by card?

Yes: Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Discover, through a vendor that charges 2.49 percent above $60 or $1.50 below it. Cash, checks and money orders are welcome too.

How do I contact the Rowan County sheriff's office?

Call (606) 784-5446 or visit 600 West Main Street in Morehead, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM.

Is a payment plan possible once a Rowan County bill is delinquent?

Yes, through the County Attorney's office: 10 percent of the bill is due on signing day and the remainder is split into monthly payments. Sign before the sale to keep investors out.

Who handles questions about a Rowan County valuation?

The Property Valuation Administrator, at (606) 784-5512. A conference there comes before any appeal at the County Clerk.

Shelby County in brief

Between Louisville and Frankfort lies Shelby County, a member of the Louisville metro area. Shelbyville is the seat, joined by the incorporated cities of Simpsonville and Pleasureville. Bagdad, Finchville, Christianburg and Clay Village are unincorporated, so only county government serves them.

The county counted 51,243 people in July 2025, compared with 48,113 in April 2020, and has 20,391 housing units. Owners occupy most homes, and the drive to Louisville shapes who buys. Interstate 64 is the main route, with U.S. 60, U.S. 421, KY 53 and KY 55 connecting to it.

Home values and ownership

Shelby County housing figures, 2020 through 2024

With nearly three quarters of homes owned, most sales here involve a long-time resident rather than a landlord.

If your house sits in Shelbyville or Simpsonville, remember that city and county governments each have a say in what the final bill looks like. Ask the PVA which taxing districts apply to your parcel, so the number you see on the bill holds no surprises when you compare it with a buyer's estimate.

What the market looks like for sellers

Shelby County homes carry a median value of $304,800, and the $82,604 median household income supports that level. Buyers are often commuters who work in Louisville and want more space and a quieter street. Houses near Interstate 64 and on the Shelbyville side tend to draw the most attention, while the smaller unincorporated communities appeal to buyers who want acreage.

An owner who needs to move fast has a few choices. A traditional listing can bring the highest price but adds showings, an inspection and a commission. A cash sale gives up some price in exchange for speed and fewer steps. Ask each buyer what they expect from you at closing before you decide, and compare the net you would actually keep.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Shelby County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the PVA values your home

The Property Valuation Administrator runs a state office at the county level. Every parcel gets a value equal to what a willing buyer and a willing seller would settle on, measured on January 1. Rate setting and payment collection are handled elsewhere, not by the PVA. Your bill combines that assessed value with rates set by state, county and city governments, school boards and special districts. You can reach the PVA at 502-633-4403.

Ownership for tax purposes is fixed on January 1 too. A parcel bought after that date still produces a bill in the former owner's name until the next year, although the PVA tries to mail it to the new owner using the recorded deed. A new owner who gets nothing should call the Sheriff. Sellers should also check that no old bill sits unpaid in their own name.

If you plan to dispute the value, call early. Waiting until the roll closes leaves no room to gather sales data, and the PVA staff can tell you which records matter for your parcel.

Due dates and penalties

One statewide schedule governs (KRS 134.015). Settle the whole bill by November 1 and you save 2 percent. After that, the face amount is due through December 31 with no penalty. Wait until January and 5 percent is added, and later still it becomes 10 percent.

The Sheriff collects the bills, and the office number is 502-633-4324. After April 15, penalties and interest keep building because unpaid claims are filed with the County Clerk, who keeps the delinquent tax records. A statutory collection fee is added to delinquent bills (KRS 134.119). The Sheriff's website has a Current Tax Bill Lookup. Anyone paying someone else's bill, such as a tenant, a lender or a person holding an interest in the property, may do so under KRS 134.119 and can ask to be treated as a transferee.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the PVA. Under KRS 133.045 the assessment roll is open to the public for 13 days starting in early May, six days a week including one Saturday. You have to request a conference with the PVA before any formal appeal. The window repeats each spring.

Bring evidence. Sales of comparable houses nearby, a recent appraisal or repair estimates carry weight, and a request without paperwork rarely moves the number. If the conference leaves you unsatisfied, the notice explains how to file with the local assessment appeals board, and a state level tax appeals board hears cases beyond that.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Shelby County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and disability exemptions

Homeowners find most of their relief in the Homestead and Disability Exemptions, since the state constitution taxes everything it does not specifically exempt. Nothing applies automatically. The PVA has to receive your application first. Call 502-633-4403 for the current exemption amount and eligibility rules, because they can change from year to year.

Property tax when a Shelby County house sells

At closing the year's tax is usually divided between buyer and seller, and any balance still owing is paid off from the sale. Check the Sheriff's website before you sign, in case an earlier year is still open. The County Clerk handles deed recording and collects the seller's deed tax of $0.50 per $500 block (KRS 142.050).

  • PVA: assessments and exemptions, 502-633-4403.
  • Sheriff, 501 Main Street, Shelbyville: collects tax bills, 502-633-4324.
  • County Clerk: deed recording and delinquent tax records. Check the county website for the number.

Gather a few things before the closing date: the latest tax bill, any exemption paperwork, and a payoff letter if there is a mortgage. The title company or closing attorney will ask for each. A seller who has these ready rarely hits a delay over taxes.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing back taxes does not block a sale. Whether you list, sell on your own or take a cash offer, the balance is paid at the closing table. The first step in every case is a current payoff figure from the Sheriff. A cash buyer can usually price in the amount owed and skip the lender's repair and appraisal steps.

Plan the order of things. First, pull the bill on the Sheriff's website or call 502-633-4324 and ask what is owed to date, including any penalty. Second, confirm with the PVA that any exemption you claim is on file. Third, bring the payoff figure to whoever handles the closing so it comes out of your proceeds. The Sheriff's office at 501 Main Street serves walk-ins on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, holidays excepted, so a quick visit can settle questions in person.

If the bill is more than one year behind, the claim may already be with the County Clerk. Ask the Clerk for the delinquent record so no year is missed. Those older years add penalties and fees, so clearing them early keeps the closing on schedule.

One more habit helps: write down every call you make and the name of the office, the date and the figure you were given. If a figure changes between your first call and the closing, that record lets you ask why. Keep the written payoff in the closing folder so the person preparing the settlement statement uses the same number you do.

Frequently asked questions

When are Shelby County property taxes due?

Pay the whole bill by November 1 and it drops 2 percent. The printed amount stands through December 31. A January payment costs 5 percent more, anything later costs 10 percent more, and penalties and interest keep building after April 15.

Who gets the bill if a Shelby County house changes hands mid-year?

The bill is mailed to whoever owned the property on January 1. If you bought after that and nothing arrives, phone the Sheriff at 502-633-4324 or search the online bill lookup.

Where can I check a Shelby County tax bill?

Open the Current Tax Bill Lookup on the Sheriff's website or phone the office. Walk-ins are welcome at 501 Main Street in Shelbyville on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30, except holidays.

What does it take to claim a homestead exemption in Shelby County?

File a formal application with the Property Valuation Administrator, because nothing is granted without one. To hear the present age or disability rules, call 502-633-4403.

What deed tax does a Shelby County seller owe?

Fifty cents on each $500 of price, counting a partial block as a full one. The County Clerk takes the money at recording.

Bracken County in brief

Bracken County is small and entirely rural, laid out along the Ohio River in northern Kentucky. Brooksville holds the courthouse, Augusta is the biggest town, and Germantown is the third incorporated city. The 2025 estimate is 8,511 residents, and the county sits inside the Cincinnati metro area.

Housing is inexpensive. The typical owner's home is valued at $125,000, and owners live in 78.5% of homes. Typical rent is $756 a month, and a mortgaged owner pays about $1,144 a month. The 2020 count found 3,839 housing units, 13.3 percent of them empty. Few residents move (95.7 percent stayed in the same house for a year), and the average trip to work is 34.5 minutes. When a value dispute comes up, the sales records kept at the PVA are what the county appeals board looks at.

Who to call about a Bracken County tax bill

Valuing and collecting happen in separate offices that share the courthouse at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville.

Bracken County tax offices
OfficePhoneHandles
Property Valuation Administrator606-735-2228Assessment, property address, name and mailing address on the bill, exemptions
Sheriff's Office (second floor)606-735-3233Collecting this year's bill
County Clerk606-735-2952Bills from earlier years, on a separate check
  • Address or name wrong: fix it on the return stub or call the PVA.
  • Disagree with the value: call the PVA before paying.

An online portal shows bills and takes payment. Cards add a 2.50 percent charge that the cardholder pays and the sheriff does not keep. By mail, the check must cover the exact amount due.

Discount period and due dates

The 2 percent discount period runs October 1 through November 1, and bills go straight to owners. The bill itself prints the later cutoffs and penalty steps, and the sheriff's office can read them to you over the phone.

Escrow causes most of the trouble. The sheriff mails the bill to the owner, never to a mortgage company. If your lender pays from escrow, pass the bill along the day it arrives, or confirm that the lender has asked the sheriff for it. A check that bounces puts the bill back to unpaid, with a returned-check fee added and the repayment schedule printed on the bill.

Why a bill may carry the previous owner's name

For tax purposes, ownership freezes on January 1. If your purchase closes after that date, the bill for the year is addressed to the person who sold. The PVA works from recorded deeds to find new owners, and a buyer whose copy never turns up can ask the sheriff for one.

As a seller, you may see a bill arrive at an address you have already left. The settlement agent normally divides the year by days of ownership and either pays the sheriff or credits whichever side will. Leave a forwarding address with the closing agent.

How to challenge an assessment

Book a conference at the PVA first, because state rules require one before any appeal. The roll opens to inspection for thirteen days beginning the first Monday of May. File the appeal with the clerk by the next workday after those days end.

If the PVA raises a value above what you listed, KRS 132.450(4) requires the office to notify you. Anyone paid to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, broker, appraiser or other qualified professional, and must show your written authorization. Hearings may be recorded on audio.

What happens to an unpaid bill after April 15?

The sheriff hands every unpaid bill to the County Clerk, who records a lien and files each one as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk gives the Department of Revenue a list by May 15, and the Department publishes each county's list by June 1. On the normal schedule a tax sale can fall on any business day between July 14 and August 28.

Before that, the county attorney sends a 30-day letter and a second letter naming the sale date. The list is advertised in the paper with the biggest paid circulation between 30 and 45 days ahead, and posted online at least 30 days ahead. An owner who still owes at the sale risks having the lien assigned to an outside buyer, who may add fees.

Interest accrues at 1 percent for every month or fraction. The total grows sharply once the bill reaches the clerk, and grows again after the June advertising, so a prior-year bill should be paid as early as you can.

Homestead relief

Owners who turn 65 during the year or are permanently disabled can claim it. The state capped the exemption at $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. The house must be your owned, occupied and maintained residence on January 1, and the application is due at the PVA by December 31.

The sheriff tells eligible owners to phone the PVA before paying a bill that lacks the exemption, since the exemption shrinks the bill.

Paying a Bracken County bill, step by step

The sheriff's office collects on the second floor of the courthouse, and you have three ways to pay.

  1. In person: take the bill to the second floor at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville.
  2. By mail: send a check that matches the amount due exactly, with the return stub, so the sheriff can apply it to the right parcel.
  3. Online: use the sheriff's portal, remembering that the 2.50 percent card charge falls on you.

Whichever route you choose, confirm the name and mailing address printed on the bill. A wrong address is the PVA's to fix, and it explains most bills that never arrive. If you have more than one parcel, check each bill separately, since the sheriff handles each one on its own.

Prior-year bills are different. They are paid to the County Clerk on a separate check, never combined with the current year's payment to the sheriff.

What to have ready before listing

A buyer's title company will look for a clean tax record, so gather the facts first. Know whether the current bill is paid and in which period. Know whether any earlier year sits at the clerk. Confirm that the name and mailing address on the bill match the deed, and ask the PVA whether a homestead exemption applies to you.

If you live in an inherited house, check the bill's owner name too. Bills follow recorded deeds, so an estate that has not recorded a transfer can leave the old owner's name on the paperwork, and the buyer's agent will ask about it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How to sell a Bracken County house that owes tax

Treat the tax as a closing item. Get the present balance from the sheriff and any older balance from the clerk, and have the closing agent pay both from the proceeds.

  1. Call the sheriff at 606-735-3233 for this year's balance.
  2. Call the clerk at 606-735-2952 for any earlier year.
  3. Give both figures to the closing agent in writing.
  4. Ask the agent to split the current year with the buyer by days of ownership.

Inherited houses, houses with tenants and houses that need more work than a retail buyer will take on often sell to cash buyers who accept the property as it stands and pay the tax at the table.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Bracken County PVA's phone number?

606-735-2228, at the courthouse in Brooksville. The office handles assessments, mailing addresses on bills and homestead exemptions.

Where do I pay a Bracken County property tax bill?

At the sheriff's second-floor office in the courthouse, by mail, or through the sheriff's online portal. Card payments add 2.50 percent.

Does my mortgage company get my Bracken County tax bill?

No. The sheriff mails only to the owner. If your lender escrows taxes, forward the bill or ask the lender to request it.

Where do I pay a prior-year Bracken County bill?

At the County Clerk's office, 606-735-2952, with a separate check from the current year's payment.

Who owes tax on a Bracken County house sold in the spring?

The bill goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. Buyer and seller normally split the year at closing, and the agent pays the sheriff.

How Caldwell County taxes a house

Three local offices touch your bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a value on the house, the Caldwell County Sheriff takes payment, and the clerk inherits whatever is still open once April 15 passes. Value is locked in on January 1, and the state expects the PVA to visit each parcel at least every four years.

Your total is a sum of several taxing districts, including the state, the county and the schools. Each one chooses its own rate, and the PVA plays no part in that choice.

This is farm country, where land in agricultural use is taxed for what it produces, not for what it would sell for. Ten or more acres kept for livestock or crops, timber included, can qualify. If you own acreage, find out from the PVA how your land is classed before you list it.

Due dates and penalties

KRS 134.015 sets a monthly ladder that opens November 1 and closes April 15. Late October is when bills go out, now as letters instead of postcards. A payment counts for a phase if it is postmarked, handed over or dropped in the box before the next phase starts.

Caldwell County payment ladder
Payment monthDiscount or penalty

January5% extra
February 1 through April 1521% extra

Inside the Princeton courthouse, look for the first door on the right off Main Street. Staff accept cash, checks, money orders and cashier's checks, plus cards at the counter for a surcharge. After hours, use the drop box by the east door, which cannot hold cash. The office keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 4 pm and publishes a holiday closing list each season.

Which office answers which tax question

Most questions end at one of three numbers: 270-365-2088 (sheriff), 270-365-7227 (PVA) and 270-365-6754 (clerk). The PVA works upstairs at 100 East Market Street, and mail for the sheriff goes to Room 25 in that building.

  • Sheriff: sends bills, takes payment through April 15, and offers an online search that only displays bills.
  • PVA: sets values, handles homestead and disability forms, and hosts the conference required before an appeal.
  • County clerk: inherits delinquent bills and records deeds.

Bills are addressed to the January 1 owner. The sheriff never receives deed transfers, so a new owner's name shows up in care-of form the first year. A buyer whose bill went to the seller can print it from the sheriff's site.

How to dispute a Caldwell County value

Your first move is a PVA conference. Next comes a filing at the clerk's office, due by the workday after public inspection ends. Inspection covers 13 days starting the first Monday in May, and the local appeals board meets for up to five days, starting 25 to 35 days after that.

The board wants paper, not opinions: lot and building descriptions, insurance documents, building costs, and listings of comparable sales. An appeal with none is denied. Going around the local board also forecloses any later review. Since bills may print while your case is pending, you are billed on your own claimed value, with a supplemental bill if the board rules higher.

The number that survives is the one a buyer's lender and title company will see. After a new roof or an addition, make sure the PVA's record matches the house today.

Homestead exemption

Owners who live in their home and are 65 or older, or totally disabled, get part of the assessed value taken off. The deduction was $46,350 for 2024 and 2025. KRS 132.810 resets it every two years, so ask the PVA for today's figure.

You must occupy the house you own, show proof of age and claim no exemption anywhere else. Filling out the form at the PVA office takes under five minutes. The benefit belongs to you, not the house, so your buyer files a new application.

Before closing, an older seller should look for the exemption on the bill. If it is absent, take it up with the PVA ahead of paying.

Paying from outside Princeton

Owners who live away from Princeton, including heirs holding a house they plan to sell, have three workable routes. Mail a check to the sheriff at 100 East Market Street, Room 25, with the bill, and aim to post it before the end of the month so the postmark falls in the phase you want. Send someone to the courthouse counter. Or leave a check in the east-door drop box, which works at any hour except that it cannot hold cash.

The online search will show you the bill and its amount, though it will not take payment, and the sheriff does not take phone payments either. Print the bill and keep the receipt, because a title company may ask to see it.

What happens to the bill at closing

The lien rides with the parcel, while the closing agent shares the year out between buyer and seller. The sheriff never hears how a sale handled it, so your agent or lender is the one to ask.

With escrow, the bill still comes to you, and passing it to the lender is your task. A periodic call to the servicer keeps a missed hand-off from turning into a penalty.

Caldwell County housing market

Princeton is the seat of a county of 12,609 residents, with 6,122 homes counted in mid-2025. A typical owner's home is valued at $118,500. Owners occupy 70.2% of homes, rent runs about $767 a month, and household income is typically $59,583.

Most residents stay put, with 93.4 percent in the same home a year earlier, so listings tend to be estates, older owners or farm families. An owner dealing with repairs or a tenant may prefer a direct cash sale in place of showings.

Steps before a Caldwell County sale

  1. Phone the sheriff (270-365-2088) to learn if this year's bill is paid, and in which phase.
  2. Phone the clerk (270-365-6754) about any earlier year still open.
  3. Phone the PVA (270-365-7227) to check for a homestead exemption and, on acreage, the farmland classification.
  4. Pass each amount to the closing agent so it can be paid from your proceeds.

A cash buyer takes the house as-is, so repairs and showings drop away. Taxes do not: back taxes and liens come out of your proceeds either way. Starting these calls early leaves time to fix a wrong name or a missing exemption before a contract is signed.

What dates matter for Caldwell County tax bills?

Payment opens November 1, and the 2% discount holds through November 30. Face value applies in December, 5% is added in January, and 21% is added from February 1 to April 15. Whatever remains on April 15 moves to the county clerk.

Where can I pay a tax bill in Princeton?

Pay at the counter inside the courthouse, mail a check to 100 E. Market St., Room 25, or leave it in the east-door drop box. The online search displays bills only, and nobody takes payment by phone.

Is there a tax break for homeowners over 65 in Caldwell County?

Yes. An owner-occupant who turns 65 during the year can claim the homestead exemption at the PVA with proof of age. It lowers the assessed value, and a buyer has to file again on their own.

What if my Princeton house sells before the bill comes?

Billing follows the January 1 owner, so it may still arrive in your name. Expect the closing agent to prorate, and a buyer missing the bill can print one from the sheriff's site.

No, a cash buyer will take the house as-is. Back taxes and liens are deducted from what you receive, so get the amounts from the sheriff and clerk early.

Which offices handle property tax

In Johnson County the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a number on your parcel, the sheriff takes your money, and the county clerk holds the liens and the appeal paperwork. Calling the wrong desk costs a day, so keep the split straight.

Key tax dates

Value is struck on January 1, the roll opens for review on the first Monday of May, and bills arrive in the fall. Those dates come from Kentucky law, and the offices that act on them are Johnson County's own.

The review window lasts 13 days and includes Saturdays. Anything you want changed has to be raised in that window, and the sheriff's discount for early payment ends November 1. Business equipment and other personal property is listed with the PVA through May 15. Ask the sheriff to confirm each year's collection dates, because the state sometimes shifts them.

When a bill goes unpaid

On April 15 the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the Johnson County Clerk. The clerk records a lien, and the bill can end up in the hands of a private buyer.

A tax sale cannot come sooner than 90 days after the handoff, under KRS 134.128, and interest of 1 percent a month runs in the meantime. The county attorney writes to the owner, and the clerk publishes the delinquent list before the sale. A county that also sells overdue oil and gas or unmined mineral bills gets 60 extra days, which suits a coalfield county where those interests are billed apart from the surface.

  • The lien rides with the land, so a buyer inherits it unless it is cleared.
  • Whoever buys the bill at the sale can add fees of their own.
  • Letters go to the address on file, so an outdated address means missed warnings.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Johnson County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Ask the PVA for a conference in May. No filing with the board is allowed until that meeting has happened, and the PVA must explain how your number was built.

If the meeting settles nothing, file at the clerk's office by the following workday. A panel of local property owners hears the case. It must turn down any appeal that shows up without proof, for instance insurance policies, building costs or sales listings.

  • Ask which sales the PVA relied on for your house.
  • Get repair quotes if damage is missing from the record.
  • A paid representative must be an attorney, CPA, appraiser or another category the state recognizes.

Past the local board, the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals is the last stop. With median values near $120,000, even a few thousand dollars off the value shifts a bill, so the call is worth making.

Homestead and other exemptions

A homeowner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled under a federal or retirement plan, can take the homestead and disability deduction. One per household is the limit, and it travels with the owner, so a purchaser has to file fresh.

Kentucky resets the dollar amount every two years, so ask the Johnson County PVA for the current figure. Owners with a service-connected total disability and people ruled disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement file once, while those classed disabled by an out-of-state agency refile every year.

Churches, schools and charities apply on Revenue Form 62A023. Farmland is taxed on use value, a break that can be large where market prices run well above farm prices. Separately from property tax, the county charges an occupational tax of 0.5 percent on wages and net profit earned inside Johnson County.

Johnson County housing at a glance

Homes cost far less here than in Kentucky's metro areas, so any one assessment change matters more to a bill than a seller might expect.

Johnson County housing measures
MeasureJohnson County
Median home value$120,200
Median household income$44,904
Median gross rent$708
Owner-occupied rate68.3%

The county counted 22,680 people in 2020 and an estimated 22,051 in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent. Of its 10,493 housing units, 12.0 percent were vacant at the 2020 census, so buyers have choices and you should price with that in mind.

Floodplain rules touch some parcels. Building in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs both a state and a local permit, and the county asks owners to call (606) 789-2550 before any development. On a rural parcel, check the access road, the exact acreage and any flood zone before you set a price.

Coal, oil and mineral rights

Coal and oil shaped this county for more than a century, and many residents sold their mineral rights cheaply during the coal boom. That history is practical for a seller. Ask the title company whether minerals were severed from the surface on your parcel, and ask the sheriff whether a separately billed mineral or oil and gas tax bill is tied to it.

A mineral bill left unpaid can trigger its own lien and sale, so settle it before closing along with the surface bill.

Before closing

Three calls cover nearly every surprise: the sheriff for the bill and a payoff, the clerk for any certificate of delinquency, and the PVA for exemption status.

The county lists separate fire and rescue units for Paintsville, Van Lear, West Van Lear and others, and a Kentucky bill can stack school, city, county and fire levies. Ask the sheriff for a line-by-line breakdown. The seller's share is settled with the buyer at closing while the owner of record pays the full bill.

If you are selling for cash and want to move quickly, get the payoffs a week or two early, since a lien at the clerk has to be cleared before the deed can pass free of it. Keep the receipts with your closing papers.

Also confirm the mailing address the sheriff and county attorney have on file for you. Letters about a late bill go there, and if you moved out after listing, a warning can sit unopened while interest runs at 1 percent a month. Update the address at the sheriff's office or forward your mail until the deed is recorded.

If you filed for an exemption, tell the PVA when the sale closes, since the buyer has to apply on their own. Ask the clerk to confirm the deed was recorded and the tax lien search shows clear.

Frequently asked questions

Which office collects Johnson County property tax?

The Johnson County Sheriff, at (606) 789-3411.

Where is a Johnson County assessment appeal filed?

At the county clerk, 230 Court Street, Suite 124, Paintsville, once the PVA conference is done. The filing falls due the workday after the May review window shuts.

When does an unpaid Johnson County bill move to the clerk?

After April 15. The clerk then carries it as a certificate of delinquency with a lien on record.

Does a Johnson County homeowner get the 65 exemption automatically?

No. The owner applies through the PVA, and the home must be a primary residence.

Who decides Johnson County tax rates?

The taxing bodies on your bill, such as the Fiscal Court and the school districts. The PVA values property and the sheriff collects.

Who collects and who values

The bill passes through two desks. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a value on the parcel. The Sheriff is where the check goes. McCreary County has no incorporated city, so nobody in the county pays a city levy or visits a city tax window. County government is the only local government covering every resident, and school and district levies fill out the rest of the bill.

Write to the PVA at PO Box 609, Whitley City, KY 42653, phone (606) 376-2514, fax (606) 376-4152. The Sheriff is at (606) 376-2322. The County Clerk, who files deeds and takes over any unpaid bill, is at (606) 376-2411. The fiscal court meets at 1 North Main Street in Whitley City on the second Thursday evening of the month, starting at six.

Due dates and penalties

Under KRS 134.015, value is fixed on January 1 and the bill is meant to be settled before the calendar year closes. The Sheriff will still accept money until April 15, but each step later costs more.

What a McCreary County bill costs by payment date
When you payWhat changes
By November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount on the bill
January5 percent added
After January10 percent added

Miss April 15 and the account goes to the County Clerk. The county attorney mails two warnings, and the tax certificate can be put up for sale three to four and a half months after that handoff. A buyer of the certificate can tack on fees, so square things with the Sheriff first.

What a McCreary County house costs in tax

Bills here are low by Kentucky standards because home values are low. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $85,300. Frankfort's 2025 rate is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value, and the fiscal court, school board and special districts each layer on a levy of their own. Ask the PVA to total them for a specific address.

Owners live in about 74.2 percent of homes. A typical rent runs $577 a month. New construction was nil in 2025, with 0 permits, so the market is almost entirely existing houses. The population was 17,124 in 2025, and the 2020 count showed 6,892 housing units, with about one in eight vacant.

Homestead exemption

The statewide homestead deduction reaches McCreary County owners too. Turn 65, or be classed as totally disabled, and $49,100 comes off the assessed value for tax years 2025 and 2026 before any rate touches it. On a house near the $85,300 median, that removes a large share of the taxable value.

File in person at the Whitley City PVA office with a birth certificate, driver's license or passport showing your age. A disability claim rests on a government or retirement-plan finding and must be filed again each year. The yearly renewal is waived for owners with a service-connected disability rating and for anyone Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems has found permanently and totally disabled.

How to appeal your assessment

Sit down with the PVA or a deputy first. Appeals from owners who skipped that meeting get turned away, and the staff are required to show how your figure was reached. Then:

  • Inspect the roll during the 13 days that follow the first Monday in May.
  • Deliver the written appeal to the County Clerk on or before the first business day after the roll closes.
  • Attach evidence about land and buildings: insurance records, construction costs, comparable sales and photographs. A survey helps with rural tracts. Appeals with no support tend to fail.
  • Go to the hearing of the local board of property owners, held about a month after the roll closes. Evidence is taken only with both sides in the room.

No-shows give up the next stage, the Kentucky Claims Commission. When bills are already printed and the board lands above your claimed value, a supplemental bill collects the gap.

Selling with taxes owed

A tax debt follows the house to closing. From January 1 the law treats it as the owner's personal obligation, and a KRS 134.420 lien can hang on for 11 years under any owner. When the account reaches the Clerk, 1 percent interest accrues monthly, and the Clerk and county attorney add commissions along with a recording fee.

Closing agents want a payoff number before funds move. The Sheriff quotes it up to April 15, then the Clerk. Order it early, since the sale price must cover it before the seller nets anything.

For an heir or an owner who has fallen behind, a cash sale as-is skips repair bills and showings and lets you pick a closing date around the payoff. The tax comes out of the proceeds in every case.

Selling a house in McCreary County

McCreary is Kentucky's newest county, carved in 1912 out of Pulaski, Wayne and Whitley, and no incorporated city sits within it. Whitley City is the seat, with Pine Knot and Stearns as the other named communities. Federal land takes up much of the map. The Daniel Boone National Forest covers roughly 43 percent and the Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area roughly 18 percent, so private land is limited.

Population peaked at 18,306 in 2010 and fell 7.7 percent to 16,888 by 2020, then rose 1.4 percent to the 2025 figure. Residents 65 and older make up 17.9 percent of the population, which matters for homestead claims. Prices sit near the county's low median home value, so price carefully and expect buyers to compare against nearby rentals.

What to bring to the office

Keep a small folder ready before you call or drive to Whitley City. For the PVA, that means a photo ID, proof of age for a homestead claim, and a copy of your deed. For the Sheriff, bring the parcel number or your last bill so staff can find the account quickly. For the County Clerk, bring any lien notice you have received. Phone ahead, since each office keeps its own hours, and ask what forms of payment the Sheriff takes before you go.

Steps to close a sale

Sales here follow a set order. Get the payoff from the Sheriff or Clerk. Ask the PVA whether a homestead claim sits on the parcel, because dropping it changes the next bill. Collect the deed and any lien papers, and give the payoff to the closing agent so tax is cleared from proceeds. The County Clerk files the new deed after closing.

A house that came through an estate usually needs extra deed work, so bring papers proving who may sell.

Before listing, compare the PVA's record with what you intend to sell: acreage, building description and owner name. A wrong acreage figure is easy to correct with PVA staff, and much harder once a buyer's lender notices it. Rural tracts are where mismatches turn up most, and a recent survey usually settles the question.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a city property tax in McCreary County?

No, since no incorporated city exists here. The bill still carries school and district levies.

Who do I pay for McCreary County property tax?

Send it to the Sheriff, (606) 376-2322, up to April 15. The PVA, (606) 376-2514, handles values and exemption forms, never payments.

What is the state rate for 2025?

It is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value. Local levies are added by the county, school board and districts.

Can a 65-year-old lower the taxable value?

Yes. Show proof of age at the Whitley City PVA office and the homestead deduction removes $49,100 for 2025 and 2026.

What happens if my bill moves to the County Clerk?

The Clerk records a lien and 1 percent monthly interest starts. An investor may buy the certificate three to four and a half months later.

Who handles Bell County property tax

Bell County bills move through the same chain of offices as any Kentucky county, and a fourth office steps in once a bill goes delinquent.

  • The Bell County PVA values real estate, takes age and disability exemption forms, and schedules appeal conferences.
  • The Bell County Sheriff sends the bills each fall and collects the money.
  • The Bell County Clerk, whose office keeps weekday hours, files deeds, mortgages and liens and takes in bills that go delinquent.
  • The county attorney mails the warning letters that follow a transfer and can set up payment plans.

The City of Pineville posts its own property tax page, and the sheriff has collected Pineville's tax on the county bill since tax year 2020. The city's page shows 27.6 cents for each $100 of assessed real property value, but call city hall for the rate on your bill.

The clerk's recording room matters to sellers for another reason. The Bell County courthouse burned in 1914 and 1918, and a 1977 flood damaged it and destroyed stored documents. If an old deed or probate record looks incomplete, ask the clerk what the recorded chain shows.

Due dates

KRS 134.015 sets the cycle. In a year when collection starts after November 1, the state grants 30 days per stage instead of the usual dates.

On the usual calendar, paying by November 1 saves 2 percent, the bill stands at face value through December, January adds 5 percent, and February 1 to April 15 carries a combined 21 percent. Payment is made to the sheriff.

The tax belongs to the person on title each January 1. A Bell County seller closing in spring therefore owes that year's bill unless the sales contract shifts it. If no bill reaches you, the sheriff can provide a duplicate.

How to challenge an assessment

Phone the Bell County PVA and request a conference during the May inspection period. Kentucky requires that meeting before any filing, and the period lasts roughly two weeks.

The conference is worth taking seriously even if you expect to lose. Bring photos, estimates and any sales you found, and ask the PVA to show what the record says about your house. Plain errors, such as a wrong square footage or a finished space that doesn't exist, are easiest to correct at this stage and cost nothing.

If the two of you stay apart, the paperwork goes to the clerk on the next business day after inspection closes. The state's own example: an inspection ending May 20 means a May 21 filing. Write your claimed value on the form.

  • A three-member local board hears the case roughly a month later.
  • Bring evidence: comparable sales, a contractor's estimate or an appraisal.
  • The PVA defends the assessed figure.
  • A certified letter reports the outcome and what to do next.

With typical values near $89,000, small gaps matter. A house with a failing roof or foundation can be valued like a sound neighbor unless you document the problem.
