Hancock County in brief

Hancock County sits on the Ohio River on Kentucky's northwest side, inside the Owensboro metro area. Hawesville is the seat and Lewisport is the largest town. The 2020 count was 9,095 residents and the July 2025 estimate is 9,050, with 3,968 housing units. Owners hold 77.2 percent of households, the typical owned home is valued at $141,200, and typical rent is $740. Only 15 building permits were counted for 2025, so a Hancock County seller is usually offering a resale house in a small market where new construction rarely sets the price.

With a typical home near $141,200, a few years of missed tax bills plus penalties can take a visible bite out of a sale price, which is why it pays to settle the account before listing.

Which office does what

Three offices share the Hancock County Administration Building at 225 Main Cross Street in Hawesville, and each has a separate job.

  • Sheriff, first floor: takes payment. Phone 270-927-6247, mail to P.O. Box 427. Posted hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.
  • PVA: values property and has no say over rates or payments. It reads the market each January 1 and aims for what a willing buyer would pay. Phone 270-927-6846, mail to P.O. Box 523.
  • County Clerk, second floor: keeps land records and processes delinquent real estate taxes. Phone 270-927-6117, mail to P.O. Box 146.

The state Department of Revenue supervises the PVA and runs yearly studies in every county to check that assessments meet constitutional standards.

Due dates and penalties

Bills reach the sheriff by mid September. Until then the PVA mails the current-year bill to whatever in-care-of address appears in the deed. KRS 134.015 sets the discount and face-value windows.

Payment windows for a Hancock County bill
Payment windowWhat you owe
On or before November 1Face amount less a 2 percent discount
Rest of the yearFace amount
January5 percent penalty added
After January 3110 percent penalty plus a 10 percent sheriff fee, described by the state as 21 percent combined

When the state delays mailing, an alternative schedule gives 30 days per stage. The bill in your hand carries the dates that apply. Whoever owned the house on January 1 is the taxpayer of record for that year, so a closing in October or November is the moment to ask the sheriff for the exact discount cutoff.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Hancock County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Occupational tax for rental owners

Rental property owners, farmers and home-based businesses with activity in Hancock County pay an occupational tax on net profits. The rate on business profits has been 1.60 percent since January 1, 2020, and an annual business license costs $10.

Employees working inside the county pay 1.60 percent of gross wages, withheld by the employer. Two exceptions apply: a company employing more than 100 people in manufacturing in the county does not owe the net profits fee, and neither does a business that pays the county a franchise tax.

A landlord selling a Hancock County rental should expect a net profits return for the year of the sale. The Occupational Tax Office, on the third floor, answers at 270-927-8788.

How to appeal your assessment

Meet the PVA first. Call 270-927-6846 to book a conference in the spring inspection window, which no appeal can skip. If the talk ends without a deal, you have one workday after the window closes to file with the clerk upstairs, along with the value you claim.

A three-person local appeals board hears the case about five weeks later and expects evidence from you. The Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals hears anything further. Ask the PVA which sales it relied on, then bring your own comparable sales.

Homestead exemption

Owners aged 65 and up, and owners classified as totally disabled, can ask the PVA to lower the taxable value of their own residence. KRS 132.810 allows one exemption per household unit and treats a manufactured house as a unit. After a sale, the old owner reports the transfer and the new owner applies separately. Ask the PVA for the dollar figure in force.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Hancock County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Timing a sale around the tax year

The bill covers a full calendar year and is owed by whoever held the house on January 1, so the seller normally carries it even after a fall closing. Many contracts split it at the table. Ask your closing agent how yours does.

If you list in spring, check where the bill stands before April 15, because after that date the clerk holds it and charges add up. If you list in summer, certificate sales begin in July, so settle any open balance first. A seller with several unpaid years and a house that needs work may find that a cash buyer buying as is can close fast enough to pay everything off from the proceeds, without repairs or lender delays.

Checklist before closing

A short checklist keeps surprises away from the table.

  • Confirm the deed carries a mailing address for the new owner's tax bill, which KRS 382.135 requires.
  • Ask the sheriff whether a current-year bill is open and who will pay it, since the bill covers a full calendar year.
  • Search the parcel through the clerk's website, which links a delinquent tax tool (DTax) and eCCLIX, a viewer for filed land records that helps when a house came through an estate.
  • Pull permits for any addition. Planning and Zoning is at 200 Court Square, P.O. Box 692, open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 8 a.m. to noon at 270-927-8169.

The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission holds evening meetings every other month, starting the first Monday of February.

What happens to an unpaid bill?

A bill still open when April 15 ends leaves the sheriff and lands with the clerk as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk's DTax tool shows what the county believes is owed on a parcel, and the clerk sets the true figure at payment or sale. Interest, a clerk commission and later an attorney commission pile on, and a buyer of the certificate adds more. A seller who plans to list in summer should pay or collect a written payoff before certificate sales begin in July.

Back taxes do not block a sale. The settlement agent pays the payoff from the proceeds, the same way it works with a cash buyer who purchases as is. Ask the clerk for the payoff in writing, dated close to the closing day, because interest keeps accruing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do rental owners in Hancock County pay occupational tax?

Yes. Rental property owners pay on net profits at 1.60 percent, plus a $10 annual business license. The Occupational Tax Office at 270-927-8788 takes the forms.

When does the Hancock County Urban Planning Commission meet?

Every other month, starting with the first Monday of February. Meetings begin at 7 p.m. on the third floor of the Administration Building, 225 Main Cross Street.

How can I view recorded deeds for a Hancock County house?

Through eCCLIX on the County Clerk's website, which lets you view or print filed documents. Questions go to 270-927-6117.

I bought a Hancock County home and never got a tax bill. Who do I call?

The sheriff at 270-927-6247 can provide a copy. The PVA mails the bill to the address in the deed until preparation begins in mid September, which is why that address matters.

Is the PVA or the sheriff the office that takes the payment?

The sheriff. The PVA's role ends at valuation, and payments go to the Hancock County Sheriff's Office on the first floor.

Who sends, values and collects the bill in Lyon County

The Lyon County Sheriff collects, the county's valuation administrator (the PVA) sets values, and the County Clerk takes over when a bill goes stale after April 15. The Sheriff's office handles about seven million dollars a year under KRS 134.140 and 160.500, which cover state, county, school and district tax on real, tangible and intangible property.

Find the Sheriff at 500 West Dale Avenue, Suite 100, Eddyville. Its mailing box is PO Box 126, Eddyville, KY 42038. The PVA operates from 500 B West Dale Avenue and answers at 270-388-7271. For prior-year delinquent bills, the Sheriff directs taxpayers to the County Clerk at 270-388-2331.

Both the Sheriff and the PVA work on West Dale Avenue, so one visit can answer two questions. Call before you go: the Sheriff cannot accept money until bills arrive from the clerk around the end of September.

Lyon County housing and the lake

Water covers a sixth of the county. Lyon County totals 257 square miles, 43 of them water, with Lake Barkley on the Cumberland River along its south side. Eddyville is the seat, and neighboring Kuttawa sits nearby. Both towns were relocated to higher ground when Barkley Dam backed up the lake. Interstates 24 and 69 cross at Eddyville, and Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area faces Kuttawa across the water.

The county had 9,123 residents in the 2025 estimate and 4,889 housing units. Owners occupy 80.4 percent of homes, and 26.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. The typical home value is $189,500, typical rent is $747 a month, and typical household income is $65,066. The 2020 census found 4,780 housing units, with 30.4 percent of them vacant. The market is small and mostly owner-held, and a seller here often prices against lake access as well as square footage.

Storms have left marks on the housing stock. An EF4 tornado tore through Eddyville and the county on December 10 and 11, 2021, damaging or destroying hundreds of homes and businesses, and an EF3 touched down near Eddyville on May 26, 2024. If your house was repaired or rebuilt, tell the PVA, because the January 1 value follows the property's condition.

Payment calendar

Your payment counts if it is received or postmarked by the date shown. The Sheriff gets bills from the clerk late in September, so statements normally land in mailboxes during early October.

Past April 15Clerk holds the bill; further penalties may apply

No bill by October 10? The Sheriff will send a duplicate. The tax year is the calendar year, so the bill covers January through December of the year printed on it.

The office accepts checks, money orders and cards, with the card processor charging a fee, and the same options are online. Partial payments are refused, though a single payment can cover several bills. For owners who find the lump sum hard, the Sheriff suggests checking for exemptions and asking a lender about escrow.

Who pays when a Lyon County house sells?

Kentucky addresses the bill to the January 1 owner, even if the house has since changed hands. The Sheriff says a closing agent or attorney usually works out each side's share of the year. Some agents then pay the Sheriff directly, and in other deals one party receives a credit and pays later.

  • Prorated payments are refused. Someone must cover the full bill.
  • Mortgage companies do not automatically get the statement. Lenders can pull data from the PVA roll, yet the owner must make sure the lender actually has the bill.
  • If a bill arrives in your name after a sale, send it on to the new owner at your former address.

Get the closing agent to confirm in writing who pays the Sheriff and by when, and keep the receipt.

How to appeal your assessment

Confer with the PVA first, then lodge the appeal at the clerk's office. State rules give you until the end of the workday after the roll's public viewing period closes, and that period opens in early May and runs about two weeks.

A local panel then takes up the matter about a month after viewing ends. It wants facts: photographs, an appraisal, insurance policies, construction costs or listings. A written decision explains any change and describes the next step to the state tax appeals board.

Bring photographs of the house, any appraisal, repair invoices and your insurance policy to the conference, and ask the PVA how the current value was reached. A conference often settles a question without a hearing, but the filing deadline at the clerk's office still applies if it does not.

Call the PVA at 270-388-7271 each spring for the exact dates, since the window can be shifted and the change is advertised locally.

Homestead and disability exemptions

A senior, or an owner classed as totally disabled, who occupies the home can deduct $49,100 from the assessed value for the 2025 to 2026 assessment years.

The Sheriff sends people who struggle to pay toward these exemptions and refers questions about them to the PVA at 270-388-7271. File with the PVA, not the Sheriff or clerk. Disability claimants normally reapply annually, except those with a service-connected disability and people whom Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement Systems has ruled permanently and totally disabled.

Selling a Lyon County house with tax owed

Get the payoff in writing from the correct office and let the closing agent pay it out of your proceeds. This year's balance comes from the Sheriff, and earlier years come from the County Clerk.

Delinquent bills get advertised before any sale, and the county attorney sends notices, so early action avoids added fees. Interest builds at one percent monthly once the clerk takes the bill, with clerk and attorney commissions on top. Have the closing agent pay any recorded lien from the sale proceeds so the house passes to the buyer with a clean tax record.

Bring the deed and your latest bill to the Sheriff's or clerk's office when you ask for the payoff, and ask how long the figure stays good. A cash sale moves fast, so having that number ready before you accept an offer keeps the closing on schedule.

Frequently asked questions

Where does Lyon County send its property tax payments?

Payments go to the Lyon County Sheriff at 500 West Dale Avenue, Suite 100, Eddyville, or by post to Box 126 in Eddyville (KY 42038). An online link on the Sheriff's tax page also works. Past April 15, pay the County Clerk.

How large is the Lyon County early-payment discount?

It is 2 percent, for money received or postmarked between October 1 and November 1. The stated amount applies through year end, and a 5 percent penalty begins in January.

Will the Lyon County Sheriff take a partial payment?

No. Partial payments are refused. A single payment may cover several bills, and the Sheriff suggests checking exemptions or lender escrow if the full amount is hard to meet.

If I sell my Lyon County home in June, who pays that year's tax?

The January 1 owner is billed, and the closing agent usually prorates each side's share at the table. The Sheriff needs the whole bill paid, so confirm in writing who sends the payment.

How much is the Lyon County homestead exemption?

The deduction is $49,100 for seniors and totally disabled owners living in their homes, set for the 2025 to 2026 assessment years. Apply through the PVA at 270-388-7271.

Courthouse offices and phone numbers

Everything runs through the courthouse at 125 East Main Street in Carlisle. The PVA (the county's property valuation office) is in the basement, answers at 859-289-3735 and keeps hours from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays. The Sheriff's Office, at 859-289-3740, collects what is owed.

Mail to the PVA goes to P.O. Box 2, Carlisle, KY 40311. The PVA website carries the certified tax roll, a tax estimator, forms and a fee schedule. The sheriff only collects. Argue a value with the PVA, and ask the sheriff where and how to pay.

Thinking of selling? Make both calls now. The PVA can tell you the classification and roll value, and the sheriff can say whether every year is paid.

The county in brief

Nicholas is a small, rural county with Carlisle as its seat. Construction is rare, which means nearly every sale is a resale, and one or two closings can move the local averages.

  • Population is 7,949 for July 2025, up 5.5% from the 2020 base.
  • There are 3,355 housing units, and only 3 building permits were issued in 2025.
  • Owners occupy 74.5% of homes.
  • The midpoint value of an owned house is $123,000.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,143 with a mortgage and $426 without.
  • Gross rent has a midpoint of $728, and household income a midpoint of $59,531.

Plenty of properties here are farms, or houses with a trade or home business on the same lot. If you own acreage, ask the PVA how the land, the barns and the house are each classed before you compare your value with a neighbor's.

Due dates and penalties

Tax statements land in mailboxes about October 1, and KRS 134.015 sets the payment schedule that follows.

Nicholas County bill totals under the state due-date statute
Date paidConsequence
No later than November 1Two percent off the total
November 2 through year endThe total printed on the bill
During JanuaryFive percent added
Past January 31Ten percent added

The statute stops at 10%, but some Kentucky sheriffs post a higher charge for the stretch between February and mid-April. Call 859-289-3740 for the figure that applies on your payment date.

That statute also treats the tax, fees, penalties and interest as the taxpayer's own debt starting on the assessment date. Closing close to a cutoff? Get the sheriff's payoff in writing instead of trusting the bill.

How to appeal your assessment

You cannot skip the first step: sit down with the Nicholas County PVA or a deputy. KRS 133.120 makes that conference a prerequisite, and it can happen before or during the inspection window or an extension of it. Staff lay out the rules and how they got your number, and the office keeps a note of the talk.

Under KRS 133.045 the roll stays open for inspection for 13 days from the first Monday in May. If you still disagree afterward, hand the County Clerk a letter or petition naming the parcel, your reasons and what you think fair cash value is. It is due the next workday after inspection ends, and you may make an audio recording when the county hears your case.

Useful evidence includes nearby sales of similar houses, contractor repair quotes and photos of problems. Filing never postpones payment. You pay on your stated value, and the final value decides what else is owed, with interest.

Homestead exemption

A homeowner who is 65 or older, or who a federal agency or retirement system has classed as totally disabled, can claim a state deduction of $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. File at the PVA in the courthouse basement. Disability claims must be renewed each year. Owners with a service-connected disability, and those found permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or the state retirement system, are exempt from that renewal.

The benefit follows the person, not the house, so a qualifying buyer files a new application after the sale.

Who receives the bill after a purchase?

Value and ownership are both fixed as of January 1. Someone who buys later in the year does not get billed until the following calendar year, so the earlier owner receives that bill. If the buyer or seller signed a tax agreement, the PVA uses it to send the buyer a duplicate. Nothing in the mail? The sheriff, at 859-289-3740, can print one.

  • Seller: make sure this year's bill is settled, and hold on to the receipt.
  • Buyer: put a mailing address on the deed, which KRS 382.135 demands.
  • Both sides: write the proration into the contract.
  • Estates: the executor files an affidavit listing heirs and estimated values with the County Clerk.

Selling with taxes owed

A sale does not wipe out unpaid tax. KRS 134.420 lets the lien from a delinquent bill last up to eleven years, attached to the parcel no matter who owns it. If you think an old year might still be open, ask the sheriff before you list, because the buyer's title agent will ask the same question.

  1. Request a payoff from the sheriff that spans each open year.
  2. Pay on or before closing day so the lien can come off.
  3. Give the closing agent a copy of the receipt.
  4. Divide the current year between you in the contract.

Carlisle sits at the center of a farm county, so many sellers are heirs or owners of older homes on a few acres. If that is you, line up the deed, the last tax receipt and a contact for the person who will sign at closing before you call a buyer.

A cash purchase avoids bank underwriting and lender repair demands. It does not avoid the lien, which has to be paid off at closing. Almost no new houses go up here, so buyers are mostly comparing older homes, and a clean tax record removes one point of haggling.

Before you list a Nicholas County house

Gather a few papers before the first showing. Start with this year's tax bill and proof it was paid. Find your parcel on the certified roll at the PVA's website and read the owner name, acreage and classification. A mismatch with your deed is something the PVA can fix, and it goes faster when no buyer is waiting.

Then settle how this year's tax gets divided. Whoever owned on January 1 gets the full-year bill, so a spring or summer seller normally gives the buyer a credit for the months after closing. Spell that out in the contract. For an estate sale, collect the executor's papers and plan the heirs-and-values affidavit with the County Clerk.

One last step: phone the sheriff a few days ahead of closing. Records can lag behind a recent payment, and a fresh figure takes two minutes.

Frequently asked questions

Where does Nicholas County keep its PVA?

The PVA works from the courthouse basement at 125 East Main Street in Carlisle, with weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30 and a phone at 859-289-3735.

Who gets a Nicholas County bill after the house sells?

The seller is billed until the next calendar year. A buyer who never gets a copy can call the sheriff at 859-289-3740.

How much does paying early save in Nicholas County?

Two percent comes off when the full bill is paid by November 1. From then through December 31 you owe the printed total.

What penalty follows January in Nicholas County?

KRS 134.015 sets 5% for January and 10% after January 31. Ask the sheriff for the exact payoff, since a higher late charge may apply in late winter and spring.

What does the homestead exemption remove in Nicholas County?

The state takes $49,100 off assessed value once a qualifying owner applies at the PVA. Qualifying means 65 or over, or totally disabled, and the figure covers tax years 2025 and 2026.

Which Stanton offices handle a tax account?

Three counters in Stanton cover nearly every question a Powell County owner will have. The PVA puts a value on each parcel. The sheriff collects the money. The county clerk holds deeds and the lien paperwork. Rates are voted elsewhere, by the fiscal court, the school board and the library, extension and health districts that appear on a bill.

The PVA sits at 525 Washington Street, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 277, Stanton, KY 40380, and a fax line at (606) 663-0947. Call before visiting, since hours at the sheriff's office and the clerk's office vary by weekday.

How the PVA values a Powell County house

The office appraises each parcel at fair market value for January 1, and it never decides what you owe, since the bill multiplies that value by rates other bodies set. Cars and trucks get the same January 1 treatment. Staff start from NADA guides and can lower a figure for high mileage or for two written repair estimates from body shops.

Owners are not obliged to relist land each spring when last year's roll described it correctly and nothing major changed. After a purchase, the price on the deed can serve as the listed value the following January 1. For Powell County buyers that means a recent sale price often becomes the next assessment.

Business equipment and other personal property goes on a list filed with the PVA between January 1 and May 15, and anything missed by May 15 is treated as omitted and billed later.

Payment dates in Powell County

KRS 134.015 sets the usual calendar for the whole state, and the sheriff collects:

  • Settle everything by November 1 and 2 percent comes off.
  • From November 2 into December, the printed amount applies.
  • January adds 5 percent.
  • February and later add 10 percent, and the Department of Revenue's examples show a sheriff's fee on top.

When mailing slips, the Department can switch to a shifted calendar that gives each stage one month from the mailing date. Which version applies in a given year is printed on the bill, and the sheriff at (606) 663-2226 can confirm it. Once April 15 passes, the sheriff hands whatever remains to the clerk, who records a lien.

What a Powell County owner pays

For 2025 the state rate fell to 10.6 cents per hundred dollars of assessment, down from 10.9 cents in 2024. County, school and district levies come on top, so only the bill for your address gives the final total. Early payment trims 2 percent.

At a sale, the bill follows the person who held title when the year began. Put the split of the year's bill into the contract, and ask the sheriff for a payoff number ahead of closing.

How to push back on a value

The sequence matters. Meet the PVA or a deputy first, because the board turns away any case that skipped that step. The tax roll lies open for inspection for thirteen days starting on May's first Monday, Saturdays included, and a higher assessment must come with written notice under KRS 132.450.

  • At the meeting the PVA explains the method and writes down your claimed number.
  • The written appeal goes to the clerk on the workday right after the inspection window shuts.
  • Hearings begin about a month after inspection and can run up to five days.
  • Bring proof: building and land details, insurance policies, construction cost, sales listings. No proof means a denial.

A paid advocate must belong to a listed profession, such as lawyer, CPA, broker or certified appraiser, and carry your signed authorization. Should the board land above your claim after bills are printed, a supplemental bill covers the gap.

Homestead deduction for older and disabled owners

The state fixed the deduction at $49,100 for assessments in 2025 and 2026. Seniors from age 65 and people classed as totally disabled receive it on the house they occupy. File at the PVA office on Washington Street and bring a document that proves your age.

A couple gets one deduction, and either spouse turning 65 is enough. After approval, an age-based claim rolls forward while the same person lives there. Disability claims are renewed every year, with exceptions for owners whose disability is service-connected and for people with a permanent finding from a federal or state retirement program.

The benefit belongs to the person, so a buyer must file again after a sale.

What if taxes on a Powell County house are never paid?

Transferring the deed does not erase them. Under Kentucky law the tax is a personal debt of the owner from the assessment date, and the lien described in KRS 134.420 lasts eleven years whoever takes title next. A title search will find it.

After April 15, 1 percent a month starts, and the clerk's and county attorney's costs are added at each stage. A clerk's sale follows roughly three to four and a half months after transfer, and whoever buys the certificate gains a lien carrying its own interest and costs. A payment to the sheriff ahead of mid April sidesteps every one of these costs.

Powell County housing in brief

Powell County, with Stanton as its seat and Clay City as its only other town, covers about 179 square miles of foothills and holds part of the Daniel Boone National Forest. Natural Bridge State Resort Park and the Red River Gorge bring walkers and climbers, and nearly all home sales involve existing houses.

  • July 2025 population estimate of 12,812, which is 2.4 percent below the 2020 base.
  • Owners occupy 68.2 percent of housing units, spread over 4,790 households.
  • Typical home value $141,100, typical rent $747.
  • Household income of $40,309 at the midpoint.
  • Five building permits in 2025.

Workers commute 26.6 minutes on average. A house that needs work or carries back tax can still move quickly through a direct cash purchase, with the bill paid at the closing table.

Steps before you sell a Powell County house

  1. Call the sheriff at (606) 663-2226 and ask whether this year's bill is paid and whether the calendar on the bill is the regular one or a shifted one.
  2. Ask the clerk, (606) 663-6444, whether any delinquent bill or lien is recorded against the parcel.
  3. Check with the PVA, (606) 663-4184, that the owner name and exemption on file match your deed.
  4. Agree with the buyer in writing on how the year's bill will be split.
  5. Get a payoff figure for any open year before the closing date, and pay it from your proceeds.

Doing these in order means the title search finds nothing new, and a buyer sees a house with a clear record.

Where does a Powell County tax payment go?

The sheriff, reachable at (606) 663-2226. The PVA, at (606) 663-4184, only assigns values and neither bills nor collects.

What does early payment save on a Powell County bill?

Two percent when the whole amount arrives by November 1 on the regular calendar. A shifted calendar gives one month from the mailing date.

How much is the older homeowner deduction in Powell County?

$49,100 for assessments in 2025 and 2026, subtracted from the home's value for owners at 65 and up or those totally disabled. The PVA supplies the form.

Can I go straight to the appeals board?

No. A meeting at the PVA office must come first. The appeal is then filed with the county clerk on the workday after inspection ends.

If I sell, do old Powell County taxes transfer to the buyer?

Delinquent amounts can. A lien lasting up to eleven years stays on the parcel, so the closing statement should pay off whatever is open.

Who handles property tax at the courthouse

Todd County puts its tax work in one building: the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street in Elkton. All three offices answer through the county switchboard at (270) 265-9966, each on its own extension.

  • Sheriff, ext. 208: takes payment of property tax bills. The sheriff's website lets owners view their bills online but not pay them, so ask the office which payment methods it accepts.
  • Property Valuation Administration (PVA), ext. 504: the place to ask about the value of a property and to dispute it.

The City of Elkton keeps a separate property tax payment link on its own website. If your address is inside the city, ask whether a city bill exists in addition to the county bill.

Todd County in brief

Todd County spans 377 square miles, and almost none of it is water. The cities are Elkton, Guthrie and Trenton, with Allensville and Fairview (mostly in Christian County) as census-designated places. Muhlenberg, Logan and Christian counties border Todd, as do Robertson and Montgomery counties in Tennessee. The county runs on Central time and has a single public school district, the Todd County School District.

Farming is a long-standing tradition. The southern lowlands, with Pembroke soil, are known for strong crop yields, and the northern high country is steeper, with oak, walnut and poplar. Buyers of rural property often care about the land as much as the house.

Home values and ownership

The county has 12,972 residents as of July 2025, a 5.9 percent rise since 2020, after a small slide during the 2010s. Population has hovered near 12,000 for decades. The housing figures matter most to a seller.

When bills go delinquent

The sheriff's file closes at the end of the day on April 15. Whatever is unpaid moves to the clerk's office, where a recorded lien attaches and the bill is renamed a certificate of delinquency. Until then the state schedule sets the price: 2 percent off if you pay by November 1, the bare amount through year end, a 5 percent surcharge in January and 10 percent afterward, with the sheriff's add-on fee on top.

Once the bill reaches the clerk, monthly interest of one percent runs, and commissions for the clerk and the county attorney follow. Waiting adds money fast, and the attorney's commission is waived only during the first five-business-day window after the transfer.

The Todd County tax sale

Under KRS 134.128 the sale falls 90 to 135 days after the sheriff hands bills to the clerk, a window the Department of Revenue puts at July 14 to August 28 on a regular schedule. Each year the clerk lists the sequence in order: a half-page notice, the published list, the deadline for outside buyers to register, and the sale itself, which begins at 9 AM.

A buyer of up to three bills registers with the county, while anyone wanting more than three registers with the state. A buyer of a bill gets a lien, not the house. Afterward the owner settles with that buyer, who may pile on costs. The county attorney mails notices to owners beforehand, and the list runs in the newspaper roughly a month before the sale.

If your bill has already been sold

An outside buyer who bought your bill holds a lien on the property, not the house itself. That lien still has to be paid before a sale can close, so the buyer's payoff becomes part of your closing figures. Ask the clerk at extension 501 who bought it and how to reach them, then request a written payoff that shows interest and any added costs.

If the sale has not happened yet, you can usually still pay at the clerk's office and stop the process. A bill paid at the clerk costs less than the same bill after an investor adds charges.

How to dispute your assessment

Valuation questions go to the PVA in the courthouse, extension 504. A conference there is mandatory. File the appeal at the clerk's office on the workday after the May viewing period ends. A panel of area owners then holds hearings a few weeks later.

The panel wants evidence: nearby sales, an appraisal, construction costs or insurance records. An owner who skips the local step or the hearing cannot continue to the Kentucky Claims Commission. Paid representatives must be professionals such as attorneys, accountants, brokers or appraisers and must hold written authorization.

Homestead exemption

For 2025 and 2026 the state lets an owner past 65, or totally disabled, subtract $49,100 from the assessed value of a home they live in. The Todd County PVA takes applications through December 31. The benefit stays with the owner, so a buyer files again.

Selling with taxes owed

Before closing, get the sheriff's payoff and ask the clerk about older certificates. Delinquent tax is the personal debt of the January 1 owner, and its lien can last eleven years, so a title agent will want a clean record before releasing funds.

Start at the courthouse. Ask the sheriff at extension 208 for the current figure, the clerk at extension 501 whether any year has gone to a certificate, and the PVA at extension 504 whether your exemption is on file. If your house is inside Elkton, add a call to the city about its bill. Put the figures together before you accept an offer, so you know the net you would walk away with. A cash buyer can take the house as is, and the tax balances come out of the proceeds at closing.

Bring a photo ID, the parcel number and the property address to the courthouse. If you hold the property through an estate, bring the paperwork showing who may sign for it. The closing agent will want to see that the person selling has authority to do so.

Allow a few days for each office to respond.

Frequently asked questions

Where is a Todd County property tax bill paid?

At the sheriff's office inside the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street, extension 208 of (270) 265-9966. The sheriff's website lets you view bills, and the office can tell you which payment methods it takes.

Who reviews a Todd County assessment I disagree with?

The PVA, at extension 504. Ask for a conference first, because the local board hears only owners who have had one.

What is the Todd County homestead deduction?

The amount is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period, available to owners past 65 or totally disabled. Applications go to the PVA before the year ends.

Can an investor buy my delinquent Todd County bill?

Yes. After April 15 the bill sits at the clerk's office, and an outside purchaser can buy it at the yearly sale and then collect from you.

Can a Todd County house with unpaid tax be sold?

Yes. The balance comes out of the sale price. Get written payoffs from the sheriff and clerk so the buyer's closing agent sees no surprises.

Carroll County, KY Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Carroll County?

Carroll County at a glance

Carroll County is a small river county where the Kentucky River meets the Ohio. Carrollton, the county seat, sits right at that confluence, about 54 miles from Cincinnati and 55 from Louisville along U.S. 42, with Interstate 71 about four miles south of town. The 2020 count was 10,810 residents, and the 2025 estimate of 11,141 is 3.1 percent higher.

Median value for a house people live in is $140,900, and 65.7 percent of Carroll homes are owner-occupied. Monthly rent runs about $910. The county counted 4,736 homes in mid-2025 but issued only 1 building permit that year, so almost every buyer here is shopping resale. Many of them commute along the river or the I-71 corridor to jobs at employers such as North American Stainless, CertainTeed and Kentucky Utilities.

Low-lying lots near the rivers carry flood risk, and the worst flood on record hit in 1937. If your lot is close to the water, the city planning office can tell you where the floodplain line falls.

Which office handles what

Who does what: the PVA values the parcel, the Sheriff's Office mails and collects, and the County Clerk gets the bill if it ends up delinquent. The clerk's counter also takes deeds, mortgages, wills and probate filings.

  • Sheriff: first floor of the courthouse at 440 Main Street, (502) 732-7010. Tax lookup and payment are online through the sheriff's page.
  • County Clerk: same building, (502) 732-7005, for delinquent taxes and deeds.
  • County administration: (502) 732-5448. This office edits or exonerates county tax amounts when a bill looks wrong.

Carroll's own FAQ puts the due date at December 31 and says to expect bills in October or November. No bill in hand? Search your parcel on the sheriff's page. The exact cutoff for the early-pay discount is printed on the bill itself, and the sheriff's office will confirm it by phone.

Due dates and penalties

Timing is set by state law, KRS 134.015. Paying early earns a small discount. Paying late costs more at two separate points.

Carroll County payment timing
When you payWhat you owe
On or before the discount dateBill less 2%
Through December 31The printed amount
During JanuaryPrinted amount plus 5%
After January 31Printed amount plus 10%

Don't count on installments: the county takes the whole bill in one transaction. You can mix tender, though, such as a check plus cash or a card. A bill lost in the mail won't get your late fees waived under the state's administrative regulations, so chase it down yourself.

Unpaid tax turns into a lien, and a buyer's title search will find it. Ask the clerk for a payoff number as soon as you decide to list.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Carroll County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How a Carroll County tax sale works

Anything still unpaid on April 15 moves from the sheriff to the County Clerk. KRS 134.128 schedules the sale 90 to 135 days after that handoff, with owner notices at the 30 and 60 day marks.

Carroll's clerk holds the sale each summer in a second-floor courthouse room, starting in the morning. Outside bidders must sign up ahead of time. For this year's dates, phone (502) 732-7005.

Settle up before the sale. Even then the bill picks up interest, a clerk commission and a recording fee. Wait longer and the county attorney's commission, postage and advertising are added, and a certificate buyer can pile on more.

How to appeal your assessment

Step one is a conference with the PVA, step two is a filing with the clerk after the roll closes. The roll sits open for 13 days beginning the first Monday in May, and no appeal counts unless you've met with the PVA or a deputy.

Whenever the PVA assesses higher than the value you reported, you're owed a notice. A recent purchase helps: your deed price may become the value for the next January 1 if the house is unchanged, so hold on to the closing paperwork.

The county board must explain any change in writing, and you're allowed to record the hearing. Go. Skip the filing or the hearing and you lose any further review.

While the appeal is pending, keep paying on the value you reported. Ignoring the bill because a hearing is coming only adds penalties. If the board changes the number, you'll get a corrected bill.

Homestead exemption

Kentucky gives a break on the main residence of owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Form 62A350 handles either case, and the PVA has copies.

What comes off is a fixed dollar figure, not the whole assessment, and the state resets that figure every other year. It doesn't pass to a buyer. Owners with a total service-connected disability rating file once, as do owners found disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement System.

The PVA can give you the current dollar figure, because published numbers can trail a reassessment. If you're 65, make sure it was actually applied before you close.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Carroll County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Yes, you can sell with back taxes. The balance is subtracted from your sale price at the table, so no cash is needed up front. Typical steps:

  • Ask the sheriff for this year's balance.
  • Ask the County Clerk at (502) 732-7005 whether any earlier year went delinquent and for a payoff figure with fees.
  • Hand both numbers to whoever runs your closing.
  • Save your old purchase paperwork in case you appeal a value.
  • If a bill looks wrong, call county administration before paying, since that office can edit or exonerate county amounts.
  • Plan the closing date around the penalty dates, because the amount owed steps up on January 1 and again after January 31.

An as-is cash sale suits owners who can't wait on a lender, are settling an estate, or hold a rental with tenants inside. It skips repairs, showings and an appraisal, and can close before the next penalty date arrives.

What happens at closing

In a standard sale the closing agent requests payoffs from the sheriff and clerk, pays them out of your price and records any release. Because values lock in on January 1, a bill can still show the prior owner's name after a mid-year sale. The year's tax should be split between you and the buyer as of the deed date.

For an office visit, carry your parcel number or street address, your deed if you have it, and the latest bill. If you're asking for a bill correction, the county administration office at (502) 732-5448 can tell you what proof it wants. For an exemption question, take photo ID and, for a disability claim, the letter from the agency that classified you.

Whichever way you sell, ask that the tax payoff and any lien release show up as separate lines on the final closing numbers.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Carroll County tax deadline?

The annual due date is December 31. Bills paid by the early cutoff on your bill get 2 percent off, January adds 5 percent, and later payments add 10 percent.

Does Carroll County allow a payment plan?

No. The county requires the full amount in a single transaction, though check, cash and card can be combined.

Whom do I call about delinquent Carroll County taxes?

Phone the County Clerk at (502) 732-7005. That office collects delinquent real estate tax and runs the sale.

Is a late fee waived if my bill never came?

No, a bill that never arrived isn't grounds for a waiver. Each fall, look yours up on the sheriff's page.

Can a Carrollton house with back taxes be sold?

Yes. A buyer can purchase it as-is and the balance is paid from your proceeds. Get the number from the County Clerk before signing.

Harlan County housing market

Harlan County lies in southeastern Kentucky against the Virginia line. Harlan is the county seat and Cumberland is the largest city. Coal built the economy, and the population has fallen with it, from 26,831 in 2020 to an estimated 24,725 in July 2025. A seller here is entering a market that has shrunk for decades. That affects the sale price more than it affects the tax bill, but it decides how much cushion a house has when unpaid taxes or repairs come out of the proceeds.

The typical owned home is valued at $73,700. Owners live in 71.6 percent of the housing, and typical rent is $678 a month. The county has 13,136 housing units against 10,731 households, about 2,400 more units than households, and no building permits were recorded for 2025. On a house this size the yearly tax bill is small in dollars. The real risk is a string of unpaid years in which interest and fees grow faster than the home's value.

Offices to call

Each office keeps its own schedule, so call before you drive in.

  • Sheriff: collects the bill. The sheriff's website links to an online public tax lookup. Call for the discount and penalty dates printed on your bill.
  • Property Valuation Administrator: write to P.O. Box 209 in Harlan (ZIP 40831) or call (606) 573-1990 between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.
  • County Clerk: phone (606) 573-3636. Monday it stays open until 6 p.m., Tuesday through Friday it closes at 4:30, and on the last Saturday of the month, holiday weekends excepted, it opens 9 a.m. to noon.

The clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page and a third-party purchaser application. The PVA's website carries the tax roll and a property search showing assessments and owners.

Real estate tax calendar

The PVA's website posts the state's cycle in a single chart.

How the Kentucky tax year runs for real estate
StepWhen
Assessment dateJanuary 1
Listing periodJanuary 1 through March 1
Tax roll open for review, conferences with the PVA13 days beginning on the first Monday of May
Appeals board hearingsFive days, beginning 25 to 35 days after review closes
Bills delivered to the sheriffNo later than September 15
Discount paymentsBy November 1
Payments at face valueNovember 2 through December 31
Bills turn delinquentJanuary 1, with 5 percent through January 31
10 percent penalty and 10 percent sheriff add-onAfter January 31
Sheriff passes bills to clerkApril 15
Clerk's certificate salesJuly 14 through August 28

A state-ordered delay can move a county to a slower plan with 30 days for each stage, so the dates on your own bill control.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the PVA. A conference in the May inspection window is mandatory, and when it produces agreement the new value flows into the fall bill.

Without agreement you have until one workday after the window shuts to file at the clerk's office. A three-member local board, appointed by the largest city's mayor, the fiscal court and the county judge executive, meets about five weeks after inspection. It must reject a claim that comes with no facts, so gather sales of similar houses and repair estimates beforehand.

At these values an appeal pays off mostly when the PVA's record is wrong about something concrete, such as a bedroom count, a shed that no longer exists, or a fire-damaged building still carried at full value.

Does the buyer get the bill after closing?

Not automatically. The bill for a year goes to the January 1 owner, so a later sale leaves it in the seller's name for that year. PVA staff read the recorded deed and mail the bill to the new owner when they can. A buyer without a copy should call the sheriff.

List a mailing address the buyer will check in the deed, since the clerk cannot take a deed without an in-care-of address for that year's bill. A seller on the homestead exemption should also tell the PVA, since the exemption does not go to the buyer.

Delinquent bills at the clerk

A bill still open when April 15 closes passes to the County Clerk, and a monthly 1 percent interest charge starts. On transfer the amount owed already includes the penalty, the sheriff add-on and an assumed commission. It climbs again within five business days, after the county attorney's first notice, and after the June advertisement.

Notices come by mail, and installment plans can be requested before a certificate is sold. If a third party buys it, the owner pays that buyer, who can add substantial fees.

An owner with unpaid years can still sell. The closing agent gets the payoff from the clerk and pays it from the proceeds. A cash offer on an older house can be weighed against a listing by comparing what is left after the payoff.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Harlan County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption

Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, and who live in the home can file for the exemption with the PVA under KRS 132.810. An owner under 65 qualifies only with a total disability. The exemption does not pass to a buyer, so report the sale to the PVA.

Ask the PVA for the current dollar figure and for the papers that prove age or disability. Because home values here are low, the saving is modest in dollars, but it is worth claiming every year you qualify.

Selling with taxes owed

Start by learning where each unpaid year sits. The sheriff's online lookup shows the current bill, and the clerk's delinquent taxes page covers anything that passed to the clerk after April 15. Then ask the clerk for a written payoff dated close to the closing day, since interest adds up monthly.

The title company will find any unpaid year, so there is no way to sell around it. What you can control is the timing. A bill paid before April 15 avoids the clerk's fees entirely. A bill already at the clerk should be cleared before certificate sales begin in July, because a third-party buyer who purchases the certificate adds charges and you then deal with that buyer instead of the county.

With low home values, a large payoff can eat much of the sale price. Compare what is left after the payoff on a listing with what a cash offer would leave, and weigh how long each route takes.

Buying near the parks and forest

Part of Cumberland Gap National Historical Park and the Blanton Forest preserve lie in the county, so a house near them may draw outdoor-minded buyers. School district boundaries, city limits and fire protection can change the taxes on a bill, so ask the sheriff which districts appear on yours.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the last day for the Harlan County discount?

November 1. After that, the chart lists face value through the end of December and a 5 percent penalty in January.

How much extra does a February payment cost in Harlan County?

Ten percent in penalty plus a 10 percent sheriff add-on, both of which start once January ends. The state describes the total as 21 percent.

Who answers questions about my Harlan County assessed value?

The PVA at (606) 573-1990 handles the conference that must come before any appeal.

Where do I check for delinquent Harlan County taxes?

The County Clerk's website has a delinquent taxes page, and the clerk's office answers at (606) 573-3636. The sheriff hands over bills after April 15.

Can a Harlan County owner under 65 get the homestead exemption?

Yes, if totally disabled. KRS 132.810 opens the exemption to age 65 and up, or total disability, for owners living in the home, filed with the PVA.

Who handles a Lawrence County tax bill

Four offices in Louisa handle the tax year between them, and the PVA and the sheriff share the same Main Cross Street address. Each covers its own step.

  • Property Valuation Administrator (PVA): 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa, KY 41230. The PVA sets the assessed value and takes homestead applications.
  • Sheriff: 122 Main Cross Street, Louisa. Phone (606) 638-4368. The sheriff takes payment.
  • County Clerk: runs the appeals board paperwork and, after April, the sale of unpaid bills. The clerk's site posts the current delinquent list.
  • County Attorney: mails the warning letters to owners whose bills have moved to the clerk.

Taxing districts set different rates, so the sheriff's bill and the PVA's assessment for your own parcel are the figures that count.

Lawrence County housing at a glance

Louisa is the lone city and holds the courthouse. The county had an estimated 15,765 residents in July 2025, down from 16,293 in 2020, spread over about 416 square miles. It holds 7,737 housing units and 6,342 households, with 77.8 percent owned by their occupants. The middle home value is $111,700. Typical owner costs run $1,216 a month for mortgaged homes and $386 for paid-off ones, and typical rent is $760. At these price levels, an unpaid bill can eat a noticeable share of the sale, so know your payoff early. Alcohol sales are limited to Louisa city limits.

Due dates and penalties

KRS 134.015 sets the year-end deadline at December 31 and gives a 2 percent discount to anyone who clears the whole bill by November 1. January costs 5 percent extra, and February onward costs 10 percent plus a sheriff's add-on fee, so a bill paid on February 1 or later runs roughly a fifth higher before any commission.

Late-mailed bills fall under a state alternative schedule that allows 30 days per stage. Oil and gas bills also exist in Lawrence County. The clerk's sale leaves out the 2023 oil and gas bills, so ask the sheriff whether one is attached to your parcel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lawrence County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

The sequence runs in order. Step one is a sit-down with the PVA's staff. Step two is the May viewing window for the roll. Step three is the written appeal, which the clerk must have by the next workday after viewing ends. Step four is a hearing before the local board about a month later. Only evidence counts at the hearing, so bring proof such as a description of the lot and buildings, insurance papers, construction costs and listings of nearby sales.

Written reasons follow any change the board makes. Hearings may be recorded, and a paid representative has to fit the categories in KRS 133.120. Skipping the board closes off the Kentucky Claims Commission.

Homestead exemption

Eligible owners are those who have turned 65 and those classified as fully disabled. The 2025-26 deduction is $49,100 off the assessed value. About 19.9 percent of local residents are past 65, so many sellers here may already have it on file.

The PVA's courthouse office takes the form. A claim built on disability has to be renewed each year. Two groups are excused from renewing: owners whose disability is service-connected, and people Social Security or a state retirement system has ruled permanently and totally disabled. Ask the PVA what happens to the exemption once the house sells.

How the clerk sells unpaid tax bills

Anything the sheriff has not collected by April 15 becomes a certificate of delinquency at the clerk's office, with interest of 1 percent a month. Letters from the county attorney go out, and the clerk publishes the list before the sale date. At the sale a registered outside buyer can buy the lien, and from then on the owner pays that buyer. The clerk's draft-style sale rules also tell an owner how much a buyer may be paying.

Lawrence County Clerk delinquent tax sale rules
Sale stepRule
RegistrationAt least 10 business days before the sale
Deposit$10 per bill, capped at $250, not refundable
Prior year certificatesSeparate list due 10 business days before the sale
Bidders per entityOne potential purchaser
Order of purchaseRandom drawing, lowest number picks first, in rounds
PaymentCash, certified check, money order or company check
RefundsNone after the sale

The lien on the land from delinquent taxes lasts eleven years under KRS 134.015, no matter who owns the property.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lawrence County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before you list a Lawrence County house

  • Ask the sheriff at (606) 638-4368 for the current bill and any earlier unpaid year.
  • Look through the clerk's delinquent list for any certificate tied to the parcel.
  • If you have the homestead exemption, find out from the PVA what becomes of it after a sale.
  • Compare your assessment with the sales of similar houses before the May inspection window opens, in case a dispute is worth filing.
  • Agree on the split of the current bill in the sales contract.
  • Because the PVA and the sheriff share one Main Cross Street address, one trip to Louisa can settle both the assessment question and the bill itself.
  • Ask whether any oil and gas bill is attached to the parcel.

Owners who want no repairs or showings can request a direct cash offer. Any tax still due is paid from the sale money at closing regardless of buyer.

Splitting the bill at closing

The assessment is made as of January 1, so the bill follows whoever owned the parcel on that date. If you sell in the spring, the bill that arrives in the fall may still carry your name. Put the split in the sales contract, and the closing agent will prorate the year on the settlement statement and send the sheriff its share from the proceeds.

A cash sale skips the buyer's lender and its separate tax search, which removes one common cause of delay. The payoff figures still have to be right, so request them from the sheriff and the clerk a few days before the closing date.

What a payoff request should include

When you call the sheriff for a payoff, give the parcel and the owner name exactly as they appear on the deed. Ask for the current-year amount, any earlier year still open, and the date through which the figure holds. Then repeat the same request at the clerk's office to see whether any certificate exists. Write down who you spoke to and when, and ask for the numbers in writing if you can.

Hand both figures to the title company before you sign a sales contract. The company deducts what is owed from your proceeds at closing and pays the offices directly, so you do not need to carry a check to Louisa yourself. If a bill has already reached the clerk, the lien follows the land, so it must be cleared whichever buyer you choose.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Lawrence County tax bill paid?

The Lawrence County Sheriff collects it at 122 Main Cross Street in Louisa. Call (606) 638-4368 to confirm the amount and the payment methods before you go.

How much does paying early save in Lawrence County?

Two percent comes off a bill paid in full by November 1, and the full printed amount is owed from November 2 to December 31 under KRS 134.015.

What comes first when disputing a value here?

A conference at the PVA's office. Without it the board that reviews assessments will not take the appeal.

How big is the homestead exemption?

It is $49,100 for 2025-26. The owner has to be at least 65 or classified as fully disabled, and the form goes to the PVA.

Can an outside buyer purchase an unpaid bill here?

Yes, when the certificate stays unpaid until the clerk's sale. A registered purchaser can buy the lien, and the owner then settles with that purchaser.

Who values, bills and collects Letcher County property tax

Letcher County runs its tax through a valuation office, the sheriff and the clerk. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets each parcel's value. The Letcher County Sheriff sends out the bill and receives the payment. The Letcher County Clerk inherits anything still unpaid in mid-April.

The PVA sits at 156 Main Street, Suite 105, in Whitesburg, with a phone line at 606-633-2182 and a fax at 606-633-3995. Ownership, like value, is fixed on January 1, so a house bought in March still shows the seller on that year's bill. A new owner who never sees a copy can phone the sheriff at 606-633-2293.

The sheriff keeps weekday hours of 8:30 to 4 and offers a web page for paying the bill. The clerk, at 606-633-2432, keeps the same hours and runs a delinquent tax section. Phone the clerk to learn when the current year's tax sale is scheduled.

Letcher County housing at a glance

Letcher is a mountain county where the land shapes how a house is priced and how long it sits. Whitesburg is the seat, Jenkins is the biggest city, and Fleming-Neon makes three. The county had an estimated 19,952 residents in July 2025, down 7.4 percent from 21,548 in 2020. It has 8,463 households, and 74.1 percent of homes are owner occupied. The middle home value is $67,400 and median rent is $669.

With almost no new construction, nearly every sale is a resale, and buyers compare each house against a small set of older homes. A tax bill on a low-value home is small in dollars, which is why a few years of neglect can feel manageable until the penalties compound. Flooding in July and August 2022 damaged homes in the county, so if a building was hit, ask the PVA how that damage shows up in the assessment.

Due dates and penalties

Kentucky's collection statute, KRS 134.015, sets one calendar for every county, and the sheriff here follows it.

Letcher County tax bill by payment date
Date paidWhat you owe
Through November 1Bill minus 2 percent
Early November to December 31Face amount
JanuaryFace amount plus 5 percent
February onwardFace amount plus 10 percent and the sheriff's fee

If the state delays a county's bills, it can swap in a schedule that allows a month per stage.

If the bill is still unpaid after April 15

Closing time on April 15 is the cliff. The sheriff hands the open bills to the clerk. Each one is reissued as a certificate of delinquency, and the lien attaches to your house. Monthly interest of one percent starts, and the clerk and county attorney each earn commissions that climb as notices go out.

The Revenue Department's sample shows the pace of growth. A $1,000 bill reaches the clerk at $1,254 once the penalty, fee and commission are added. If it is still open after the June newspaper ad, the sample total is $1,659.90. A public sale follows three to four and a half months after the handoff, where investors may buy the debt. The lien can last eleven years whoever owns the house.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin with a sit-down at the PVA's office. The appeals panel refuses any case that skipped that meeting, and the meeting must happen before or during the viewing window.

The roll opens for public viewing on May's first Monday and stays open thirteen days. Once you have held your conference, you must file with the Letcher County Clerk by the end of the workday that follows the window. The local appeals panel then sits in Whitesburg, the county seat, roughly a month later, within 25 to 35 days of the window closing.

  • Evidence to bring: lot and building details, insurance policies, construction costs and listings of comparable houses. An appeal with no evidence is denied.
  • A paid advocate has to be a lawyer, accountant, consultant, broker, appraiser, your own employee or a holder of a state-recognized designation, and needs your authorization in writing.
  • Audio recording is allowed, and the panel must explain any change in writing.
  • If bills were printed before the ruling and the value rises, a supplemental bill follows.

Homestead exemption for seniors and disabled owners

The deduction for assessment years 2025 and 2026 is $49,100 of taxable value. The home must be the applicant's residence, and the applicant must either reach 65 during the tax year or hold a total disability rating from a federal program or a retirement system. Roughly one resident in five is past 65, so many owners may qualify.

Apply at the Letcher County PVA. Owners under 65 who claim disability usually renew yearly. The exceptions, who document the disability a single time, are owners with a service-connected disability and owners ruled permanently disabled by Social Security or the state retirement system. A buyer cannot inherit the break, since the exemption belongs to the person.

What a Letcher County seller owes at closing

The bill follows the January 1 titleholder, and the settlement statement decides who reimburses whom. A common Kentucky practice is for the seller to credit the buyer for the months of ownership, with the buyer paying the full bill when it arrives.

The state's deed transfer tax (KRS 142.050) falls on the seller. The charge is fifty cents per $500 of the price on the deed, and a partial block counts as a whole one. The clerk takes it at the recording window. Foreclosure transfers, spouses splitting in a divorce and nominal parent-child transfers are exempt. Because delinquent tax is a lien, closing agents insist on paying it out of the proceeds. Before closing, line up the sheriff's payoff figure and the clerk's answer on any delinquency certificate.

Selling a house with back taxes

Start with two phone calls. Dial the sheriff at 606-633-2293 for this year's amount plus any older year left open. Then dial the clerk at 606-633-2432 to learn if a certificate already exists on the parcel. Request each figure in writing and note the date it stays good, because interest runs monthly.

Pass both figures to the title company ahead of signing any contract. Whatever is owed comes out of your sale money at closing, so no cash needs to change hands beforehand. A cash buyer can still close on a house carrying a lien once the payoff is pinned down, and the lien is cleared at the table.

Frequently asked questions

Who gets the Letcher County tax payment?

Send it to the Letcher County Sheriff, who answers at 606-633-2293 on weekdays from 8:30 to 4. The county website also links to an online payment page. Anything unpaid after April 15 shifts to the county clerk.

Is there an early-payment discount in Letcher County?

Yes. Paying the whole bill by November 1 of the tax year takes 2 percent off. From then through year end you pay the printed figure, and two penalty steps come next: 5 percent, then 10.

I bought in Letcher County and no bill came. What now?

Phone the sheriff at 606-633-2293 and ask for a copy. Bills are written to the owner on January 1, so yours may be under the seller's name. Not receiving the bill does not cancel what is owed.

Who hears a property tax appeal in Letcher County?

The local board of assessment appeals, meeting in Whitesburg. You first meet the PVA at 156 Main Street, Suite 105, then file with the clerk. The filing deadline is the workday after the thirteen-day roll inspection ends.

Who pays the year's tax when a Letcher County house changes hands?

The settlement statement decides. The sheriff bills the January 1 owner, and sellers commonly credit the buyer for their months of ownership. Delinquent amounts are a lien that has to be cleared for the title to pass clean.

Who to call about Livingston County property tax

Three offices share the work, all in or near the courthouse square in Smithland. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets the value of each parcel. The sheriff sends and collects the bill. The county clerk takes over once a bill is certified as delinquent. Knowing which office owns which question saves you a few wasted calls.

Livingston County offices
OfficeCall aboutPhoneAddress and hours
Property Valuation AdministratorValue disputes, exemptions, ownership records270-928-2524PO Box 77, Smithland, KY 42081
SheriffAmount owed, payoff figures, payment270-928-2122321 Court Street (PO Box 340); weekdays 8 to 4
County ClerkRecorded liens, delinquent bills, tax sales270-928-2162321 Court Street (PO Box 400); Monday 8 to 5, Tuesday through Friday 8 to 4

The sheriff also handles court security and civil papers, so the tax counter is one of several things happening at that desk.

Housing and the local market

Livingston is a small rural county with settled households, and it belongs to the Paducah metro area. The middle owner-occupied home is worth $125,600, and owners live in 81.2 percent of the homes. Median gross rent is $926. Few people move in a given year, since 93.8 percent stayed at the same address, and one resident in four (25.1 percent) is 65 or older.

Population was 8,888 in the 2020 census, and the July 2025 estimate of 8,863 is almost flat. Few listings come up, and buyers often come from nearby Paducah. The community of Ledbetter sits across the Tennessee River from that city and is the largest place in the county. If you own farmland or river acreage, expect the buyer pool to be smaller and more local than for a house in town.

When the tax bill is due

Kentucky gives owners until December 31 of the assessment year to pay. Paying early earns a discount: 2 percent off for a full payment made by November 1. The next two months carry the plain amount, January adds 5 percent, and 10 percent applies after that. If the state approves a late schedule for a county, each stage lasts about a month instead.

The sheriff turns over what remains unpaid on April 15. The clerk then records the lien, and the debt picks up 1 percent interest each month. The state's walk-through of a $1,000 bill shows $1,254 at the handoff, $1,627.61 if paid in May after a second month of interest, and $1,704.21 for a buyer at the clerk's sale. That last figure becomes the base on which the buyer later charges interest and fees.

Before any sale the clerk must run the delinquent list in a newspaper and on a county-sponsored site. The county attorney also mails a 30-day warning to each owner, with a second warning if needed. Ask the Livingston County Clerk for the date of the current sale and the list of bills certified as delinquent.

How the PVA sets a value

Kentucky recognizes three main methods. For homes the PVA leans on the sales comparison approach, adjusting nearby sales up or down for differences such as a basement. Barns, fences and commercial buildings are valued at replacement cost minus depreciation. Rental properties are valued by the income they produce. Every parcel gets a physical look from the PVA's staff at least every four years.

Farmland is different. Under Section 172A of the Kentucky Constitution, it is assessed at agricultural value, not market value. The state's own example taxes an acre that would sell for $50,000 on an agricultural value of $750. The Revenue Department builds per-acre values for cropland, pasture, woodland and waste ground. Ask the PVA whether your parcel is classed as farm use before you assume a market-based figure.

Federal, state, county and city property is exempt, as are schools run by nonprofits and the buildings and personal property of religious institutions. A nonprofit or religious group applies on Revenue Form 62A023 through the PVA, and a denial can go to the local board.

How to appeal your assessment

Talk to the PVA first, and do it before the inspection period ends. Public viewing of the roll starts the first Monday of May and lasts thirteen days. After your conference, the clerk needs the paperwork by the end of the next workday. The board then sits at the county seat, Smithland, 25 to 35 days later.

Evidence wins or loses these cases. The board considers only what is presented while both sides are in the room, and it denies an appeal that arrives without documents. Photographs of the building, its construction cost, insurance policies, nearby listings and sales all help. A paid representative must hold one of the credentials Kentucky lists, such as attorney, accountant, broker or appraiser, and present your written authorization.

If the board changes a value, it must explain why in writing. A value that rises after bills have printed produces a supplemental bill.

Homestead exemption

Seniors can cut their bill. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 the homestead exemption removes $49,100 from the assessed value of the owner's home. Apply through the PVA and bring a license, birth certificate or passport that proves your age. A buyer cannot inherit the exemption and must file separately, so a sale ends it for you. If you are 65 or older and planning to sell, ask the PVA how the exemption will be handled for the year of the sale so the closing figures are not a surprise.

Selling with taxes owed

The year's bill belongs to whoever held title when January 1 arrived, and the closing statement divides the cost between buyer and seller. The seller also owes Kentucky's transfer tax under KRS 142.050, $0.50 on each $500 of price, collected as the deed is filed in Smithland. Foreclosure transfers and transfers between divorcing spouses are among the exemptions.

A delinquent amount stays attached to the property as a lien for up to eleven years, so expect the title agent to want it paid first. Before listing, get a payoff from the sheriff or, if the bill has been certified, from the clerk. A cash sale skips the wait for a buyer's lender to order title work, but the lien still has to be cleared from the proceeds at closing.

Bring the deed, your most recent tax bill and a photo ID when you visit the sheriff or clerk. Ask for the payoff in writing and for the good-through date, since interest accrues every month the debt stays open. Hand that figure to the title agent so it can be deducted at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Livingston County sheriff's tax office?

It is at 321 Court Street in Smithland; mail goes to PO Box 340. Call 270-928-2122 on a weekday between 8 and 4.

What phone number reaches the Livingston County PVA?

Call 270-928-2524. The mailing address is PO Box 77, Smithland, KY 42081, and the office handles values, exemptions and ownership records.

Does Livingston County give a discount for paying early?

Yes. Pay the full bill by November 1 and it drops by 2 percent. After that you owe the printed amount until year end, and then penalties begin.

What happens to a Livingston County tax bill I never pay?

The sheriff sends it to the clerk after April 15, and a lien goes on record with interest and commissions piling up. Investors may buy the debt at a sale a few months later.

Is farmland taxed differently in Livingston County?

Yes. Kentucky assesses farmland at agricultural value rather than market value, using per-acre figures for cropland, pasture and woodland. Ask the PVA whether your acreage qualifies as farm use.

Who handles property tax in Menifee County

Three offices in Frenchburg share the work. The elected appraiser, called the PVA, values each house. The sheriff mails the bill and collects it. The clerk takes over whatever is still unpaid when April 15 closes. Matching your question to the right desk gets you a payoff figure or a corrected value sooner.

The PVA, clerk and county attorney all use 12 Main Street, while the sheriff keeps a post office box of its own.

Offices and phone numbers

Each office has its own mailing box, so check the address before anything goes in the mail. Call ahead for office hours before you drive in.

Payment deadlines

The sheriff follows the statewide calendar in KRS 134.015. Bills arrive in the fall and go to whoever held title on January 1.

  • Through November 1: pay 2 percent less.
  • November 2 to December 31: pay the bill as printed.
  • During January: 5 percent extra.
  • February 1 to April 15: a 21 percent combined penalty applies.
  • After April 15: the clerk holds the bill.

A house sold partway through the year still carries the earlier owner's name on that year's bill. Settle the split in the sales contract and ask the sheriff for the balance.

Menifee County housing and the market

Menifee is mountain country with about 204 square miles of land. Frenchburg is both the seat and the only city. Cave Run Lake and the Red River Gorge flank the county, and Lexington is under 70 miles away by the Mountain Parkway. National forest covers much of Menifee and farms cover about a tenth, so sellers mostly offer hillside lots, small tracts and cabins.

The county counted 6,113 residents in 2020, down from 6,306 ten years earlier, and a mid-2025 estimate of 6,430 would be a 5.2 percent rise. The 2020 count showed 3,277 housing units, 24.3 percent of them empty. Owners live in 75.5 percent of homes. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $125,800 and typical rent is $675. Monthly owner costs run $996 with a mortgage and $299 without one. If a remote address is for sale, ask what internet service it can get.

How to contest a Menifee County value

Sit down with the PVA first, and go to the clerk only if the two of you can't agree. Inspection starts on the first Monday in May and lasts two weeks, and filing closes one workday later.

A local board then hears the case within 25 to 35 days and gets five sitting days without state permission. A claim with no evidence must be denied, so bring paper:

  • Photos and contractor quotes for a worn roof or a shifting foundation on a slope.
  • Prices that comparable houses nearby fetched this past year.
  • Insurance policies or construction costs.

Audio recording of the hearing is allowed. A paid representative must belong to a group listed in KRS 133.120 and carry your signed authorization.

Homestead exemption

Owners aged 65 or older, and those classified as totally disabled, can claim it. File at the Menifee County PVA for the house you occupy. Each residential unit gets just one exemption under KRS 132.810, and manufactured homes count as units.

The exempt amount tracks a federal price index, so ask the PVA for the current figure. An approval granted after you paid brings a refund on the exempt slice. Report a sale or a death to the PVA, and whoever takes the house files anew.
